1.q: What were the seafarers called who set out from Scandinavia in longships about 1000 years ago?
1.e: The Vikings lived in the area of today’s Norway, Sweden and Denmark. With their fast longships they sailed the seas as traders, explorers and warriors, even as far as North America.
1.m: The Vikings were seafarers from the north.

2.q: Why did the ancient Egyptians build the great pyramids?
2.e: The kings of ancient Egypt were called pharaohs. The Egyptians believed in life after death, so they built huge tombs for them: the pyramids.

3.q: Since which year has Switzerland been a modern federal state with a Federal Constitution?
3.e: 1291 is the year of the Federal Charter of the first cantons, remembered on 1 August. But the modern federal state with a shared constitution, Parliament and Federal Council has only existed since 1848.
3.m: The Federal Charter dates from 1291, the modern federal state from 1848.

4.q: In which city do the Federal Council and the Swiss Parliament sit?
4.e: Bern is the federal city of Switzerland. The Federal Palace is there, where the Federal Council works and Parliament meets.
4.m: The Federal Palace is in Bern.

6.q: Which event in 1989 became the symbol of the end of the Cold War?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
The start of the First World War
6.e: The Berlin Wall divided East and West Berlin. When it was opened in November 1989, it was the beginning of the end of Europe’s division into East and West.

7.q: How many national languages does Switzerland have?
7.e: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Romansh is spoken mainly in the Grisons.
7.m: The national languages are German, French, Italian and Romansh.

8.q: How many members does the Federal Council, the Swiss government, have?
8.e: The Federal Council has seven members. They run the country together, and each member heads a department, for example for finance or defence.

9.q: What is the difference between electing and voting on an issue?
a: In an election you choose people, in a vote you decide on an issue
9.e: In elections you choose who represents you, for example in the National Council. In votes you say Yes or No to an issue yourself. In Switzerland this happens several times a year.
9.m: You elect people and vote on issues.

12.q: Which festival do Christians celebrate for the birth of Jesus?
12.e: At Christmas, Christians remember the birth of Jesus. Easter is another important festival: it remembers his resurrection.
12.m: At Christmas people celebrate the birth of Jesus.

13.q: What is the place of worship for Muslims called?
13.e: Muslims pray together in a mosque. Christians go to church, and Jews go to the synagogue.
13.m: Muslims pray in the mosque, Christians in the church, Jews in the synagogue.

14.q: Which five religions are often called the major world religions?
a: Christianity, Islam, Viking religion, Hinduism, Buddhism
Judaism, Christianity, Islam, the Olympics, Buddhism
14.e: These five religions have many followers worldwide and a long history. There are also many other religions and people with no religion.
14.m: The major world religions are Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism.

15.q: What is the festival at the end of the month of fasting, Ramadan, called?
15.e: During Ramadan many Muslims fast during the day. At the end they celebrate Eid al-Fitr, the ‘Sugar Festival’, with family, visits and sweets.
15.m: At the end of Ramadan people celebrate Eid al-Fitr.

16.q: What is the holy scripture of Judaism that contains the five books of Moses called?
16.e: The Torah is the most important part of the Jewish Bible. In the synagogue it is read from a handwritten scroll.
16.m: The Torah is the holy scripture of Judaism.

20.q: What happens to water when it gets colder than 0 °C?
20.e: Water has three states: solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (steam). Below 0 °C, liquid water becomes solid; it freezes.

21.q: Which poles of two magnets attract each other?
21.e: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Unlike poles attract each other, like poles repel each other.
21.m: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel.

22.q: Why do you see the lightning first in a thunderstorm and only hear the thunder afterwards?
a: Light is much faster than sound
Your ears are slower than your eyes
The lightning is closer than the thunder
22.e: Lightning and thunder happen at the same time. But light is extremely fast, while sound takes around three seconds to travel a kilometre. If you count the seconds and divide by three, you know roughly how many kilometres away the storm is.

23.e: Metals such as copper let electricity through well, which is why cables are made of copper inside. Rubber and plastic hardly conduct at all and are therefore used as a protective covering.

24.q: Why does a large steel ship float?
a: It pushes aside so much water that the upthrust carries it
Because steel is lighter than water
Because the engine holds it up
24.e: A ship is mostly hollow inside and pushes a lot of water aside. The water pushes back with a force called upthrust. If it is as big as the weight of the ship, the ship floats.
24.m: Pushing aside lots of water gives lots of upthrust.

25.q: Why do you lurch forwards when a bus suddenly brakes?
a: Because of inertia: your body wants to keep moving
Because the bus pushes you forwards
Because the air in the bus flows forwards
25.e: According to Newton's law of inertia, a body keeps moving as long as no force slows it down. The bus slows down, but your body wants to keep going, so you lurch forwards. That is why seat belts are so important.
25.m: Because of inertia, everything that is moving wants to keep moving.

26.q: In which unit is force measured?
26.e: Forces are measured in newtons, named after Isaac Newton. The watt is the unit of power, the joule of energy and the volt of voltage.

27.q: Roughly how fast is light in a vacuum?
27.e: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres every second. The sunlight hitting you right now left the sun about eight minutes ago.
27.m: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second.

28.q: You see something on the internet that frightens you. What do you do?
a: Tell an adult you trust about it
Send it to all your friends
Keep watching until it is over
28.e: Nobody has to deal with something like that alone. Tell your parents, a teacher or someone else you trust. In Switzerland, children and young people can also contact Pro Juventute on 147.
28.m: If something feels wrong, tell someone.

29.q: Can you simply put a photo of someone else on the internet?
a: Yes, if the photo is funny
Yes, if I took the photo myself
29.e: Everyone has the right to decide whether a picture of them ends up on the internet. So always ask first, and remember: once something is online, it is very hard to delete completely.

30.q: According to their own rules, from what age do TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat allow you to have an account?
30.e: The big platforms require a minimum age of 13 in their terms of use. Many contents and features are not meant for younger children, for example messages from strangers.
30.m: Social media is usually only allowed from 13.

31.q: What does the algorithm on TikTok and similar apps do?
a: It chooses which videos you see, based on what you watch
It checks whether videos are true
31.e: The app remembers how long you watch which videos and shows you more of them. That makes it easy to stay on longer than planned. If you know this, you can decide more consciously when to stop.
31.m: The algorithm wants to keep you in the app.

32.q: Someone is being picked on again and again in a group chat. What is a sensible thing to do?
a: Take screenshots, block or report, and involve someone you trust
Delete the chat and say nothing
32.e: This is called cyberbullying. Save the evidence, block or report the person and get help from parents, teachers or, in Switzerland, Pro Juventute on 147. Anyone who watches and says nothing makes it worse for the person affected.
32.m: Save evidence, report it and get help.

33.q: You read a surprising piece of news on social media. How do you check whether it is true?
a: Check the source and see whether reliable media report the same
See how many likes it has
Believe the person who posted it
33.e: Lots of likes do not mean something is true. Ask yourself: who is behind it? Are well-known newspapers, radio or TV reporting it too? If not, be careful.
33.m: Check the source, compare, and only then share.

a: They make money from adverts and your data
Because the government pays for them
Because companies do not need money
35.e: If you pay nothing, the app usually earns money from adverts. The more it knows about you, the more targeted the adverts can be. That is why it is worth looking at the privacy settings.
35.m: With free apps, you pay with your attention and your data.

36.q: An influencer is paid by a company for a post. What applies?
a: The post should be clearly marked as advertising
She has to keep it secret
Only TV adverts count as advertising
36.e: Paid posts are advertising. So that followers are not misled, this should be clearly marked, for example with “ad” or “advert”. Look out for this before you believe a recommendation.

37.q: Which job suits someone who really loves working with animals?
37.e: Animal keepers feed and look after animals, for example at the zoo or in an animal shelter. Many jobs fit well with what you like doing in your free time.
37.m: What you like doing can become your job.

38.q: How is an apprenticeship in Switzerland organised?
a: You work at the training company and also go to vocational school
You only work, with no school
You learn everything on your own online
38.e: The official name for an apprenticeship is basic vocational education. You learn the job at the company, go to vocational school one or two days a week, and also attend inter-company courses.
38.m: In an apprenticeship you learn at the company and at school.

a: A few days at a company to get to know a job
The final exam of the apprenticeship
39.e: On a taster placement you work alongside others at a company for a few days. You find out whether you like the job, and the company gets to know you. It is often the first step towards an apprenticeship.
39.m: On a taster placement you try out a job.

40.q: What does the abbreviation EFZ stand for?
40.e: You receive the EFZ after a three- or four-year apprenticeship. It shows that you have learned a trade and is recognised throughout Switzerland.
40.m: The EFZ is the qualification from a 3- to 4-year apprenticeship.

44.q: Which of these animals is a mammal?
44.e: The dolphin lives in the sea but is not a fish: it breathes air with its lungs, gives birth to live young and feeds them with milk. That is exactly what makes a mammal.
44.m: Mammals feed their young with milk.

45.q: What do plants need to make their own food?
45.e: Using sunlight, water and air, plants make sugar in their green leaves. As they do this, they give off oxygen, which we breathe.
45.m: Plants make their food with light, water and air.

46.q: How many planets are there in our solar system?
46.e: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Pluto used to be counted as the ninth planet, but since 2006 it has been a dwarf planet.
46.m: 8 planets; Pluto is a dwarf planet.

47.q: Why are bees so important to us?
a: They pollinate many plants that give us food
47.e: While collecting, bees carry pollen from flower to flower. Only then do many plants produce fruit, for example apples or cherries.
47.m: Bees pollinate; without them there would be less fruit.

49.q: Which organ pumps blood around your body?
49.e: The heart is a strong muscle. It beats without a break and pumps blood through the blood vessels so that every part of your body gets oxygen.
49.m: The heart is the body's pump.

53.q: What is the money in Switzerland called?
53.e: In Switzerland people pay with Swiss francs, CHF for short. One franc is worth 100 rappen.

54.q: You get 5 francs every week and would like a game that costs 20 francs. What helps?
a: Spending it all on sweets straight away
Hiding the money and forgetting it
54.e: If you put your pocket money aside every week, you will have 20 francs after four weeks. Saving means going without now so you can buy something bigger later.
54.m: If you save today, you will have more later.

a: A plan of how much money comes in and what you spend it on
55.e: In a budget you write down how much money you get and what you want to spend it on. That way you can see early on whether the money will be enough, and you do not suddenly run out.
55.m: A budget is a plan for income and spending.

56.q: Which of these is a real need and not just a want?
56.e: Needs are things you require to live, for example food, a home or clothing. Wants are nice but not necessary. If you can tell the two apart, you are better at managing your money.

59.q: Where can you keep money safely?
59.e: In a bank account your money is protected from theft and fire. You can always see how much you have and withdraw it when you need it.
59.m: A bank account is a safe place for money.

60.q: What is interest on a savings account?
a: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money there
60.e: The bank works with your money, for example by lending it out. In return it pays you a small amount: the interest. How much depends on the bank and the period of time.
60.m: Interest is a reward for saving.

61.q: What is the difference between a debit card and a credit card?
a: A debit card takes money straight from your account, a credit card bills you later
A debit card gives you credit
A credit card is only for children
61.e: With a debit card the amount is taken from your account straight away, so you only spend what is there. With a credit card you get a bill at the end of the month. That is handy, but it is easier to lose track.
61.m: With a debit card you pay now, with a credit card later.

63.q: What does a Swiss IBAN start with?
63.e: The IBAN is your international account number. Swiss IBANs start with the country code CH. Other people can use it to send you money.
63.m: A Swiss IBAN starts with CH.

64.q: What does the state need taxes for?
a: For schools, roads, hospitals and much more
64.e: With taxes we all pay together for things everyone needs: school buildings, teachers, roads, police, fire brigade and much more.
64.m: Taxes are shared money for everyone.

65.q: Which three levels collect taxes in Switzerland?
65.e: In Switzerland you pay taxes to the Confederation, to your canton and to your municipality. That is why people pay different amounts depending on where they live.
65.m: The Confederation, canton and municipality collect taxes.

a: A tax that is included in the price of many goods and services
66.e: You pay VAT with almost every purchase, even without noticing. It is often shown in small print on the receipt. A lower rate applies to food than to most other things.
66.m: VAT is included in the price.

a: It helps pay the costs of doctors, hospitals and medicines
70.e: When people get ill, they sometimes need expensive treatment. Many people pay a little into their health insurance every month. This pays the costs for those who need help.
70.m: With health insurance everyone pays in, and whoever is ill gets help.

71.q: Do you have to have basic health insurance in Switzerland?
a: Yes, it is compulsory for everyone living in Switzerland
Only people who are often ill
71.e: Basic insurance is compulsory for everyone who lives in Switzerland, including children. Every health insurer must accept you for it, and the benefits are the same everywhere.
71.m: Basic insurance is compulsory for everyone.

a: The amount you pay the health insurer every month
The money for a visit to the doctor
A present from the health insurer
72.e: You pay the premium regularly, whether you are ill or not. How much it is depends on the health insurer, where you live, your age and your insurance model.
72.m: The premium is a monthly payment.

76.q: Which number do you call for the fire brigade in Switzerland?
76.e: Switzerland has three important emergency numbers: 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade and 144 for the ambulance. 112 also works everywhere in Europe.
76.m: The police number is 117, the fire brigade 118 and the ambulance 144.

77.q: What do you do when the pedestrian light is red?
a: Go if no car is coming
77.e: Red means stop. You may only go when it is green, and even then look left and right quickly to check that all the cars really stop.
77.m: At red you stop, at green you look and then go.

a: A long sentence with numbers and symbols that only you know
78.e: Long passwords are hard to guess. A whole sentence like “My dog eats 3 carrots!” is easy to remember and hard to crack. Never use the same password everywhere.
78.m: A safe password is long, unique and secret.

80.q: What is the name of the hero who, according to legend, shot an apple off his son's head?
80.e: William Tell is the best-known legendary figure in Switzerland. According to the legend, he had to shoot an apple off his son's head on the orders of the bailiff Gessler. Whether Tell really lived has not been proven.
80.m: Tell is the legendary hero with the crossbow.

81.q: What do we call the long period when people did not yet know about metal?
81.e: In the Stone Age there was no metal yet. People made tools and weapons from stone, bone and wood. It is the longest period in human history.
81.m: In the Stone Age people made tools from stone.

82.q: Who lived in castles in the Middle Ages?
82.e: Castles were well-protected homes of nobles and knights. Thick walls, towers and often a moat protected them from attackers. In Switzerland there are still many castles, for example Chillon Castle on Lake Geneva.

83.q: Which animal did knights ride into battle?
83.e: Knights were warriors on horseback. Horses and armour were very expensive, so knights usually came from rich families.

84.q: Which empire built towns such as Aventicum (Avenches) in what is now Switzerland?
84.e: About 2000 years ago, the area of present-day Switzerland belonged to the Roman Empire. Aventicum was an important town with a theatre and a town wall, and you can still see remains of it today.

85.q: Who reached America in 1492, even though he was really looking for a sea route to India?
85.e: Columbus sailed west from Spain and believed he had landed in India. That is why the people there were long called “Indians”. But people had already been living in America for thousands of years.

86.q: Which invention by Johannes Gutenberg around 1450 changed the world?
86.e: Before that, books were copied by hand, which took a very long time. With Gutenberg’s printing method, books could be made quickly and more cheaply. This made knowledge spread much faster.

87.q: In which year did the Second World War begin?
87.e: The Second World War began in 1939 with Germany’s attack on Poland and ended in 1945. Switzerland stayed neutral but was surrounded by the war.
87.m: The Second World War lasted from 1939 to 1945.

88.q: In which year did people first walk on the Moon?
88.e: On the Apollo 11 mission, the Americans Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon in 1969. Millions of people watched it on television.
88.m: In 1969 people walked on the Moon for the first time.

91.q: What is meant by the Industrial Revolution?
a: The change to working with machines and factories from the 18th century
A revolution against the King of France
The founding of the first cities
91.e: From the 18th century, first in England, machines like the steam engine replaced a lot of handwork. Factories, railways and new towns appeared. Switzerland, too, with its textile and machine industries, changed greatly.
91.m: The Industrial Revolution brought machines and factories.

92.q: Who started the founding of the Red Cross?
92.e: In 1859, Henry Dunant witnessed the Battle of Solferino and saw the suffering of the wounded. His book about it led to the founding of the Red Cross in Geneva in 1863. In 1901 he received the first Nobel Peace Prize.
92.m: Henri Dunant started the founding of the Red Cross in Geneva.

93.q: What does the Swiss flag look like?
a: White cross on a red background
Red cross on a white background
93.e: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on a red background and is square, which is rare. By the way, the Red Cross reversed the colours in honour of Switzerland.
93.m: The Swiss flag is square and shows a white cross on red.

94.q: How many cantons does Switzerland have?
94.e: Switzerland is made up of 26 cantons. Each canton has its own government, its own parliament and its own laws, for example for schools.

96.q: Which two chambers make up the Swiss parliament?
a: National Council and Council of States
96.e: The parliament is called the Federal Assembly. The National Council represents the people, the Council of States represents the cantons. New laws need the approval of both chambers.
96.m: The National Council represents the people, the Council of States the cantons.

97.q: How many members does the National Council have?
97.e: The National Council has 200 seats. Large cantons with many inhabitants have more seats than small ones. It is elected every four years.

98.q: Who elects the members of the Federal Council?
98.e: The National Council and the Council of States meet together as the United Federal Assembly and elect the seven members of the Federal Council. So the people do not elect the Federal Council directly.

99.q: What happens at a municipal assembly?
a: The voters of a municipality decide directly on its business
99.e: Many municipalities, especially smaller ones, have no municipal parliament. There the voters meet and decide, for example, on the budget or a new school building.
99.m: At the municipal assembly, voters decide directly on the spot.

103.q: What does separation of powers mean?
a: Law-making, government and courts are kept separate
The police share out the work
Every canton has its own army
103.e: The power of the state is split into three branches: parliament makes laws (legislature), the government carries them out (executive), the courts give judgements (judiciary). This way they keep a check on each other.
103.m: With separation of powers, legislature, executive and judiciary are kept apart.

106.q: What is the Jewish place of worship called?
106.e: In the synagogue Jewish people pray together and read from the Torah. The most important day of the week is the Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday evening.
106.m: The synagogue is the Jewish place of worship.

107.q: At which Christian festival do many children look for painted eggs?
107.e: Easter is the most important festival in Christianity and remembers the resurrection of Jesus. Eggs stand for new life.
107.m: At Easter, Christians celebrate the resurrection, and children look for Easter eggs.

108.q: According to the Christmas story, where was Jesus born?
108.e: According to the Bible, Jesus was born in a stable in Bethlehem. The town is in the West Bank. Many nativity scenes show this story.
108.m: According to the Christmas story, Jesus was born in Bethlehem.

109.q: What is the holy book of Islam called?
109.e: For Muslims the Quran is the word of God, passed on to the Prophet Muhammad. It is written in Arabic and divided into chapters called surahs.
109.m: The holy book of Islam is the Quran.

110.q: What is the eight-day Jewish festival of lights called?
110.e: At Hanukkah families light one more candle each evening for eight evenings on a special candlestick. The festival remembers the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem.
110.m: Hanukkah is the eight-day Jewish festival of lights.

111.q: Which big festival of lights do Hindus celebrate in autumn?
111.e: For Diwali Hindus decorate their homes with lights and lamps. The festival stands for the victory of light over darkness and of good over evil.
111.m: Diwali is the big Hindu festival of lights.

112.q: In which city is the Kaaba, the most important holy site of Islam?
112.e: The Kaaba is in Mecca in Saudi Arabia. Muslims pray facing it, and many go on pilgrimage there once in their life.

113.q: What makes up the ‘Five Pillars of Islam’?
a: Declaration of faith, prayer, charity, fasting and pilgrimage
Baptism, communion, confirmation, marriage and confession
Sabbath, Torah, synagogue, Passover and Hanukkah
Yoga, meditation, karma, temple and sacrifice
113.e: The five pillars are the most important duties in Islam: the declaration of faith, daily prayer, giving to those in need, fasting in Ramadan and, for those who can, the pilgrimage to Mecca.
113.m: The five pillars of Islam are faith, prayer, charity, fasting and pilgrimage.

114.q: In which religion is nirvana, the end of the cycle of rebirth, a central goal?
114.e: In Buddhism people believe in a cycle of birth, death and rebirth. According to the teaching, whoever overcomes greed, hatred and ignorance can reach nirvana and leave this cycle.
114.m: In Buddhism nirvana is a central goal.

117.q: What do you call a person who does not believe in a god?
117.e: Atheists do not believe in God or gods. Agnostics, on the other hand, say we cannot know whether there is a god. In Switzerland each of these views is protected by freedom of religion.
117.m: Atheism means not believing in a god.

118.q: What is the largest animal in the world?
118.e: The blue whale can grow over 30 metres long, longer than a tennis court is wide. It is the largest animal that has ever lived and eats tiny crustaceans called krill.
118.m: The blue whale is the largest animal in the world.

119.q: What does a caterpillar turn into?
119.e: The caterpillar eats a lot, then turns into a pupa and changes into a butterfly inside it. This change is called metamorphosis.
119.m: A caterpillar becomes a pupa and then a butterfly.

120.q: What do you call an animal that only eats plants?
120.e: Cows, rabbits and roe deer are herbivores. Foxes mainly eat meat; bears and humans are omnivores.

121.q: Which animal often lives in Swiss forests, with the male having antlers?
121.e: In roe deer only the buck has small antlers. He sheds them every year and they grow back again.
121.m: The roe buck has antlers that grow back every year.

122.q: Why do marmots hibernate for a long time?
a: Because they can hardly find food in winter and save energy this way
Because they are afraid of snow
Because they have to work in summer
122.e: In the Alps there is hardly any grass in winter. So marmots sleep for many months in their burrow. Their heartbeat and body temperature drop a lot, so their fat reserves last until spring.

123.q: What is the highest mountain in Switzerland called?
123.e: At 4,634 metres, the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif in Valais is the highest peak in Switzerland. The more famous Matterhorn is a little lower.
123.m: The highest mountain in Switzerland is the Dufourspitze.

a: Water evaporates, forms clouds and falls again as precipitation
Clouds are made of cotton wool and get wrung out
124.e: The sun warms water from seas, lakes and plants, and it evaporates. High up, the water vapour cools and forms clouds. When the droplets get heavy enough, they fall as rain or snow.
124.m: Water evaporates, forms clouds and falls back down as precipitation.

125.q: Which planet is closest to the sun?
125.e: Mercury is the smallest planet and orbits closest to the sun. You can remember the order with: My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming.
125.m: Mercury is closest to the sun.

126.q: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
126.e: Jupiter is a gas giant and so big that the Earth would fit inside it more than a thousand times. Its best-known feature is the Great Red Spot, a huge storm.
126.m: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system.

a: The variety of species, genes and habitats
The number of trees in a park
127.e: Biodiversity describes the variety of life: different animal and plant species, differences within a species and different habitats. A high variety makes nature more resilient.
127.m: Biodiversity means the variety of life.

128.q: What does a food chain show?
a: Who eats whom, from plant material to predator
128.e: An example: grass → mouse → fox. Plants are at the start because they make energy using sunlight. If one link is missing, the whole chain gets out of balance.
128.m: In the food chain herbivores eat plants and carnivores eat herbivores.

a: A community of living things together with their habitat
130.e: A forest, a pond or a meadow is an ecosystem. Plants, animals, fungi and bacteria there depend on each other and on soil, water and climate.
130.m: An ecosystem is made up of living things and their habitat.

131.q: Which sense organ do you smell with?
131.e: There are lots of smell cells in the nose. They detect scents in the air and send messages to the brain. Smelling also helps with tasting.

132.q: Traditionally, how many senses do humans have?
132.e: The five classic senses are sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Today we know that we sense even more, for example balance.
132.m: The five senses are sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.

133.q: What is the frame of bones that supports your body called?
133.e: The skeleton holds the body up and protects organs, for example the skull protects the brain. Muscles move the bones at the joints.
133.m: The skeleton is the body's frame of bones.

134.q: Which organ takes in oxygen from the air when you breathe?
134.e: When you breathe in, air gets into the lungs. There, oxygen passes into the blood, and carbon dioxide is breathed out.
134.m: The lungs bring oxygen into the blood.

135.q: Which is the largest organ of the human body?
135.e: The skin covers the whole body. It protects against germs and sun, helps control temperature and lets us feel touch.
135.m: The skin is the largest human organ.

136.q: What are white blood cells responsible for?
136.e: White blood cells are the body's police. They recognise bacteria and viruses and fight them. Oxygen is carried by the red blood cells.
136.m: White blood cells are for defence, red ones carry oxygen.

137.q: Roughly how many bones does an adult human have?
137.e: An adult human has about 206 bones. Babies have more, because some bones only grow together later.
137.m: An adult human has about 206 bones.

138.q: How many teeth does an adult have, including all the wisdom teeth?
138.e: The permanent set has 32 teeth, 4 of them wisdom teeth. Children have a set of 20 milk teeth.

a: It trains the immune system to recognise a germ before you get ill
It kills all the bacteria in the body
It only works against broken bones
139.e: A vaccination shows the body a harmless part or a weakened form of a germ. The immune system gets to know it and can react faster to a real infection.
139.m: A vaccination is training for the immune system.

144.q: What is needed for a shadow to form?
a: Light and an object that blocks the light
144.e: Light travels in straight lines. If something is in the way, less light gets behind it, and that is where a shadow forms.
144.m: When light hits an obstacle, a shadow forms.

a: Sunlight is split into its colours in raindrops
It is painted on the sky
145.e: Sunlight looks white but is made up of many colours. In raindrops it is bent and fanned out into red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet. For this, the sun has to be behind you.
145.m: A rainbow forms when sunlight is split into its colours.

146.e: A thermometer measures how warm or cold something is, for example the air or a fever. In Switzerland temperature is measured in degrees Celsius.

147.q: Why can you see yourself in a mirror?
a: The mirror throws the light back
The mirror gives off its own light
A picture lives inside the mirror
147.e: Light coming from you hits the smooth surface of the mirror and is thrown back. This is called reflection. That is why you see yourself the wrong way round.
147.m: A mirror reflects light, which is why you can see yourself in it.

149.q: Which of these energy sources is renewable?
149.e: Renewable energy does not run out, for example sun, wind and water power. Switzerland gets a large part of its electricity from hydropower.
149.m: Sun, wind and water are renewable energy sources.

150.q: When does a bulb light up in a simple circuit?
150.e: Electricity only flows if there is a closed path from the battery through the bulb and back to the battery. A switch opens or closes this circuit.
150.m: A bulb only lights up when the circuit is closed.

155.e: The 5-franc coin is the largest and most valuable coin in Switzerland. It is also called the “Fünfliber”. Larger amounts are paid with banknotes from 10 francs upwards.
155.m: The Fünfliber is the largest Swiss coin.

156.q: What is a piggy bank good for?
156.e: In a piggy bank you collect coins until there is enough for something bigger. Later you might also get a savings account at the bank.
156.m: A piggy bank helps you save for small goals.

157.q: In a mobile game you can pay for “jewels”. What is true?
a: That costs real money, so ask your parents first
You get the money back later
157.e: In-app purchases like this cost real money, even if they look like play money. Many games are designed to make you buy again and again. So always ask first.
157.m: Game currency in mobile games costs real money.

158.q: Why is it worth comparing prices?
a: The same product can cost different amounts in different shops
Because prices are the same everywhere
Because more expensive is always better
Because you get more pocket money that way
158.e: Comparing in the shop or online often shows big differences. Also look at the price per kilo or litre, which is usually in small print on the price label.

a: Borrowed money that you have to pay back with interest
159.e: With a loan, a bank lends you money. You pay it back in instalments and also pay interest. So in the end you pay back more than you received.
159.m: A loan is borrowed money that you pay back with interest.

160.q: What is a warning sign of debt?
160.e: If you pay old debts with new loans, you can easily slide into a debt spiral. In Switzerland, debt advice centres help free of charge and in confidence.
160.m: Taking out a loan to pay off debts is a warning sign.

a: You also get interest on interest you received earlier
A penalty fee charged by the bank
162.e: If interest stays in the account, it earns interest itself the following year. So money grows faster and faster over time. That is why it pays to start saving early. With debts, unfortunately, the effect works the other way round.
162.m: With compound interest, the interest earns interest too.

167.q: What do people in Switzerland call the machine where you can withdraw cash?
167.e: In Switzerland people usually say Bancomat. With a card and your PIN you can withdraw cash from your account there.
167.m: You can withdraw cash at a Bancomat.

168.q: What do you do with the PIN for your card?
a: Keep it secret and tell nobody
168.e: The PIN is a secret number. Anyone who knows it and has the card can withdraw your money. Cover the keypad when you type it in.

169.e: The Swiss National Bank (SNB) is Switzerland's central bank. It issues the banknotes and makes sure the franc stays stable. It has offices in Bern and Zurich.

a: A Swiss app for paying with your phone
170.e: With TWINT you can pay with your smartphone or send money to friends. The app is linked to your bank account or a prepaid balance.
170.m: With TWINT you can pay with your phone.

a: A regular automatic payment, for example for the rent
An order that is never carried out
171.e: With a standing order the bank automatically transfers the same amount every month. Handy for rent or a phone contract, so you never forget a payment.
171.m: A standing order pays an amount automatically every month.

172.q: What replaced the old orange payment slip in Switzerland?
172.e: Since autumn 2022 there has only been the QR-bill. You scan the QR code with your banking app and all the payment details are filled in automatically.
172.m: You can simply scan and pay a QR-bill.

173.q: What does a bank statement show?
a: All the money coming into and going out of your account
173.e: On the bank statement or in the app you can see when money came in or went out. If you check it regularly, you will also spot wrong payments.
173.m: A bank statement gives an overview of your account.

178.q: Which of these things is paid for with tax money?
178.e: With taxes, municipalities, cantons and the Confederation pay for things for everyone: schools, roads, parks, the fire brigade and much more. Everyone buys private things themselves.
178.m: With tax money the state pays for things that serve everyone.

179.q: Do children sometimes pay taxes too?
a: Yes, for example VAT when shopping
Only with their own tax return
Only once they have a bank account
179.e: When you buy something in a shop, VAT is already included in the price. So everyone pays a little, including children.
179.m: When shopping you also pay VAT.

180.q: What has the standard rate of Swiss VAT been since 2024?
180.e: Since 2024 the standard rate has been 8.1 per cent. A reduced rate applies to food, books and medicines. Compared with many countries in Europe, VAT in Switzerland is low.
180.m: The standard VAT rate has been 8.1% since 2024.

181.q: Which tax do dog owners pay in many municipalities?
181.e: Many municipalities charge a dog tax for every dog every year. The money pays for things like dog waste bins and emptying them.
181.m: If you have a dog, you pay a dog tax to the municipality.

182.q: When do you usually have to fill in your own tax return for the first time in Switzerland?
a: From the year you come of age
Only if you own a house
182.e: When you come of age you become liable for tax yourself, even if you are still in education. Details depend on the canton, for example apprentices with a wage may have to do it earlier.
182.m: At 18 comes your first tax return.

190.q: Where do you go when you are ill and need help?
190.e: The doctor examines you and helps you get well. The health insurance helps to pay the costs.
190.m: When you are ill, you go to the doctor.

191.q: What is the lowest deductible (franchise) that adults can choose in basic health insurance?
191.e: Adults can choose a deductible between 300 and 2500 francs. The higher the deductible, the lower the premium, but the more you pay yourself when you are ill.
191.m: Adults can choose a deductible of 300 to 2500 francs.

192.q: What is the standard deductible (franchise) for children?
192.e: For children the deductible is normally 0 francs. Parents can choose a higher one voluntarily, up to 600 francs.
192.m: For children the deductible is usually 0 francs.

193.q: Can a health insurer turn you down for basic insurance?
a: Yes, if you are often ill
193.e: In basic insurance, health insurers must accept everyone, and the benefits are the same for all. Only for supplementary insurance may they reject applications.
193.m: In basic insurance, every health insurer must accept you.

194.q: By when must notice to cancel basic insurance usually reach the health insurer to switch at the start of the year?
194.e: The new premiums are announced in autumn. Anyone who wants to switch must give notice so that it arrives no later than the last working day of November. Comparing can be worthwhile because the benefits are the same everywhere.
194.m: If you want to switch health insurer, you usually have to give notice by the end of November.

202.q: What should you never share with strangers on the internet?
202.e: Personal details such as your address, phone number or school do not belong on the internet or in chats with strangers. You never know exactly who is behind them.
202.m: Your address and number stay private.

203.q: Someone you only know online wants to meet you. What do you do?
a: Tell your parents or someone you trust, and do not go alone
203.e: Online, anyone can pretend to be someone else. Always tell an adult you trust. If someone asks you to keep something secret, that is a warning sign.
203.m: Meeting someone from online? Always ask an adult first.

204.q: Why are breaks from the screen good?
a: They are good for your eyes, head and body
So that the game loads faster
204.e: After looking at a screen for a long time, your eyes get tired and it is harder to concentrate. Playing outside, moving and meeting friends is good for your whole body.
204.m: Breaks from the screen are good for you.

a: Sensational headlines or pictures meant only to get you to click
205.e: Headlines like “You won't believe what happens next!” are meant to make you curious. Often the content does not deliver what it promises; it is about clicks and advertising money.
205.m: Be careful with sensational headlines, as they are often clickbait.

206.q: Why is it good to put your phone away before going to sleep?
a: Light and exciting content keep the brain awake
Because the phone breaks at night
Because messages are forbidden at night
206.e: The bright light of the screen and exciting videos wake your head up. If you put your phone away before sleeping, or charge it outside your room, you usually fall asleep more easily.
206.m: If you put your phone away, you sleep better.

208.q: A classmate secretly films you and wants to post the video. What applies?
a: He needs your permission, otherwise he breaks your right to your own image
There are no rules about it
208.e: In Switzerland, the right to your own image is protected by personal rights law. Anyone who publishes pictures or videos of others without their consent can be held responsible.
208.m: You decide about your own image.

213.q: In Switzerland, who checks whether journalists keep to ethical rules?
213.e: The Press Council is a complaints body of the media industry. It checks, for example, whether facts are correct and privacy has been respected. Such rules usually do not apply to social media posts.
213.m: The Press Council keeps an eye on ethics in journalism.

214.q: Who repairs cars at the garage?
214.e: At the garage, car mechanics check and repair engines and brakes. Today the job is called automotive mechatronics technician.

215.e: Hairdressers advise customers and cut and colour hair. Creativity and enjoying contact with people are important here.

216.q: Which path do most young people in Switzerland choose after compulsory school?
216.e: About two thirds of young people in Switzerland do an apprenticeship. The dual system with company and school is seen as a model internationally.
216.m: An apprenticeship is the most common path.

a: A written contract between apprentice and company, approved by the canton
217.e: The apprenticeship contract sets out the length, wages, holidays and working hours. For under-18s, the parents sign too. The cantonal vocational training office must approve the contract.
217.m: An apprenticeship contract is written and approved by the canton.

a: Courses outside the training company where basic skills are practised
218.e: In the üK, all apprentices in a trade learn the most important basics, no matter which company they work for. That way everyone has the same foundation.
218.m: In inter-company courses (üK) you learn shared basics.

219.q: What belongs in an application for an apprenticeship?
a: A cover letter, CV and school reports
219.e: In the cover letter you explain why the job interests you. Add your CV, school reports and often taster placement reports or test results.
219.m: An application includes a letter, CV and reports.

224.q: What should you wear when you ride a bike?
224.e: A helmet protects your head if you fall. It is important that it fits well and the strap is fastened.
224.m: When you ride a bike, you put on a helmet.

225.q: Which side of the road do people drive on in Switzerland?
225.e: Switzerland drives on the right: bikes and cars use the right-hand side. In Great Britain, on the other hand, people drive on the left.
225.m: In Switzerland people drive on the right.

226.q: Where does an empty PET bottle go?
226.e: You can return PET bottles to many shops. New bottles are made from the material. That saves raw materials and energy.
226.m: Empty PET bottles go back to the collection.

227.q: Why do you wash your hands before eating?
a: To make the food taste better
227.e: Bacteria and viruses collect on your hands. Washing with soap and water for about 20 seconds removes most of them. That way you get ill less often.
227.m: Washing your hands means fewer germs.

228.q: Which number do you call in Switzerland in case of poisoning?
228.e: Tox Info Suisse gives advice on 145 day and night in cases of poisoning, for example if a child has swallowed cleaning products or tablets. If someone is unconscious, call 144 straight away.

229.q: Which number do you call to alert Rega, the Swiss air rescue service?
229.e: Rega flies injured people to hospital in helicopters and air ambulance jets, for example after an accident in the mountains. You can reach it on 1414.

230.q: According to the food pyramid, what should you eat or drink the most of?
230.e: The base is unsweetened drinks like water, then come vegetables and fruit, then cereals. Sweet and salty foods are at the top, so only a little of those.
230.m: Drink plenty of water, eat lots of vegetables and fruit and few sweet things.

231.q: Why do many municipalities charge a fee for rubbish bags?
a: Whoever makes more rubbish should pay more
So that rubbish costs more than food
231.e: The bag fee follows the polluter pays principle: whoever produces lots of rubbish pays more. That encourages people to collect glass, paper and PET separately.
231.m: Whoever makes rubbish pays for it: the bag fee follows the polluter pays principle.

237.q: Which animals lived millions of years ago and are extinct today?
237.e: Dinosaurs ruled the Earth for more than 150 million years. Today we know about them from fossils, that is, bones and tracks turned to stone. By the way, birds are descended from dinosaurs.
237.m: Dinosaurs are extinct, and their descendants are the birds.

238.q: Where did people in the Stone Age paint pictures of animals?
238.e: Tens of thousands of years ago people painted horses, bison and deer on cave walls. They used paints made from earth, charcoal and plants. These pictures are the oldest works of art made by humans.
238.m: In the Stone Age people painted pictures in caves.

240.q: According to what we know today, roughly how old is the universe?
240.e: From observations, scientists calculate that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago with the Big Bang. It has been expanding ever since.
240.m: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old.

241.q: Roughly how old is the Earth?
241.e: The Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago from dust and rock that circled the young Sun. Humans have only existed for a tiny fraction of this time.
241.m: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.

242.q: According to what we know today, what was the main reason the dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago?
a: The impact of a huge asteroid
242.e: An asteroid about ten kilometres across struck what is now Mexico. Dust darkened the sky, the climate changed greatly, and many kinds of animals died out.
242.m: An asteroid led to the end of the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.

a: A glacier mummy more than 5000 years old
A mountaineer from the Middle Ages
243.e: Ötzi was found in 1991 in the ice of the Ötztal Alps. Because he lay in glacier ice, his body, clothes and tools were amazingly well preserved.
243.m: Ötzi is a glacier mummy more than 5000 years old.

244.q: What does the Big Bang theory describe?
a: That the universe expanded from an extremely hot, dense state
That the Earth was formed by a volcanic explosion
That stars grow out of the Earth
That the universe keeps getting smaller
244.e: According to the Big Bang theory, all the matter in the universe was unimaginably hot and dense at the beginning. Since then it has been expanding and cooling. Important evidence for this is the galaxies moving apart and the cosmic background radiation.
244.m: The expansion of the universe began with the Big Bang.

245.q: According to what we know today, on which continent did modern humans (Homo sapiens) first appear?
245.e: The oldest finds of Homo sapiens come from Africa and are about 300,000 years old. From there people later spread all over the world.
245.m: Africa is seen as the cradle of humankind.

247.q: What are the pile dwellings that have been found at many Swiss lakes?
a: Remains of villages from the Stone and Bronze Ages
247.e: On lake shores and in bogs, wooden posts, tools and even food remains were preserved for thousands of years. The pile dwellings around the Alps have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011.
247.m: Pile dwellings were prehistoric villages by lakes.

248.q: What were the first living things on Earth like?
248.e: The first living things appeared in water more than 3.5 billion years ago and were made of just one cell. Over a very long time all plants and animals developed from them.
248.m: Life began with single-celled organisms in water.

249.q: What were the kings of ancient Egypt called?
249.e: The pharaohs ruled ancient Egypt and were worshipped like gods. One of the best known is Tutankhamun, whose tomb full of treasure was discovered in 1922.
249.m: The kings of ancient Egypt were called pharaohs.

250.q: Where do the Olympic Games originally come from?
250.e: The first Olympic Games took place about 2800 years ago in Olympia in Greece, in honour of the god Zeus. The modern Games have existed since 1896.

251.q: What is the picture writing of the ancient Egyptians called?
251.e: Hieroglyphs are made up of small pictures for sounds and words. For a long time nobody could read them. Only with the Rosetta Stone were they deciphered in the 19th century.
251.m: The writing of the ancient Egyptians is called hieroglyphs.

252.q: What did the Romans build to carry water into their towns?
252.e: Aqueducts were water channels with a gentle slope, often running over high arched bridges. This way fresh water flowed for many kilometres to fountains and baths.
252.m: The Romans built aqueducts to carry water into their towns.

253.q: In which ancient city did an early form of democracy develop?
253.e: In ancient Athens, free men could take part in decisions in the people's assembly. Women, slaves and foreigners, however, were excluded. The word democracy means ‘rule by the people’.

254.q: Which volcano buried the Roman town of Pompeii in the year 79?
254.e: When Vesuvius erupted, Pompeii was buried under ash. This preserved the town, and today you can visit its streets, houses and wall paintings.

255.e: Caesar conquered Gaul and became the most powerful man in Rome. Because many feared he wanted to become king, he was murdered on the Ides of March in 44 BC.
255.m: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and was murdered in 44 BC.

258.q: What do Socrates, Plato and Aristotle have in common?
a: They were famous philosophers in ancient Greece
258.e: The three thinkers lived in Greece about 2400 years ago. They asked questions such as what justice is and how to live a good life. Their ideas still shape our thinking today.
258.m: Socrates, Plato and Aristotle were Greek philosophers.

259.q: Who lived in a monastery or convent in the Middle Ages?
259.e: Monks or nuns lived in monasteries and convents by fixed rules. They prayed, worked and copied books by hand. In this way they preserved a lot of knowledge.
259.m: Monks or nuns lived in a monastery or convent.

260.q: Which disease killed a large part of the people in Europe around 1350?
260.e: The plague, also called the Black Death, was spread by bacteria, often through fleas from rats. According to estimates, about a third of Europe’s population died.
260.m: Around 1350 the plague raged in Europe.

261.q: Which king of the Franks was crowned emperor in the year 800?
261.e: Charlemagne ruled over a huge empire, which also included parts of today’s Switzerland. He supported schools and monasteries. According to legend, he founded the Grossmünster in Zurich.
261.m: In the year 800 Charlemagne was crowned emperor.

262.q: Whose expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world?
262.e: Magellan set off in 1519 with five ships. He himself died on the way, but one ship returned in 1522 under Juan Sebastián Elcano. This proved that you can sail around the Earth.
262.m: The first voyage around the world took place from 1519 to 1522.

a: A league of merchants and trading cities in northern Europe
263.e: In the Middle Ages the Hanseatic League linked cities such as Lübeck, Hamburg and Bergen. Together they protected their trade across the North Sea and the Baltic and became very rich.
263.m: The Hanseatic League was a trading league in the north.

a: Military campaigns by Christian armies for religious reasons, mainly to the Holy Land
264.e: From 1096, Christian armies marched towards Jerusalem to conquer the “Holy Land”. The Crusades brought much suffering, but also contact with the Arab world and its knowledge.
264.m: From 1096 the Crusades went to the Holy Land.

265.q: Which Renaissance artist painted the Mona Lisa?
265.e: Leonardo da Vinci was a painter, inventor and scientist. In the Renaissance, from the 15th century, artists and scholars looked back to ancient times and put human beings at the centre.
265.m: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa.

266.q: Which new picture of the universe did Nicolaus Copernicus describe?
a: The Sun is at the centre and the Earth goes round it
The Earth is a flat disc
The Sun goes round the Earth
The stars are holes in the sky
266.e: People used to believe that the Earth was at the centre. In 1543 Copernicus showed that the movements of the planets can be explained better with a model that puts the Sun at the centre. This changed people’s thinking completely.
266.m: Copernicus put the Sun at the centre of the universe.

267.q: What did not exist yet 100 years ago?
267.e: Smartphones have only existed for about 20 years. 100 years ago many families did not even have a telephone at home.

268.q: In which year did the French Revolution begin?
268.e: In 1789 people in Paris stormed the Bastille, a prison. The Revolution called for liberty, equality and fraternity and changed all of Europe, Switzerland too.

269.q: In which year did the First World War begin?
269.e: The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918. New weapons made it especially destructive. Switzerland stayed neutral but suffered from hunger and hardship.
269.m: The First World War lasted from 1914 to 1918.

270.q: Which organisation was founded in 1945 to keep peace in the world?
270.e: After the Second World War, 51 countries founded the United Nations. Today almost every country in the world is a member. Geneva is an important seat of the UN.

271.q: When did the USA declare its independence from Great Britain?
271.e: On 4 July 1776, 13 American colonies declared their independence. That is why 4 July is the national holiday in the USA.
271.m: The USA declared its independence on 4 July 1776.

a: A conflict lasting decades between the USA and the Soviet Union without direct war between them
A war in the winter of 1914
272.e: After 1945 the West, led by the USA, faced the East under the Soviet Union. They built up weapons but did not fight each other directly. The Cold War ended with the fall of the Berlin Wall.
272.m: In the Cold War, from 1947 to 1991, the USA and the Soviet Union faced each other.

273.q: Where was the World Wide Web invented?
273.e: The British researcher Tim Berners-Lee developed the Web in 1989 at CERN, the research centre near Geneva. It was meant to help researchers share information; today almost the whole world uses it.
273.m: The Web was created at CERN in 1989.

274.q: What did Martin Luther King fight for in the USA?
a: For equal rights for Black people, without violence
For the independence of the USA
274.e: In the 1950s and 1960s Martin Luther King campaigned without violence against racial segregation. His speech “I have a dream” is world-famous. In 1964 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
274.m: Martin Luther King fought without violence for equal rights.

a: A fighter against apartheid and later South Africa’s first Black president
275.e: Mandela spent 27 years in prison because he fought against racial segregation in South Africa. In 1994 he was elected president and worked for reconciliation.
275.m: Nelson Mandela fought against apartheid and became president in 1994.

276.q: Which three places are seen as the founders of the Swiss Confederation?
276.e: According to tradition, the three “original cantons” joined together in 1291 to help each other. Unterwalden is now divided into Obwalden and Nidwalden.
276.m: The original cantons are Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.

277.q: On which lake is the Rütli meadow?
277.e: The Rütli is on Lake Lucerne. According to legend, men from the original cantons swore eternal loyalty to each other there. Celebrations take place there on 1 August.
277.m: The Rütli is the symbolic place of the Swiss Confederation.

278.q: Which battle did the Confederates win against a Habsburg army in 1315?
278.e: At Morgarten, men from Schwyz surprised a Habsburg army of knights on a narrow path between the mountain and the lake. The victory strengthened the alliance of the Confederates.
278.m: In 1315, the Confederates won at Morgarten.

279.q: What happened to the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1798?
a: French troops marched in, and the Helvetic Republic was created
The Habsburgs conquered the whole country
The cantons founded the federal state
279.e: In 1798, revolutionary France occupied Switzerland. The old order with subject territories was abolished and a unified state, the Helvetic Republic, was founded. It lasted only a few years.
279.m: The Helvetic Republic was created in 1798.

280.q: When was Switzerland's neutrality recognised by the great powers of Europe?
a: In 1815 at the Congress of Vienna
280.e: After the end of the Napoleonic Wars, in 1815 the great powers recognised Switzerland's permanent neutrality. Today's borders also largely date from this time.

285.q: In which year was the Gotthard Base Tunnel, the longest railway tunnel in the world, opened?
285.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long and was opened in 2016. Since then, goods and people can travel through the Alps faster and on a flatter route. The first Gotthard railway tunnel dates from 1882.
285.m: The 57 km Gotthard Base Tunnel was opened in 2016.

286.q: Which snowman is burned at the Zurich Sechseläuten?
286.e: At the Sechseläuten in spring, the guilds parade through Zurich. At the end, the Böögg is set alight on a bonfire. The faster its head explodes, the nicer the summer is supposed to be.
286.m: The Böögg burns at the Sechseläuten.

287.q: What was Zurich called in Roman times?
287.e: Where the Limmat flows out of Lake Zurich, the Romans had a customs station called Turicum. The name Zurich developed from it.
287.m: In Roman times, Zurich was called Turicum.

288.q: In which year did Zurich join the Swiss Confederation?
288.e: In 1351 Zurich formed an alliance with the forest cantons and Lucerne. This gave the Confederation an important trading city.
288.m: Zurich has been part of the Confederation since 1351.

290.q: Which animal is on Bern's coat of arms?
290.e: The bear has been the symbol of Bern for centuries. In the Bear Park by the Aare you can still see live bears today.
290.m: Bern's heraldic animal is the bear.

291.q: Which noble family founded the city of Bern in 1191?
291.e: Duke Berthold V of Zähringen founded Bern on a peninsula in a loop of the Aare. The Zähringens also founded Fribourg.
291.m: Bern was founded by the Zähringens in 1191.

294.q: Which famous covered wooden bridge is in Lucerne?
294.e: The Chapel Bridge dates from the 14th century and is one of the oldest wooden bridges in Europe. In 1993 it partly burnt down and was rebuilt. Next to it stands the Water Tower.
294.m: The Chapel Bridge is in Lucerne.

295.q: What does the Lion Monument in Lucerne commemorate?
a: Swiss Guards who died in Paris in 1792
A lion that escaped from a zoo
295.e: The dying lion in the rock commemorates Swiss mercenaries who defended the French king during the storming of the Tuileries in Paris in 1792. Many Swiss served in foreign armies at that time.
295.m: The Lion Monument commemorates the Swiss Guards of 1792.

296.q: Which battle took place in 1386 in what is now the canton of Lucerne?
296.e: At Sempach in 1386 the Confederates defeated a Habsburg army. Duke Leopold III of Austria was killed. The legend of Winkelried is linked to this battle.
296.m: The Battle of Sempach took place in 1386.

298.q: In which place in Uri does the famous Tell Monument stand?
298.e: The Tell Monument in Altdorf shows William Tell with his crossbow and his son Walter. According to legend, Tell shot the apple in Altdorf.
298.m: The Tell Monument stands in Altdorf.

299.q: According to legend, which animal did the people of Uri send across the Devil's Bridge in the Schöllenen Gorge first?
299.e: According to legend, the Devil built the bridge over the Reuss and demanded the first soul to cross it. The clever people of Uri sent a billy goat across.
299.m: According to legend, the Devil got a billy goat for the Devil's Bridge.

301.q: Which canton gave the whole of Switzerland its name?
301.e: After the people of Schwyz, who stood out in many battles, all the Confederates were soon called “Schwyzer”. This became the name Switzerland (in German Schweiz).
301.m: The name Switzerland comes from Schwyz.

302.q: Where is the Federal Charter of 1291 kept?
a: In the Museum of the Swiss Charters in Schwyz
In the Federal Palace in Bern
In the National Museum in Paris
302.e: The Federal Charter is a document in Latin in which Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden promise to help each other. The original is kept in the Museum of the Swiss Charters in Schwyz.
302.m: The Federal Charter is kept in a museum in Schwyz.

304.q: Which founding canton did Obwalden and Nidwalden form together?
304.e: Obwalden and Nidwalden together formed Unterwalden, one of the three founding cantons. However, they were governed separately from early on.
304.m: Obwalden and Nidwalden together formed Unterwalden.

305.q: Which hermit from Obwalden helped to settle a dangerous quarrel between the Confederates in 1481?
305.e: Nicholas of Flüe lived as a hermit in the Ranft. In 1481 his advice contributed to the Covenant of Stans, an agreement that prevented the Confederation from breaking apart. He is the patron saint of Switzerland.
305.m: In 1481, Brother Klaus brought peace among the Confederates.

307.q: Which legendary hero from Nidwalden is said to have grabbed the enemies' spears at Sempach?
307.e: According to legend, Winkelried opened a gap in the enemy lines at the Battle of Sempach by pulling many spears towards himself. It is not certain whether he really lived. There is a monument to him in Stans.
307.m: According to legend, Winkelried was the hero of Sempach.

308.q: What is the capital of Nidwalden?
308.e: Stans is the capital of Nidwalden. The Covenant of Stans was agreed there in 1481. Sarnen is the capital of Obwalden.
308.m: The capital of Nidwalden is Stans; the capital of Obwalden is Sarnen.

310.q: Which saint is shown on the flag of Glarus?
310.e: Glarus is the only canton whose coat of arms shows a person: Saint Fridolin as a traveller with a staff and a Bible. He is said to have brought Christianity to the area in the early Middle Ages.
310.m: Saint Fridolin is shown on the Glarus coat of arms.

311.q: Who did the people of Glarus defeat at the Battle of Näfels in 1388, which the Näfelser Fahrt commemorates?
311.e: In 1388 the people of Glarus defeated a Habsburg army at Näfels. Since then they have remembered this victory every year in April with a pilgrimage, the Näfelser Fahrt.
311.m: The Näfelser Fahrt commemorates the victory over the Habsburgs in 1388.

313.q: Which sweet speciality is named after Zug?
313.e: The Zuger Kirschtorte is made of sponge, buttercream and meringue-nut layers and is soaked in kirsch. Many cherry trees have grown around Zug for a long time.
313.m: Zug is famous for the Zuger Kirschtorte.

314.q: In which year did Zug join the Swiss Confederation?
314.e: Zug was admitted to the alliance in 1352, the same year as Glarus. Bern followed a year later.

316.q: Which two languages are spoken in the canton of Fribourg?
316.e: Fribourg lies on the language border. Most people speak French, some speak German. In German the city is called Freiburg.
316.m: The canton of Fribourg is bilingual.

317.q: Who did the Swiss Confederates fight against at the Battle of Murten in 1476?
a: Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy
317.e: In the Burgundian Wars, the Confederates defeated the powerful Duke Charles the Bold at Grandson and Murten. The victory brought great booty and respect in Europe.
317.m: In 1476 the Confederates defeated Burgundy at Murten.

319.q: Which number plays a special role in Solothurn?
319.e: Solothurn was admitted to the Confederation as the eleventh member. Since then the number 11 appears everywhere: there are 11 churches and chapels, 11 fountains, and the cathedral has 11 bells. There is even a clock with only 11 hours.

320.q: What was Solothurn called in Roman times?
320.e: Solothurn is one of the oldest towns in Switzerland. The Romans called the settlement on the Aare Salodurum.
320.m: In Roman times, Solothurn was called Salodurum.

322.q: Which big festival in Basel begins with the Morgestraich at 4 o'clock in the morning?
322.e: At the Morgestraich, the lights in the city are switched off at 4 in the morning, and groups called cliques set off with lanterns, piccolos and drums. Basel Carnival is UNESCO cultural heritage.
322.m: Basel Carnival begins with the Morgestraich.

323.q: Which is the oldest university in Switzerland?
a: The University of Basel, founded in 1460
323.e: The University of Basel was founded in 1460. Famous scholars such as Erasmus of Rotterdam worked in Basel, which was also a centre of book printing.
323.m: Switzerland's oldest university was founded in Basel in 1460.

324.q: Which city on the Rhine joined the Swiss Confederacy in 1501?
324.e: Basel was admitted in 1501, in the same year as Schaffhausen. As a trading city on the Rhine it was an important partner. Geneva only joined in 1815.

326.q: Which Roman town can you visit in Augst in the canton of Basel-Landschaft?
326.e: Augusta Raurica was a large Roman town. Today you can see a theatre, temples and a reconstructed Roman house there. A Roman festival takes place every year.
326.m: The Roman town of Augusta Raurica is in Augst.

327.q: What is the capital of Basel-Landschaft?
327.e: Since the canton was split in 1833, Liestal has been the capital of Basel-Landschaft. It is known for the fire custom “Chienbäse” at carnival.
327.m: The capital of Basel-Landschaft is Liestal.

329.q: Which big waterfall is near Schaffhausen?
329.e: The Rhine Falls is one of the largest waterfalls in Europe. You can take a boat right up to the rock in the middle.
329.m: The Rhine Falls is near Schaffhausen.

330.q: What is the name of the round fortress above the old town of Schaffhausen?
330.e: The Munot was built in the 16th century. Every evening the little Munot bell rings there. In summer, balls are held on the battlements.
330.m: The Munot stands above the old town of Schaffhausen.

332.q: Which cheese bears the name of the Appenzell region?
332.e: Appenzeller cheese is treated with a secret herbal brine, which gives it its spicy taste. The region is also known for customs such as Silvesterchlausen.
332.m: The Appenzell region is known for Appenzeller cheese.

333.q: Why was the state of Appenzell divided in 1597?
a: Because of religion: Ausserrhoden became Protestant, Innerrhoden stayed Catholic
Because of a quarrel about cheese
333.e: After the Reformation there were Protestant and Catholic communities in Appenzell. To keep the peace, the state was divided in 1597 into Ausserrhoden and Innerrhoden.
333.m: In 1597 Appenzell was divided by religion.

335.q: Which canton has the fewest inhabitants?
335.e: Appenzell Innerrhoden is the smallest Swiss canton by population. It is rural and known for its traditions.
335.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden is the canton with the fewest inhabitants.

336.q: What is the capital of Appenzell Innerrhoden, where the Landsgemeinde takes place?
336.e: On the Landsgemeinde square in Appenzell, the people of Innerrhoden vote by raising their hands every April. Herisau is the capital of Ausserrhoden.
336.m: The capital of Appenzell Innerrhoden is Appenzell.

338.q: Which monk gave the city of St Gallen its name?
338.e: The Irish monk Gallus settled in the Steinach valley around 612. According to legend, a bear helped him build his cell, which is why there is a bear on the city's coat of arms.
338.m: St Gallen is named after the monk Gallus, and there is a bear on its coat of arms.

339.q: Which treasure in St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
a: The Abbey District with the Abbey Library
339.e: The Abbey Library is one of the oldest libraries in the world and owns precious medieval manuscripts. You enter the magnificent Baroque hall wearing felt slippers.
339.m: The Abbey Library of St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

342.q: Which Swiss canton has the largest area?
342.e: The Grisons makes up about a sixth of the whole of Switzerland. It has a great many valleys and mountain peaks.
342.m: The Grisons is the largest canton by area.

343.q: Which three languages are official languages in the Grisons?
343.e: The Grisons is the only trilingual canton. Romansh is spoken almost only here.

346.q: Which powerful ruling dynasty takes its name from a castle in Aargau?
346.e: Habsburg Castle stands near Brugg in Aargau. The family named after it later became one of the most powerful in Europe and ruled over Austria and Spain.

347.q: Which large Roman legionary camp was near Windisch in Aargau?
347.e: Thousands of Roman soldiers were once stationed at Vindonissa. It was the only Roman legionary camp on the territory of present-day Switzerland.
347.m: The Roman legionary camp of Vindonissa was near Windisch.

349.q: Because of which fruit is Thurgau jokingly called “Mostindien” (Cider India)?
349.e: A particularly large number of fruit trees grow in Thurgau. The apples are made into cider (Most). Because the shape of the canton looks a little like India, the nickname came about.
349.m: Thurgau is jokingly called Mostindien because of its apples.

350.q: On which large lake does Thurgau lie?
350.e: Lake Constance borders Switzerland, Germany and Austria. Places such as Kreuzlingen, Romanshorn and Arbon lie on the Thurgau shore.

352.q: Which language is mainly spoken in Ticino?
352.e: Ticino is the only canton where Italian is the only official language. Together with southern Grisons, it forms Italian-speaking Switzerland.

353.q: Which castles in Bellinzona are a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
353.e: In the Middle Ages, the three castles guarded the way to several Alpine passes. The Dukes of Milan extended them. They have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.
353.m: The three castles of Bellinzona are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

355.q: Which famous water castle stands near Montreux on Lake Geneva?
355.e: Chillon Castle stands on a rock in the lake. For a long time it belonged to the Counts of Savoy and later to Bern. It is one of the most visited historic buildings in Switzerland.
355.m: Chillon Castle stands in Lake Geneva.

356.q: Which international sports organisation has its headquarters in Lausanne?
356.e: The IOC has been based in Lausanne since 1915. There is also a big Olympic Museum there. That is why Lausanne calls itself the “Olympic Capital”.
356.m: The IOC has its headquarters in Lausanne.

357.q: Which vineyard terraces on Lake Geneva are a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
357.e: The steep vineyard terraces of Lavaux were built by monks and farmers from the Middle Ages onwards. They have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.
357.m: The vineyard terraces of Lavaux are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

359.q: Which famous mountain stands near Zermatt in Valais?
359.e: Because of its pyramid shape, the Matterhorn is one of the best-known mountains in the world. It lies on the border with Italy.

360.q: Which is the largest glacier in the Alps?
360.e: The Aletsch Glacier is about 20 kilometres long. Like all Alpine glaciers, it is melting because of global warming and gets shorter every year.
360.m: The Aletsch Glacier is the largest glacier in the Alps.

363.q: Which industry is the canton of Neuchâtel especially famous for?
363.e: A famous watch industry developed in the Neuchâtel Jura from the 18th century onwards. Many families made watch parts at home.
363.m: Neuchâtel is famous for its watches.

364.q: Which two watchmaking towns in Neuchâtel are UNESCO World Heritage Sites?
364.e: After fires in the 19th century, both towns were rebuilt entirely around watchmaking: with straight streets and houses with large windows for good light. They have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 2009.
364.m: La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are UNESCO World Heritage watchmaking towns.

366.q: Which festival does Geneva celebrate every December, often with chocolate pots?
366.e: The Escalade recalls the night in December 1602 when Geneva fought off an attack by Savoy. According to legend, Mère Royaume poured hot soup on the attackers. That is why chocolate pots are smashed today.
366.m: Geneva celebrates the Escalade of 1602 with the soup pot.

367.q: Which reformer shaped Geneva in the 16th century?
367.e: Calvin made Geneva a centre of the Reformation. Many religious refugees came to the city. That is why Geneva was also called the “Protestant Rome”.

370.q: Which is the youngest canton in Switzerland?
370.e: The canton of Jura has only existed since 1979. That makes it the youngest of the 26 cantons.
370.m: Jura is the youngest canton in Switzerland.

371.q: Which canton did Jura separate from?
371.e: The northern Jura had belonged to the canton of Bern since 1815. Many French-speaking, Catholic people of the Jura did not feel represented and fought for decades for their own canton.

373.q: Who leads the municipal government in many Swiss municipalities?
373.e: Every municipality has its own government, usually called the municipal council. At its head is the municipal president. In towns the role is often called town president.
373.m: Many municipalities are led by the municipal president.

374.q: How often is the National Council elected?
374.e: National Council elections take place every four years in October. In most cantons the members of the Council of States are elected on the same day.
374.m: The National Council is elected every four years.

376.q: Which animal has feathers and lays eggs?
376.e: All birds have feathers and lay eggs. The hen is a bird, even though it can hardly fly.
376.m: An animal with feathers that lays eggs is a bird.

377.q: Which is the largest lake that lies entirely in Switzerland?
377.e: Lake Geneva and Lake Constance are bigger, but parts of them lie in France, or in Germany and Austria. The largest lake entirely on Swiss soil is Lake Neuchâtel.
377.m: Lake Neuchâtel is the largest lake lying entirely in Switzerland.

379.q: At least how often should you brush your teeth?
379.e: Dentists recommend brushing your teeth in the morning and in the evening. That removes bits of food and plaque, which could otherwise cause tooth decay.
379.m: You should brush your teeth in the morning and in the evening.

a: Food is mixed with gastric juice and broken down
380.e: In the stomach, food is mixed with acid and digestive juices and kneaded. Then the mush moves into the gut, where the nutrients pass into the blood.
380.m: In the stomach, food is partly digested.

381.q: Why is getting enough sleep important?
a: The body recovers, and the brain processes what you have learnt
So that your hair grows faster
381.e: During sleep the body and brain recover. What you learnt during the day is strengthened in your memory. That is why children and teenagers need particularly a lot of sleep.
381.m: Sleep is for recovery and strengthens what you have learnt.

383.q: What colour is the current 10-franc note?
383.e: Every Swiss banknote has its own colour: 10 francs yellow, 20 red, 50 green, 100 blue, 200 brown and 1000 purple. This makes them easy to tell apart.
383.m: The 10-franc note is yellow, the 20 red, the 50 green and the 100 blue.

384.q: Why is it worth checking your subscriptions regularly?
a: Small monthly amounts add up to a lot of money over the year
Because subscriptions become free every year
384.e: Streaming, music, games, mobile phone: each subscription may only cost a few francs a month. But added together over a whole year, they quickly come to a large amount.
384.m: Check your subscriptions, small amounts add up.

385.q: What is an emergency fund for?
a: To pay for unexpected costs without getting into debt
To go on holiday every month
385.e: A broken phone, a dentist's bill or an extra payment: unexpected costs happen. If you have money put aside, you do not need to take out an expensive loan. It is often recommended to save several months' worth of spending.
385.m: An emergency fund protects you from debt.

386.q: What is a savings account for?
a: To put money aside for longer
386.e: In a savings account you put aside money you don't need straight away. There is often a little more interest than on an everyday account.
386.m: In a savings account you put money aside.

a: Sending money from one account to another
387.e: With a transfer you tell the bank to send money to another account, for example to pay a bill. You need the IBAN of the person receiving it.
387.m: With a transfer, money goes from one account to another.

388.q: What do many banks offer especially for young people?
388.e: Many banks have accounts for children and young people, often without account fees and with their own card. That way you learn early how to handle money. For under-18s, the parents usually have to agree.
388.m: A youth account is a cheap way to start.

391.q: Who levies the direct federal tax on income?
a: The Confederation, but the cantons collect it
391.e: The direct federal tax is a tax of the Confederation. So that people don't have to fill in two tax returns, the cantons assess and collect it together with their own taxes.
391.m: Federal tax, collected by the canton.

394.q: Where do you get medicines that the doctor has prescribed for you?
394.e: At the pharmacy you get medicines and can also ask for advice. You should only take medicines the way the doctor or the pharmacy explains.
394.m: You get medicines at the pharmacy and take them as prescribed.

395.q: What do you need your health insurance card for?
a: You show it at the doctor's or pharmacy so the costs can be billed
395.e: Your insurance card shows your insurance number and your health insurer. Doctors' surgeries and pharmacies need this information to bill the costs.
395.m: Always have your insurance card with you.

a: You first phone a medical advice line before seeing a doctor and get a lower premium for it
You may only be ill by phone
You get a free mobile phone
The health insurer phones you every day
