396.e: With Telmed, you first contact a telephone advice service before visiting a doctor. The experts tell you whether and where treatment is needed. In return the premium is cheaper. Emergencies are excluded.
396.m: With the Telmed model you phone first and pay less for it.

398.q: Who makes bread and croissants in the bakehouse?
398.e: Bakers and confectioners often start very early in the morning so that the bread is fresh. The apprenticeship lasts three years and ends with the EFZ.
398.m: The bakery makes bread and croissants.

399.q: What can you do at a careers fair?
a: Get to know lots of jobs and talk to apprentices and companies
399.e: At careers fairs, many jobs and companies present themselves. You can try out tasks and ask apprentices directly what their everyday working life is like.
399.m: At a careers fair you can discover jobs.

400.q: What is true about apprentices' wages?
a: They are set in the apprenticeship contract and usually rise each year
They are always as high as for fully trained workers
400.e: Apprentices receive a wage that is written in the apprenticeship contract. It is lower than for trained workers, because you are still learning, and usually rises from year to year. There are big differences between jobs.
400.m: An apprentice's wage rises each year of training.

402.q: What is the rule at a zebra crossing in Switzerland?
a: Pedestrians have right of way, but always look first
Cars always have right of way
You must not cross the road there
402.e: Anyone clearly wanting to cross at a zebra crossing has right of way. Even so: wait until the cars stop and make eye contact with the drivers.
402.m: At a zebra crossing you have right of way, but look first.

403.q: Which emergency number works all over Europe, including Switzerland?
403.e: 112 is the European emergency number. In Switzerland it puts you through to the police. The ambulance (144) and fire brigade (118) have their own numbers.
403.m: 112 is the emergency number all over Europe.

a: Edible food that is thrown away
404.e: A large share of food ends up in the bin even though it could still be eaten. Tips against it: shop carefully, use up leftovers and, at the best-before date, smell and taste rather than throwing food away at once.
404.m: You avoid food waste by planning and using up leftovers.

406.q: What does the abbreviation CH stand for?
406.e: CH is the abbreviation of the Latin name of Switzerland: Confoederatio Helvetica, the Swiss Confederation. Latin is neutral and is not one of the four national languages.

407.q: Since when has the franc been the shared currency of Switzerland?
407.e: Before 1850, there were lots of different coins from the cantons and towns in Switzerland. With the new federal state, the franc was introduced as a single currency.

408.q: Who gave Switzerland a new order with the Act of Mediation in 1803?
408.e: The Helvetic Republic was divided by quarrels. In 1803, Napoleon arranged a new constitution, the Act of Mediation. New cantons were created, such as Aargau, Thurgau, St Gallen, the Grisons, Ticino and Vaud.
408.m: In 1803, Napoleon gave Switzerland the Act of Mediation.

409.q: Which route did the first railway running entirely in Switzerland travel in 1847?
409.e: In 1847, the first railway inside Switzerland connected Zurich with Baden. It is called the “Spanish Bun Railway” because it supposedly brought a popular pastry from Baden quickly to Zurich.
409.m: In 1847, the Spanish Bun Railway ran from Zurich to Baden.

411.q: Which dinosaur was a huge meat-eater with strikingly small arms?
411.e: Tyrannosaurus rex was one of the largest meat-eaters on land. Its arms were tiny compared with its body, but its bite was extremely strong.
411.m: T. rex had a big head and small arms.

a: Remains or traces of prehistoric living things turned to stone
412.e: If animals or plants are quickly covered with mud after they die, fossils can form over millions of years. This is how we know what dinosaurs looked like.
412.m: A fossil is a prehistoric remain turned to stone.

413.q: Which large, hairy animal with long tusks lived in the Ice Age?
413.e: Mammoths were related to elephants and had thick fur against the cold. Mammoth bones and teeth have also been found in Switzerland.
413.m: The mammoth was a furry Ice Age elephant.

414.q: What did the Ice Age glaciers shape in Switzerland?
a: Many valleys and lakes, for example Lake Zurich
414.e: During the ice ages huge glaciers covered large parts of Switzerland. They carved out valleys and left behind lakes, hills and big boulders.
414.m: Ice Age glaciers shaped the landscape.

415.q: Which kind of human lived in Europe before modern humans?
415.e: Neanderthals lived in Europe for hundreds of thousands of years and were adapted to the cold. Homo habilis and Australopithecus lived only in Africa, Peking Man in Asia.
415.m: Neanderthals were early humans in Europe.

416.q: What was typical of an ice age?
a: Large parts of the Earth were covered with ice, and it was much colder
416.e: During ice ages it was much colder on average, and glaciers spread far. The last ice age ended about 12,000 years ago.
416.m: In the Ice Age it was cold and there was a lot of glacier ice.

417.q: Bronze gave its name to a whole period. What is it made of?
417.e: Bronze is a mixture of copper and a little tin and is harder than pure copper. From about 2200 BC people made tools, weapons and jewellery from it.
417.m: Bronze is made of copper and tin.

419.q: Who was the highest god of the ancient Greeks?
419.e: The Greeks believed in many gods who lived on Mount Olympus. Zeus was their king and, according to legend, hurled thunderbolts. Thor and Odin are Norse gods.
419.m: The father of the Greek gods was Zeus.

420.q: With which special war animals did the general Hannibal cross the Alps?
420.e: More than 2000 years ago, Hannibal of Carthage crossed the Alps with an army and war elephants to attack Rome. Many of the animals did not survive the cold.
420.m: Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants.

421.q: What is the famous amphitheatre in Rome where gladiators fought called?
421.e: The Colosseum had room for tens of thousands of spectators. Gladiator fights and animal hunts took place there. Today it is one of the best-known buildings in the world.

422.q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is still standing today?
422.e: Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, only the Pyramids of Giza have survived. The others were destroyed by earthquakes, fire or decay.
422.m: The pyramids are the only surviving wonder of the ancient world.

423.q: Which language did the ancient Romans speak?
423.e: The Romans spoke Latin. Italian, French, Spanish and Romansh developed from it. Many German and English words also come from Latin, for example the German ‘Fenster’ (window) and ‘Mauer’ (wall).

a: The last queen of ancient Egypt
A pharaoh who built the pyramids
424.e: Cleopatra ruled in the 1st century BC. She allied herself with Caesar and later with Mark Antony. After her death in 30 BC, Egypt became a Roman province.
424.m: Cleopatra was the last queen of Egypt.

425.q: What is Alexander the Great known for?
a: He conquered a huge empire from Greece to India
He built the Great Wall of China
425.e: Alexander became king of Macedonia at 20. In only about ten years he conquered the Persian Empire and marched as far as India. He died aged just 32.
425.m: Alexander the Great conquered an empire reaching as far as India.

426.q: Which huge border fortification was built in China from ancient times onwards?
426.e: The first sections of wall were built more than 2000 years ago. Over many centuries they were extended and strengthened. Most of the parts you can see today date from the later Ming period.
426.m: The Great Wall of China was built over centuries.

427.q: What is the protective metal clothing that knights wore called?
427.e: Armour protected the knight in battle. It was heavy and expensive. You needed help to put it on.

428.q: What did monks write their books on in the Middle Ages?
a: On parchment made from animal skin
428.e: Parchment was made from animal skin. With a quill and ink, monks carefully copied books and decorated them with colourful pictures.
428.m: In the Middle Ages books were written with a quill on parchment.

a: A merchant from Venice who travelled all the way to China
429.e: Marco Polo travelled to China in the 13th century and lived there for many years. His account of his travels made Europe curious about Asia.
429.m: Marco Polo travelled from Venice to China.

a: A young Frenchwoman who led an army in the Hundred Years’ War
430.e: In 1429 Joan of Arc helped France to free the city of Orléans. Later she was captured and burned in 1431. Today she is a national heroine of France.
430.m: Joan of Arc was the heroine of Orléans.

431.q: What were serfs in the Middle Ages?
a: Farmers who depended on a lord and were not free to move away
431.e: Serfs worked the land of a lord and had to give him payments and services. Without his permission they could neither move away nor marry.
431.m: Serfs were farmers who were not free.

433.q: In which year did the Ottomans conquer Constantinople, today’s Istanbul?
433.e: With the conquest of Constantinople, the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire came to an end. The city became the capital of the Ottoman Empire.

435.q: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
435.e: In 1969 Neil Armstrong was the first to climb out of the lunar module. Buzz Aldrin followed shortly after him. Yuri Gagarin was the first person in space in 1961.
435.m: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.

436.q: Which means of transport changed travel in the 19th century and runs on rails?
436.e: With the railway people could suddenly travel much faster and further. Goods could be transported cheaply. In Switzerland a dense rail network grew up from 1847.
436.m: The railway took over in the 19th century.

437.q: Who received a patent for the telephone in 1876?
437.e: Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876. Other inventors were working on it too. Today almost everyone carries a phone in their pocket.
437.m: Bell received the patent for the telephone in 1876.

438.q: Which French ruler crowned himself emperor in 1804?
438.e: Napoleon was a successful general of the Revolution and became emperor in 1804. He conquered large parts of Europe, and Switzerland too was under his influence. In 1815 he was finally defeated.

439.q: What is meant by the Holocaust?
a: The genocide of about six million European Jews by Nazi Germany
439.e: In the Second World War the Nazis systematically persecuted and murdered Jews and other groups, such as the Sinti and Roma. Remembering this should help make sure it never happens again.
439.m: The Holocaust was a genocide that we must never forget.

441.q: What is Mahatma Gandhi known for?
a: His non-violent struggle for India’s independence
Being the first person on the Moon
441.e: Gandhi relied on peaceful resistance, such as boycotts and protest marches. In 1947 India became independent from Great Britain. His example also influenced Martin Luther King.
441.m: Gandhi led India to independence without violence.

443.e: Magnets mainly attract iron and steel, for example paper clips or nails. Wood, paper and plastic do not react to magnets.

444.q: What is the force called that slowly brings a rolling bike to a stop when you stop pedalling?
444.e: Friction arises between the tyres and the road and in the air. It works against the movement and slows it down. But without friction you could not brake or walk either.

445.q: Which organisation aims to keep peace all over the world?
445.e: Almost all the countries in the world work together in the UN. They want to prevent wars, protect human rights and help people in need.
445.m: In the UN, countries work together for peace.

446.q: In which Swiss city do especially many international organisations have their headquarters?
446.e: The UN, the Red Cross, the World Health Organization and many other organisations work in Geneva. That is why peace talks are often held there.
446.m: Geneva is the city of international organisations.

447.q: Roughly how many states are members of the UN?
447.e: Almost all the states in the world are members of the United Nations: there are 193. Switzerland has been a member since 2002.

448.q: In which city are the UN headquarters?
448.e: The UN headquarters are in New York. Its most important seat in Europe is in Geneva.
448.m: The UN headquarters are in New York.

449.q: Which statement about the European Union (EU) is true?
a: Many European states work closely together; Switzerland is not a member
All the countries in the world are members
449.e: In the EU, 27 European states work closely together politically and economically. Switzerland is not a member, but it has many agreements with the EU.
449.m: Switzerland is not in the EU, but is linked to it through agreements.

a: A defence alliance of states from North America and Europe
450.e: In NATO the members promise to stand by each other if one is attacked. Neutral Switzerland is not a member.

a: Represents their own country in another state
454.e: Ambassadors look after the relations between two countries. They work in an embassy, usually in the capital of the host country.
454.m: An embassy represents a country abroad.

455.e: The word comes from Greek: ‘demos’ means people, ‘kratos’ means power. In a democracy people help decide who governs and what the rules are.
455.m: Democracy means that the people decide.

456.q: What is especially important in a democracy?
a: Freedom of opinion and freedom of the press
That only one party is allowed
456.e: In a democracy you may say what you think freely, and the media may report critically. Only then can everyone form their own opinion.
456.m: Democracy needs free opinions and free media.

457.q: What is the basic idea of communism?
a: Factories and land should belong to everyone together, with no rich and poor classes
Everyone should own as much as they like
457.e: Communism is a political idea according to which factories, land and machines belong to the community. In practice, communist states were usually ruled by a single party and its leaders.
457.m: The aim of communism is shared ownership.

458.e: In it Marx and Engels described the inequality between workers and factory owners and called for a new society. The book had a great influence on the 20th century.
458.m: Marx and Engels wrote the Communist Manifesto in 1848.

459.q: Which large state was ruled by communists from 1922 to 1991?
459.e: The Soviet Union was a huge state, with Russia as its largest part. In 1991 it broke up into many independent countries.
459.m: The Soviet Union existed from 1922 to 1991.

a: A communist-ruled state in eastern Germany from 1949 to 1990
460.e: After the Second World War Germany was divided. The GDR (East Germany) was ruled by the SED, and people were not allowed to travel freely to the West. Germany was reunified in 1990.
460.m: The GDR was the state in East Germany from 1949 to 1990.

464.q: In which large country does a communist party still rule as the only party today?
464.e: The Communist Party has ruled China since 1949. Today the economy is partly a market economy, but politically the party is in charge.
464.m: China is a one-party state of the Communist Party.

a: One person or a small group has all the power and the people may not vote freely
465.e: In a dictatorship one person or a small group decides alone. Anyone who disagrees can be punished. The opposite is democracy.
465.m: In a dictatorship a few have the power and there are no free elections.

466.q: Where does the word “dictator” come from?
a: From ancient Rome: an office with great power in times of emergency
466.e: In ancient Rome a dictator could be appointed in times of emergency and had almost unlimited power for a short time. Today the word is used for rulers who govern without any checks.
466.m: The dictator was originally a Roman office for emergencies.

a: The state controls or bans what may appear in the media, in books or on the internet
467.e: In dictatorships critical newspapers, books or websites are often banned. In Switzerland the constitution protects freedom of expression and freedom of the media.
467.m: Censorship is the control of opinion.

469.q: Who ruled Germany as a dictator from 1933 to 1945?
469.e: The National Socialists under Hitler set up a dictatorship, persecuted people who thought differently and committed the Holocaust. The Second World War, which Germany started, cost millions of people their lives.
469.m: From 1933 to 1945 Germany was ruled by the Nazi dictatorship.

473.q: What is the Christian place of worship called?
473.e: In church, Christians hold services, for example on Sundays, at Christmas and at Easter.

474.q: What is the holy scripture of Christians called?
474.e: The Bible is made up of the Old and the New Testament. The New Testament tells about the life of Jesus.
474.m: The holy scripture of Christianity is the Bible.

475.q: What do Christians remember at Pentecost?
a: The sending of the Holy Spirit
475.e: Pentecost is celebrated 50 days after Easter. According to the Bible, the disciples received the Holy Spirit and began to spread the message of Jesus.

476.q: What is the head of the Roman Catholic Church called?
476.e: The Pope leads the Catholic Church around the world and lives in the Vatican in Rome. He is elected by the cardinals.
476.m: The head of the Catholic Church is the Pope in Rome.

477.q: Who has protected the Pope in the Vatican for over 500 years?
477.e: The Pontifical Swiss Guard was founded in 1506. Its members are young Catholic Swiss men and wear colourful uniforms.
477.m: The Swiss Guard has protected the Pope since 1506.

478.e: The original word comes from Greek. The four Gospels in the New Testament tell about the life and teaching of Jesus.

479.q: What is the month of fasting in Islam called?
479.e: During Ramadan many devout Muslims eat and drink nothing from dawn until sunset. In the evening people often eat together.
479.m: The month of fasting in Islam is called Ramadan.

480.q: Who is the most important prophet for Muslims?
480.e: According to Islamic belief, Muhammad received the revelations written in the Quran in the 7th century.
480.m: The most important prophet in Islam is Muhammad.

481.q: According to tradition, how many times a day do devout Muslims pray?
481.e: Prayer at set times is one of the five pillars of Islam. On Fridays there is a special shared prayer in the mosque.
481.m: Devout Muslims pray five times a day.

482.q: In which language was the Quran originally written?
482.e: The Quran was passed down in Arabic. It has been translated into many languages, but in prayer it is usually recited in Arabic.
482.m: The Quran was written in Arabic.

483.q: What is the great pilgrimage to Mecca called?
483.e: Anyone who is healthy and can afford it should make the pilgrimage to Mecca once in their life. Millions of people gather for it every year.
483.m: The pilgrimage to Mecca is called the Hajj.

a: A tower at a mosque from which the call to prayer is traditionally made
484.e: The muezzin traditionally calls people to prayer from the minaret. In Switzerland a popular vote in 2009 decided that no new minarets may be built.
484.m: A minaret is the tower of a mosque.

486.q: In which religion are the gods Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva worshipped, among others?
486.e: Hinduism is mainly found in India and has many gods and goddesses. Among the most important are Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.
486.m: Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are Hindu gods.

487.q: What is the weekly day of rest in Judaism called?
487.e: The Sabbath lasts from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Many Jewish people rest, pray and eat together with their family.
487.m: The Sabbath lasts from Friday evening to Saturday evening.

488.q: What is the Hindu place of worship called?
488.e: In a Hindu temple there are statues of gods. Believers bring flowers, fruit or light as offerings.
488.m: The Hindu place of worship is the temple.

498.q: Which animal is seen around the world as a symbol of peace?
498.e: The white dove, often with an olive branch, is a well-known symbol of peace. You can see it on posters, flags and stamps.
498.m: The white dove is a symbol of peace.

499.q: What does peace between countries mean?
a: There is no war; disputes are settled without violence
All countries have the same flag
499.e: Peace means that countries solve their problems through talks and treaties instead of with weapons. The UN and Switzerland work for this.
499.m: Peace means settling disputes without violence.

500.q: How many neighbouring countries does Switzerland have?
500.e: Switzerland borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
500.m: Switzerland has five neighbouring countries: Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.

a: The rights and well-being of children around the world
501.e: UNICEF is the United Nations children’s agency. It helps children with vaccinations, schools, clean water and protection in emergencies.
501.m: UNICEF is the UN’s children’s agency.

502.q: Which UN organisation based in Geneva looks after health around the world?
502.e: The WHO supports countries in the fight against diseases, for example with vaccination programmes. Its headquarters are in Geneva.
502.m: The WHO looks after health and is based in Geneva.

a: A person who has had to leave their home because of war or persecution
A sportsperson running away from the ball
503.e: Refugees flee from danger to life and limb. The Geneva Refugee Convention protects their rights, and the UN refugee agency UNHCR supports them.
503.m: A refugee flees from war or persecution.

504.q: In which city are the most important EU institutions based?
504.e: The EU Commission and the Council of the EU are based in Brussels in Belgium. The EU Parliament also meets in Strasbourg.
504.m: The most important EU institutions are based in Brussels.

505.q: What are sanctions in world politics?
a: Penalties against a state, for example trade bans
505.e: With sanctions, states want to put on pressure, for example when a country breaks international law. Often trade is restricted or assets are frozen.
505.m: Sanctions are penalties meant to put on pressure.

509.q: Which colour is often linked with communism?
509.e: The red flag was the sign of many workers' movements and communist states, for example the Soviet Union and China.
509.m: The colour red is often linked with communism.

510.q: What used to separate East and West Berlin?
510.e: The communist government of the GDR built a wall right through Berlin so that people would not go to the West. It was opened in 1989.
510.m: Berlin was divided by a wall.

511.q: Which sign was on the flag of the Soviet Union?
a: A hammer and sickle with a star
511.e: The hammer and sickle stood for the workers in the factories and the farmers in the fields. The star above them stood for the party.
511.m: The Soviet flag had a hammer, a sickle and a star.

512.q: In which year was the Berlin Wall built?
512.e: In August 1961 the GDR sealed off East Berlin. The Wall stood for 28 years until it was opened in November 1989.
512.m: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 and fell in 1989.

513.q: Which Caribbean island has been ruled by communists since the revolution of 1959?
513.e: After the revolution Fidel Castro took power in Cuba. To this day the Communist Party rules there as the only party.
513.m: Cuba has been ruled by communists since 1959.

514.q: Who led the revolution in Cuba in 1959?
514.e: Fidel Castro ruled Cuba for almost 50 years. After that his brother Raúl took over the leadership.
514.m: Fidel Castro led the revolution in Cuba in 1959.

515.q: What was known as the “Iron Curtain”?
a: The heavily guarded border between Eastern and Western Europe in the Cold War
A suit of armour from the Middle Ages
515.e: The border between the communist states in the east and the democracies in the west was secured with fences, mines and watchtowers. It opened in 1989.
515.m: The Iron Curtain was the border between East and West in the Cold War.

a: The dictator of the Soviet Union, under whom millions of people were persecuted
516.e: Stalin ruled from the 1920s until his death in 1953. Under his rule millions of people were arrested, locked up in camps or killed.
516.m: Stalin led a dictatorship in the Soviet Union.

a: A system of prison and labour camps in the Soviet Union
517.e: In the camps prisoners had to work in very harsh conditions, and many died. Often just criticising the government was enough to be arrested.
517.m: The Gulag was a system of labour camps in the Soviet Union.

518.q: Who proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949?
518.e: Mao led the Communist Party to victory in the civil war and ruled China until 1976. His policies, such as the “Great Leap Forward”, led to a famine in which a huge number of people died.
518.m: In 1949 Mao founded the People's Republic of China.

519.q: Which Soviet politician introduced reforms such as “glasnost” (openness) from 1985?
519.e: Gorbachev wanted to open up and modernise the Soviet Union. His reforms helped to end the Cold War. In 1990 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
519.m: Gorbachev introduced reforms such as glasnost and perestroika.

521.q: In a dictatorship, can you usually say freely what you think about the government?
521.e: In dictatorships criticism of the rulers is often forbidden. In a democracy like Switzerland you may say your opinion freely.
521.m: In a dictatorship you cannot say your opinion freely.

522.q: In which form of government can the people freely choose who governs?
522.e: In a democracy people freely elect their government and can also vote it out again. In a dictatorship that is not possible.
522.m: In a democracy the people can vote freely.

a: A ruler is excessively worshipped, for example with huge pictures and statues
A club for a singer’s fans
523.e: Many dictators have themselves shown and praised everywhere. This is meant to give the impression that they cannot be replaced and that nobody may criticise them.
523.m: A personality cult is the excessive worship of one person.

524.q: What did the “Stasi” do in East Germany (GDR)?
a: As secret police it spied on the population
524.e: The Stasi tapped phones, read letters and had many informers. Anyone seen as an opponent could be arrested. Today people can look at their Stasi files.
524.m: The Stasi was the secret police of East Germany.

a: The army or generals rule the country without free elections
A democracy with compulsory military service
525.e: The military often takes power in a coup. Parliaments are dissolved and opponents are persecuted.
525.m: In a military dictatorship generals are in power.

a: Rights that every person has, for example freedom and protection from torture
526.e: In 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Dictatorships often violate these rights, for example through arbitrary arrests.

533.q: Who visits many children in Switzerland on 6 December?
533.e: Samichlaus goes back to St Nicholas, a bishop who is said to have helped children and the poor. He is often accompanied by Schmutzli.

534.q: According to the Bible, how many disciples (apostles) did Jesus have?
534.e: The twelve apostles went with Jesus and spread his teaching after his death. Well-known apostles are Peter and John.

535.q: How many candles does an Advent wreath have?
535.e: On each of the four Sundays of Advent before Christmas, one more candle is lit. This is how people count the time until Christmas.

536.q: What is the best-known prayer of Christians called?
a: The Ave prayer in the Quran
536.e: According to the Bible, Jesus taught his disciples the Lord’s Prayer. It is prayed in Catholic and Reformed services.
536.m: The most important Christian prayer is the Lord’s Prayer.

537.q: What does baptism mean in Christianity?
a: Being welcomed into the Christian community, usually with water
537.e: At baptism, water is usually poured over the head. Many children are baptised as babies, some people only as adults.

538.q: What is confirmation in the Reformed Church?
a: Young people confirm their baptism and become full members of the church
538.e: Confirmation usually takes place at about 15 or 16. The Catholic Church has its own confirmation, called Firmung in German.
538.m: Reformed Protestants and Catholics both celebrate confirmation.

539.q: What is the Arabic word for God?
539.e: ‘Allah’ is the Arabic word for God. Arabic-speaking Christians also call God by this name.
539.m: The Arabic word for God is Allah.

540.q: Which meat do devout Muslims not eat?
540.e: According to Islamic food rules, pork is forbidden. Food that is allowed is called ‘halal’.
540.m: Allowed food is called halal, pork is forbidden.

541.q: What does the Islamic Feast of Sacrifice recall?
a: Abraham (Ibrahim), who was ready to obey God
The building of the first mosque
541.e: The Feast of Sacrifice is the most important festival in Islam and takes place during the pilgrimage season. Families celebrate together and share food with those in need.
541.m: The Feast of Sacrifice recalls Abraham.

542.q: In which direction do Muslims pray?
542.e: When praying, Muslims all over the world turn towards the Kaaba in Mecca. In the mosque, a niche in the wall shows the direction.

a: Someone who leads prayer in the mosque
543.e: The imam stands at the front during shared prayer and leads it. He often also gives the sermon on Fridays.
543.m: An imam leads prayer in the mosque.

544.q: On which day of the week does the important shared prayer take place in the mosque?
544.e: Friday prayer at midday is the most important service of the week for many Muslims.
544.m: In Islam the important shared prayer takes place on Friday.

545.q: Which person is equally important in Judaism, Christianity and Islam?
545.e: Abraham, called Ibrahim in Islam, is seen in all three religions as the father of faith. That is why they are also called the ‘Abrahamic religions’.
545.m: Abraham is important in Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

549.q: Which animal is especially respected in Hinduism?
549.e: In Hinduism the cow is seen as sacred because it gives milk and stands for life and kindness. That is why many Hindus do not eat beef.
549.m: In Hinduism the cow is sacred.

550.q: In which country do most Hindus live?
550.e: The great majority of Hindus live in India and Nepal. There are also Hindu temples in Switzerland, for example in Bern.

551.q: What does the Jewish festival of Passover remember?
551.e: According to the Torah, Moses led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt. At Passover people eat unleavened bread called matzah.
551.m: Passover remembers the exodus from Egypt.

552.q: What is the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism called?
552.e: The Dalai Lama works for peace and non-violence. In 1989 he received the Nobel Peace Prize.
552.m: The leader of Tibetan Buddhism is the Dalai Lama.

554.q: What do Jewish boys celebrate at the age of 13?
a: Bar Mitzvah, becoming religiously of age
554.e: With the Bar Mitzvah (for girls the Bat Mitzvah, usually at 12) young people take on responsibility for the religious commandments. They often read from the Torah.
554.m: With a Bar or Bat Mitzvah you count as a religious adult.

555.q: What is the star that the Earth orbits called?
555.e: The sun is a huge star. It gives light and warmth; without it there would be no life on Earth.

556.e: The order is spring, summer, autumn, winter. In spring the first flowers bloom and the days get longer.

a: A body in space that orbits the Earth
A small star that shines by itself
A planet like Earth with cities
557.e: The moon does not shine by itself; it is lit up by the sun. That is why we sometimes see it as a crescent and sometimes as a full moon.

558.e: When it is very cold in the clouds, the water freezes into ice crystals. Lots of them together fall as snowflakes.
558.m: Snow is made of ice crystals.

559.q: Why are there day and night?
a: The Earth spins once on its own axis in about 24 hours
The sun goes out every night
559.e: The side of the Earth facing the sun has day. The side facing away has night.
559.m: Because the Earth spins, there are day and night.

560.q: How long does the Earth take to go once all the way round the sun?
560.e: The Earth takes about 365 days for one orbit. Because it is actually about 365 and a quarter days, there is a leap year every four years.
560.m: The Earth takes 1 year to go once round the sun.

561.q: Which is the longest river that flows entirely within Switzerland?
561.e: The Aare rises in the Bernese Oberland and flows into the Rhine at Koblenz in the canton of Aargau. The Rhine is longer overall, but it also flows through other countries.
561.m: The Aare is the longest river that flows only in Switzerland.

563.q: Why is the natural greenhouse effect important for life?
a: Without it the Earth would be far too cold
563.e: Gases in the atmosphere hold back some of the heat. Without this effect, the average temperature would be well below zero degrees. The problem is that humans are making the effect stronger.
563.m: The natural greenhouse effect is good; too much of it leads to climate change.

564.q: What is the fastest land animal in the world?
564.e: A cheetah can reach over 90 kilometres per hour over short distances. But it cannot keep up this speed for long.
564.m: The fastest land animal is the cheetah.

565.e: Fish take in water through their mouth. In the gills, the oxygen dissolved in the water passes into the blood.

566.q: Which bird can even fly backwards?
566.e: Hummingbirds beat their wings extremely fast. This lets them hover in the air and even fly backwards while they drink nectar.
566.m: The hummingbird can also fly backwards.

567.q: Which Alpine animal has large, curved horns on the male and is a very skilful climber?
567.e: The ibex was almost wiped out in Switzerland and was reintroduced. Today many thousands live in the Alps again. It is also on the coat of arms of the Grisons.
567.m: The ibex is a climbing expert of the Alps.

568.q: How many legs does a spider have?
568.e: Spiders have eight legs and are not insects. Insects such as beetles or bees have six legs.
568.m: A spider has 8 legs, an insect has 6 legs.

569.q: What does it mean when an animal species is “threatened with extinction”?
a: There are only a few animals left, and the species could disappear completely
The animals are dangerous to humans
The species has just been discovered
The animals only live in zoos
569.e: The Red List shows which species are endangered. The reasons are often loss of habitat, poaching or climate change.
569.m: If a species is threatened, it could disappear.

570.q: Why do many birds fly south in autumn?
a: Because they can't find enough food here in winter
Because they are going on holiday
Because they want to see the sea
Because their feathers fall out in winter
570.e: Swallows and storks, for example, eat insects, which are hard to find in winter. That is why they fly thousands of kilometres to Africa and return in spring.

571.q: What do all vertebrates have in common?
571.e: Vertebrates include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Insects, snails and worms have no backbone.
571.m: Vertebrates are animals with a backbone.

572.e: Bats fly with skin membranes between their fingers. At night they find their way with ultrasound, in other words with echoes.
572.m: The bat is a flying mammal.

579.q: Which organ cleans the blood and makes urine?
579.e: The two kidneys filter large amounts of blood every day. Waste products and extra water leave the body as urine.

580.q: Which is the largest internal organ of the human body?
580.e: The liver sits on the right in the upper belly. It breaks down poisons, stores energy and makes bile for digestion.
580.m: The largest internal organ is the liver.

581.q: What do red blood cells carry?
581.e: Red blood cells contain the red pigment haemoglobin. It picks up oxygen in the lungs and releases it all over the body.

583.q: Which large lake lies near Geneva and Lausanne?
583.e: Lake Geneva is the largest lake in the Alps. The southern shore belongs to France, the northern shore to Switzerland.
583.m: Geneva and Lausanne lie on Lake Geneva.

584.q: Which mountain range covers a large part of Switzerland?
584.e: About 60 per cent of Switzerland lies in the Alps. There are high mountains, glaciers and many valleys there.

585.q: Which is the largest city in Switzerland?
585.e: Zurich has the most inhabitants. Bern is the federal city, but much smaller.
585.m: The largest city in Switzerland is Zurich.

586.q: Which neighbouring country lies to the north of Switzerland?
586.e: Switzerland borders Germany to the north, France to the west, Italy to the south and Austria and Liechtenstein to the east.
586.m: Germany lies to the north, Italy to the south.

587.q: Which river flows in a large loop around the old town of Bern?
587.e: Bern’s old town lies on a peninsula in a loop of the Aare. In summer many people swim in the Aare.

588.q: What colour are the signposts for normal hiking trails in Switzerland?
588.e: Yellow signposts show hiking trails. Mountain trails are marked white-red-white, alpine trails white-blue-white.
588.m: Signposts for hiking trails are yellow.

589.q: Which three large landscapes make up Switzerland?
589.e: The Jura lies in the north-west, the flatter Central Plateau in the middle and the Alps in the south. The Alps cover the largest area.
589.m: Switzerland consists of the Jura, the Central Plateau and the Alps.

590.q: In which landscape do most people in Switzerland live?
590.e: The Central Plateau is flatter and easy to reach. That is why most cities, such as Zurich, Bern and Lausanne, are there.
590.m: Most people live on the Central Plateau.

591.q: Into which sea does the Rhône flow?
591.e: The Rhône flows from Valais through Lake Geneva to France and into the Mediterranean.
591.m: The Rhône flows through Valais and Lake Geneva into the Mediterranean.

592.q: Into which sea does the Rhine flow?
592.e: The Rhine rises in the Grisons, flows via Basel to Germany and in the Netherlands into the North Sea.
592.m: The Rhine flows into the North Sea.

593.q: Which Alpine pass connects Valais with Italy and has a famous railway tunnel from 1906?
593.e: When it opened, the Simplon Tunnel was the longest railway tunnel in the world. A road also runs over the pass.
593.m: The Simplon connects Valais with Italy.

594.q: In which canton do people mainly speak Italian?
594.e: Ticino lies south of the Alps and is the only purely Italian-speaking canton. Italian is also spoken in some valleys of the Grisons.

595.q: Where is the lowest point in Switzerland?
595.e: Lake Maggiore lies only about 193 metres above sea level. The highest point, the Dufourspitze, is over 4600 metres high.
595.m: The lowest point in Switzerland is on Lake Maggiore.

596.q: Which is the largest city in French-speaking Switzerland?
596.e: Geneva is the second largest city in Switzerland. Lausanne follows as the second largest city in Romandy.
596.m: The largest city in Romandy is Geneva.

597.q: About how many people live in Switzerland?
597.e: Switzerland’s population has grown strongly in recent decades and is now about 9 million people.

598.q: About how large is the area of Switzerland?
598.e: Switzerland covers about 41,300 square kilometres. Even so, it is a long journey from Geneva to the Engadine, because there are many mountains in between.
598.m: Switzerland has an area of about 41,000 km².

a: A warm, dry wind that blows down from the Alps
A cold north wind in winter
A fog on the Central Plateau
601.e: With the föhn, air rises over the Alps, loses its moisture as rain on one side and comes down warm and dry on the other side. The view is then often very clear.
601.m: The föhn is a warm wind blowing down the mountains.

602.q: About how much of Switzerland is covered by forest?
602.e: About a third of Switzerland is forest. In the mountains it also protects against avalanches and rockfall.
602.m: About a third of Switzerland is covered by forest.

604.q: What is the capital of France?
604.e: Paris is the biggest city in France. The Eiffel Tower and the Louvre are there.
604.m: The capital of France is Paris.

605.q: What is the capital of Italy?
605.e: Rome was once the centre of the Roman Empire. Vatican City lies in the middle of Rome.
605.m: The capital of Italy is Rome.

606.q: What is the capital of Germany?
606.e: Berlin is the biggest city in Germany. The Berlin Wall stood here until 1989.
606.m: The capital of Germany is Berlin.

607.q: What is the capital of Austria?
607.e: Vienna is on the Danube and is famous for palaces, music and coffee houses.
607.m: The capital of Austria is Vienna.

608.q: Which sea lies to the south of Spain, Italy and Greece?
608.e: The Mediterranean lies between Europe, Africa and Asia. Many people from Switzerland spend their holidays there.
608.m: The Mediterranean lies to the south of Europe.

609.q: Which language is spoken in France?
609.e: French is also one of the four national languages of Switzerland. It is spoken in western Switzerland, the Romandy.

610.q: Which is the longest river in Europe?
610.e: The Volga flows through Russia and is about 3500 kilometres long. It flows into the Caspian Sea.
610.m: The longest river in Europe is the Volga.

611.q: Which is the highest mountain in the Alps?
611.e: Mont Blanc is on the border between France and Italy and is over 4800 metres high.
611.m: The highest peak in the Alps is Mont Blanc.

612.q: Which Italian city is built on many islands and has canals instead of streets?
612.e: In Venice people travel through the canals by boat and gondola. There are no cars in the old town.
612.m: Venice is famous for canals and gondolas.

613.q: Which country is shaped like a boot on the map?
613.e: Italy sticks out into the Mediterranean like a boot. The island of Sicily lies off the “toe of the boot”.
613.m: Italy is shaped like a boot.

614.q: Which river flows through Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade?
614.e: The Danube flows through ten countries, more than any other river in the world, and into the Black Sea.
614.m: The Danube flows through many capitals into the Black Sea.

615.q: What is the capital of Spain?
615.e: Madrid lies almost exactly in the middle of Spain. Barcelona is the second-largest city.
615.m: The capital of Spain is Madrid.

616.e: Crete is the largest Greek island. Majorca belongs to Spain, Sardinia to Italy and Corsica to France.

617.q: Which is the smallest country in the world?
617.e: Vatican City lies in the middle of Rome and is much smaller than one square kilometre. The Pope lives there, guarded by the Swiss Guard.
617.m: The smallest country in the world is Vatican City.

620.q: Which strait separates Spain from Africa?
620.e: At the narrowest point, Europe and Africa are only about 14 kilometres apart. The strait connects the Mediterranean with the Atlantic.
620.m: The Strait of Gibraltar separates Europe and Africa.

621.q: Which big city lies on two continents, in Europe and in Asia?
621.e: Istanbul lies on both sides of the Bosporus. One part of the city belongs to Europe, the other to Asia.
621.m: Istanbul lies in Europe and in Asia.

622.q: What is the capital of Norway?
622.e: Stockholm is the capital of Sweden, Copenhagen that of Denmark and Helsinki that of Finland.
622.m: The capital of Norway is Oslo.

623.q: Which mountain range is often seen as the border between Europe and Asia?
623.e: The Urals run from north to south through Russia. West of them counts as Europe, east of them as Asia.
623.m: The Urals are seen as the border between Europe and Asia.

624.q: What is the capital of Liechtenstein?
624.e: Liechtenstein lies between Switzerland and Austria and uses the Swiss franc. Its capital is Vaduz.
624.m: The capital of Liechtenstein is Vaduz.

625.q: How many continents are usually counted?
625.e: Usually people count Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America. In some countries continents are counted a little differently.

626.e: Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe, surrounded by Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.

628.e: Antarctica, around the South Pole, is almost completely covered in ice. Penguins and seals live there, for example.

629.q: Where do penguins live in the wild?
a: Mainly in the southern hemisphere, for example in Antarctica
629.e: Penguins live almost only in the southern hemisphere. There are no penguins at the North Pole; polar bears live there.
629.m: Penguins live in the south, polar bears in the north.

630.q: Which is the highest mountain in the world?
630.e: Mount Everest in the Himalayas is about 8850 metres high. It lies on the border between Nepal and China.
630.m: The highest mountain in the world is Mount Everest.

631.q: Which river is usually thought to be the longest in the world?
631.e: The Nile flows through Africa to Egypt and into the Mediterranean. Depending on how it is measured, the Amazon in South America is about as long.
631.m: The Nile is usually seen as the longest river in the world.

632.q: What is the largest hot desert in the world called?
632.e: The Sahara lies in northern Africa and is almost as big as the USA. Antarctica counts as an even bigger cold desert.
632.m: The largest hot desert is the Sahara.

633.q: Which country has the most inhabitants?
633.e: Since 2023 India has had more inhabitants than China, over 1.4 billion people.

634.q: Which is the largest country in the world by area?
634.e: Russia stretches from Europe to the Pacific and has eleven time zones.
634.m: The largest country in the world is Russia.

a: An imaginary line around the middle of the Earth
635.e: The equator divides the Earth into a northern and a southern hemisphere. It is warm there all year round.
635.m: The equator runs around the middle of the Earth.

636.q: Where is the largest rainforest in the world?
a: Along the Amazon in South America
636.e: The Amazon rainforest lies mainly in Brazil. Countless species of animals and plants live there.
636.m: The largest rainforest is along the Amazon.

637.q: What is the capital of the USA?
637.e: New York is the largest city in the USA, but the capital is Washington, D.C. The White House is there.
637.m: The capital of the USA is Washington, D.C.

638.e: Asia is the largest continent and also has the most people. It includes China, India and Japan, for example.

639.q: What is the capital of Australia?
639.e: Sydney and Melbourne are bigger, but Canberra was built as the capital, partly as a compromise between those two cities.
639.m: The capital of Australia is Canberra.

640.q: Where is the deepest known point in the world's oceans?
a: In the Mariana Trench in the Pacific
640.e: The Mariana Trench is almost 11 kilometres deep. Mount Everest would fit inside without its peak sticking out of the water.
640.m: The deepest point in the oceans is the Mariana Trench.

641.q: What are lines of longitude and latitude used for?
a: To pinpoint any place on Earth exactly
641.e: Lines of latitude run parallel to the equator, lines of longitude from the North Pole to the South Pole. With both numbers you can find any point on Earth; that is also how GPS works.

642.q: Why is it summer in Australia in December?
a: Because Australia is in the southern hemisphere and the Earth's axis is tilted
Because Australia is closer to the sun
Because there are no seasons there
Because a different calendar is used there
642.e: The Earth's axis is tilted. In December the southern hemisphere is tilted towards the sun and has summer, while we have winter.
642.m: In the southern hemisphere the seasons are the other way round.

643.q: Which canal links the Atlantic with the Pacific?
643.e: The Panama Canal in Central America saves ships the long journey around South America. The Suez Canal links the Mediterranean with the Red Sea.
643.m: The Panama Canal links the Atlantic with the Pacific.

645.q: Which emergency number belongs to this vehicle?
645.e: This is a fire engine. In Switzerland you can reach the fire brigade on 118.
645.m: You can reach the fire brigade on 118.

646.q: What does this symbol stand for?
646.e: The three arrows in a circle stand for recycling. New products are made from collected glass, paper or PET.

647.q: What does the bee do at the flower?
a: It collects nectar and pollinates the flower
It builds a nest out of the flower
647.e: Bees collect nectar and pollen. In doing so they carry pollen from flower to flower, and this is how fruit develops.

648.e: Inside the pupa the caterpillar becomes a butterfly. This complete transformation is called metamorphosis.
648.m: The transformation of a caterpillar into a butterfly is called metamorphosis.

649.q: What appears when the sun shines on raindrops?
649.e: Sunlight is bent in the raindrops and split into its colours. For this, the sun has to be behind you.
649.m: Sun and rain make a rainbow.

a: The magnet is attracting the paper clip
650.e: Paper clips are usually made of steel, which means iron. This is attracted by magnets.

651.q: Which three states of water can you see?
651.e: Water can be solid (ice), liquid (water) or a gas (steam). These are called states of matter.
651.m: Water exists as ice, as a liquid and as steam.

652.q: Why do you see the lightning first in a thunderstorm and only then hear the thunder?
a: Your ears are slower than your eyes
652.e: Lightning and thunder happen at the same time. The light reaches you almost instantly, while the sound takes about three seconds per kilometre.

653.e: You collect coins in a piggy bank for a bigger goal.
653.m: You save money with a piggy bank.

654.q: What is the Swiss app called that lets you pay with your phone?
654.e: With TWINT you pay in shops or send money to friends, straight from your phone.
654.m: With TWINT you can pay with your phone.

656.q: Which ancient civilisation do these pictures make you think of?
656.e: Pyramids, camels and desert sun go with ancient Egypt on the Nile.

657.e: This is a Tyrannosaurus rex, one of the best-known dinosaurs.

658.q: Which event do these pictures remind you of?
658.e: In 1969, with Apollo 11, people landed on the Moon for the first time.
658.m: People landed on the Moon in 1969.

659.e: Knights lived in the Middle Ages, fought on horseback and often lived in castles.
659.m: A castle, a sword and a horse belong to a knight.

660.q: Which legendary figure goes with these pictures?
660.e: William Tell is said to have shot an apple off his son's head with a crossbow.
660.m: An apple and a crossbow belong to William Tell.

661.q: Which Swiss holiday is celebrated with bonfires on the hills and fireworks?
661.e: On the national holiday, 1 August, there are bonfires on the hills, paper lanterns and fireworks.
661.m: On 1 August, Switzerland celebrates its National Day.

662.q: Which Zurich custom is meant here?
662.e: At the Sechseläuten, the snowman Böögg is burned. The faster its head explodes, the nicer the summer is supposed to be.
662.m: The Böögg burns at the Sechseläuten.

663.q: Which Geneva festival is meant here?
663.e: At the Escalade, chocolate pots are smashed in memory of Mère Royaume's soup in 1602.
663.m: The chocolate pot is part of the Escalade.

a: Putting the phone away before sleeping
664.e: Bright screen light and exciting videos keep you awake. Without a phone, you fall asleep more easily.
664.m: If you put your phone away, you sleep better.

665.q: Which festival goes with these pictures?
665.e: A Christmas tree, presents and a star belong to Christmas, the festival of the birth of Jesus.

666.q: Which festival does this candlestick belong to?
666.e: At the Jewish festival of lights, Hanukkah, one more light is lit each evening for eight evenings.

667.q: At least how often a day should you do this?
667.e: Brushing your teeth in the morning and evening protects against tooth decay.
667.m: You should brush your teeth twice a day.

668.q: What are the voters doing here?
a: They are voting or electing someone
668.e: In Switzerland you can vote and elect by post or at the ballot box.
668.m: You vote at the ballot box.

669.q: What are these things paid for with?
669.e: We pay for schools, roads and the fire brigade together with taxes.
669.m: Taxes pay for what everyone needs.

670.e: Doctor's visits and medicines are paid for to a large extent through health insurance.

671.e: Bread and croissants are baked at the bakery.

672.q: Which canton does this coat of arms belong to?
672.e: This is the coat of arms of Zurich: divided diagonally, white at the top and blue at the bottom. (Drawn in a simplified way here.)
672.m: The Zurich coat of arms is divided diagonally.

673.q: Which country does this flag belong to?
673.e: This is the flag of Switzerland: a white cross on a red background. The Swiss flag is square.
673.m: The Swiss flag shows a white cross on red.

674.q: Why are squirrels important for the forest?
a: Because when they hide seeds, new plants can grow
Because they drive away other animals
674.e: When squirrels forget buried nuts, new trees can grow from them. In this way they help the forest to renew itself.
674.m: Squirrels help the forest to grow.

a: Yes, it is a good swimmer
No, it sinks straight away in water
675.e: The grass snake swims well and also dives to catch prey. It wriggles its way through the water.
675.m: Grass snakes swim and dive well.

676.q: Can pigs sweat well like we humans do?
a: No, they have hardly any sweat glands
Yes, just as well as humans
No, they only sweat on their ears
676.e: Pigs have almost no working sweat glands. That is why they cool down in mud or water instead.

677.q: Why do wolves in North America and in Europe often look somewhat different?
a: They are not related at all
677.e: The wolf is divided into different subspecies, which differ in size and fur colour depending on their habitat. North American and European wolves belong to different subspecies.
677.m: There are different subspecies of wolf.

678.q: What loud sound does a stag make during the rut?
678.e: During the rut the stag lets out loud, deep roars. In this way it shows its strength and attracts females.
678.m: During the rut the stag roars loudly.

679.q: Why is it important for people to protect dolphins and the sea?
a: Dolphins need clean water to live
Dolphins don't need any water at all
679.e: Dolphins live in the sea and need clean, healthy water to find food. Polluted water and rubbish can harm them.
679.m: Dolphins need clean seawater to live.

680.q: How many barbels does the wels catfish have?
680.e: Two long barbels sit on the upper jaw and four short ones on the lower jaw. That makes six altogether.
680.m: The wels catfish has six barbels.

681.q: In which country does the Iberian lynx mainly live?
681.e: Today the Iberian lynx is only found in small areas of Spain and Portugal. Protection programmes are helping it recover.
681.m: Spain and Portugal are its home.

682.q: How is the female Alpine newt fertilised?
a: She takes up a sperm packet from the male with her cloaca
682.e: The male deposits a sperm packet, the spermatophore, on the bottom of the pond. The female then takes it up with her cloaca, without mating as in mammals.

683.q: Which animals sometimes eat stag beetles?
a: Birds such as crows and woodpeckers
683.e: Martens, foxes and wild boar can also eat the beetles or their larvae. Flying beetles in particular are easy prey.
683.m: Birds and mammals eat stag beetles.

684.q: In lions, which is usually bigger and heavier, the male or the female?
684.e: Male lions are usually bigger and heavier than lionesses. Also, only the males have a mane.
684.m: Male lions are bigger than lionesses.

685.q: What does a donkey like to eat best?
685.e: Donkeys are pure herbivores and especially like dry grass and hay. They also like eating straw and herbs.

686.q: What do ring-tailed lemurs have on the second toe of their hind feet?
686.e: Instead of a nail they have a claw there. They use it to scratch and groom their fur.
686.m: The grooming claw helps with caring for the fur.

687.q: What role does the great crested grebe's dance play in addition to courtship, when the pair are already together?
a: It strengthens the bond between the partners throughout the breeding season
It is only used for finding food
It drives fish out of the territory
It helps directly with building the nest
687.e: Even after pairing, great crested grebes keep performing courtship rituals. This strengthens the relationship throughout the whole breeding season.
687.m: Dancing strengthens the bond for the long term.

689.q: How does a brown bear usually react when it meets a human?
a: It is usually shy and prefers to withdraw
It stands completely still and falls asleep
It always follows humans home in a friendly way
689.e: Brown bears are naturally rather shy and avoid contact with humans. Only in certain situations, for example when they are surprised or protecting their cubs, can they react aggressively.
689.m: Brown bears usually avoid humans of their own accord.

690.q: Why is it important that a goldfish pond does not freeze over completely in winter?
a: So that the fish still get enough oxygen
So that the water gets warmer
So that the fish can fly
So that they become more colourful
690.e: If a pond freezes over completely, no more oxygen can get into the water and the fish could suffocate. That is why a small area is often kept open.
690.m: The pond needs an open area in winter.

701.q: What forms on a wound so that it can heal?
701.e: When blood dries in the air, a firm crust forms: the scab. It protects the wound while it heals.

704.q: What does “Desaparecidos” mean in the Argentine military dictatorship?
a: People who disappeared without trace because the government persecuted them.
704.e: During the military dictatorship in Argentina (1976 to 1983) the rulers had thousands of government critics secretly disappear. Many were never found again.

705.q: What is the big building in Geneva where many international conferences take place called?
705.e: The Palais des Nations is the biggest UN site in Europe and is in Geneva. Representatives from many countries meet there.
705.m: The Palais des Nations is the UN site in Geneva.

707.q: What is a renewable energy source?
a: For example solar or wind power
707.e: Renewable energies such as sun, wind or water power are available practically without limit and constantly renew themselves. They harm the climate much less than fossil fuels.
707.m: Sun and wind are renewable energies.

711.q: What is the tower of a mosque called, from which people are called to prayer?
711.e: From the minaret the muezzin calls people to prayer several times a day. Many mosques have one or more of these towers.
711.m: The call to prayer comes from the minaret.

752.q: Which device turns electricity into light?
752.e: In a light bulb, electricity flows through a wire, which makes it glow brightly. This is how electricity becomes light.
752.m: The light bulb turns electricity into light.

770.q: Which symbol is in the centre of the Israeli flag?
770.e: The blue Star of David between two blue stripes is the central symbol of the Israeli flag, introduced in 1948. It is a traditional symbol of Judaism.
770.m: Israel's flag shows the Star of David.

777.e: The Star of David is a six-pointed star made of two triangles. You see it on synagogues and on the flag of Israel.
777.m: The Star of David is the symbol of Judaism.

779.q: What is a greenhouse used for?
a: To let plants grow warm in any weather
779.e: In a greenhouse made of glass or plastic, the warmth stays inside. That way plants can grow protected even in winter.
779.m: In a greenhouse it is always warm for plants.

785.q: What is the difference between the UN General Assembly and the Security Council?
a: All states are represented in the General Assembly, only a few in the Security Council
Both are exactly the same body
The Security Council only meets every ten years
The General Assembly has only five members
785.e: Every UN member country has a seat and one vote in the General Assembly. The Security Council, on the other hand, consists of only 15 countries and makes important decisions about peace and security.
785.m: All states are in the General Assembly, only 15 in the Security Council.

804.q: What does the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation (SDC) do?
a: It supports projects in poorer countries
804.e: The SDC is part of the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs and funds projects that reduce poverty or promote education, for example in Africa or Asia. In this way Switzerland takes part in international development cooperation.
804.m: The SDC supports development projects abroad.

811.q: What was a “Five-Year Plan” in the Soviet Union?
a: A state economic plan that set production targets for five years
A school plan for five years
811.e: With Five-Year Plans the Soviet government wanted to build up industry quickly. The state decided exactly what should be produced and how much.

860.e: A municipality is like a village or a town where people live. The people who live there can have a say on many questions.
860.m: The municipality is the smallest political unit.

873.q: What does the ‘militia system’ mean in Swiss politics?
a: Many politicians do their political job alongside another job
Politics is a full-time main job for everyone
873.e: In Switzerland many politicians, especially in municipalities and in parliament, do this work part-time.
873.m: Politics is often a part-time job.

900.e: Unlike in votes, children and teenagers may also take part in a petition. This way everyone can show their opinion.

916.q: How big can a fully grown carp get?
916.e: Some carp grow very big and heavy, more than a metre long. But it takes them many years to get that big.

917.q: What helps the red fox most when it catches mice in the snow?
917.e: Foxes can hear mice rustling even under a thick layer of snow. Then they leap high into the air and dive head first into the snow.
917.m: Foxes can hear mice under the snow.

919.q: What do great crested grebe chicks love to do soon after hatching?
a: They ride on their parents’ backs
They build their own nest straight away
They fly after just a few hours
They bury themselves in the mud
919.e: The chicks like to climb onto a parent’s back, where they are protected and kept warm. They often stay there even while the parent looks for food.
919.m: Chicks love riding on their parents.

920.q: How much can an ant carry compared with its own weight?
a: Exactly as much as it weighs
920.e: Ants are incredibly strong. They can carry much more than they weigh themselves.

921.q: Why do woodlice often gather in groups?
a: In groups it stays damper and they are better protected
Because they form a colony like ants
921.e: Huddled close together, woodlice lose less moisture. However, they do not form a colony where jobs are shared.
921.m: Groups protect woodlice from drying out.

922.q: Which habitat does the chamois like best?
922.e: Chamois are perfectly adapted to steep, rocky mountain landscapes. There they find shelter and can climb quickly.

923.q: How many eyes does a garden cross spider have?
923.e: The garden cross spider has eight small eyes on the front part of its body. Even so, it does not see very sharply.

924.q: What is the name of the smallest and most endangered lynx in the world?
924.e: The Iberian lynx now lives only in small populations on the Iberian Peninsula. It is one of the most endangered cat species in the world.
924.m: The Iberian lynx is highly endangered.

926.q: What does a hamster often do when it gets a fright?
a: It stands up on its back legs and hisses
It lies flat and goes to sleep
926.e: A frightened hamster may rear up, hiss or even bite. This is how it shows that it is scared.

927.q: What sound do reindeer often make when they walk?
927.e: When reindeer walk, the tendons in their legs crack or click. This helps animals in the herd stay in touch during a snowstorm.

928.q: What colour is the head of a male mallard, the drake?
928.e: The drake has a bright green head that shines in the sun. This makes it easy to recognise from far away.

929.q: What do meerkats mainly use their long claws for?
929.e: Their strong claws are good for digging burrows and scratching for food. They are not built for climbing.
929.m: They dig tunnels with their claws.

930.q: Where can the edible dormouse sometimes cause trouble for homeowners?
a: In lofts, where it gnaws on cables
In the cellar, where it drinks water
In the garden, where it eats flowers
In the cowshed, where it bothers the cows
930.e: Edible dormice sometimes move into lofts and gnaw on cables or insulation there. This can be annoying for homeowners.
930.m: In lofts it sometimes gnaws on cables.

932.q: What is a baby rhino called?
932.e: A young rhino is called a calf, just like a baby elephant. It stays with its mother for a long time.
932.m: A baby rhino is called a calf.

933.q: What does a red fox like to eat most?
a: Mice, birds, insects, fruit and berries
933.e: The red fox is an omnivore and eats very different things depending on the season. In autumn it also enjoys ripe berries and fallen fruit.

934.q: What happens when a fox hears people or dogs in a garden at night?
a: It usually runs away quickly and quietly
It stands still and barks back loudly
It calls its whole family to fight
934.e: When a fox is surprised, it would rather run away quickly and silently than risk a fight. By nature it is more cautious than brave.
934.m: Foxes would rather flee than fight.

935.q: Why can cats still see well in very little light?
a: A special layer in the eye (tapetum lucidum) boosts the light
They smell their surroundings and need no light
935.e: Behind the retina, cats have a mirror-like layer called the tapetum lucidum. It reflects incoming light back and greatly improves night vision.
935.m: The tapetum lucidum improves night vision.

936.q: Which sense helps reindeer find lichen under the snow?
936.e: Reindeer can smell food even under a layer of snow. That way they know where it is worth scraping.

937.q: Roughly how much does an adult bearded vulture weigh?
937.e: Despite its huge wingspan, a bearded vulture weighs only about five to seven kilograms. Its body is built very light for efficient flying.
937.m: A light body despite big wings.

938.q: What is the meeting called where all the residents of a municipality gather to make decisions?
938.e: In many small municipalities the voters meet and decide together, often by a show of hands.
938.m: Deciding together at the municipal assembly.

939.q: What role does the herd play for a buffalo calf?
939.e: In the middle of the herd, calves are better protected. That makes things harder for lions.

940.q: Which animals are enemies of the common toad?
a: Grass snakes, hedgehogs and grey herons
940.e: Grass snakes, hedgehogs and some birds such as the grey heron eat common toads. So despite its poison, the toad is not completely safe.

941.q: Which two main species of gorilla do scientists distinguish?
941.e: There is the western gorilla and the eastern gorilla. They live in different parts of Africa.
941.m: There are two main species of gorilla.

942.q: In which canton were women only given the vote in 1990, by a court ruling?
942.e: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to give women the vote, and only after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court.
942.m: Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton to give women the vote, in 1990.

944.q: What covers the body of a carp?
a: Bare, smooth skin with nothing on it
944.e: The carp’s body is covered with scales that protect it. The scales often shine golden or brownish.

945.q: What is the oldest age a raven can reach in human care?
945.e: In captivity, for example in zoos, ravens can live much longer than in the wild because there are no dangers and they are well looked after. Ages of over 40 years have been recorded.
945.m: Over 40 years is possible in captivity.

946.q: Where does the wood mouse like to live best?
a: Only high in the mountains above the snow line
946.e: The wood mouse feels at home wherever there are plants and hiding places. It is found most often in woods, hedges and gardens.
946.m: The wood mouse lives in woods and gardens.

947.q: How many young does a female chamois usually have?
947.e: A female chamois usually has only one kid a year. Twins are rare.
947.m: Female chamois usually have just one kid.

948.q: How often does the common earwig fly?
948.e: It has working wings but hardly uses them. Most of the time it prefers to walk.
948.m: It can fly but rarely does.

949.q: How are the jaguar’s legs built compared with other big cats?
949.e: The jaguar has a stocky, muscular build. This helps it climb, swim and overpower prey.

950.q: Does the golden eagle also eat carrion as well as live prey?
a: Yes, sometimes it eats dead animals too
950.e: Golden eagles are flexible hunters and will eat carrion when they get the chance, especially in winter when live prey is scarce. So they are not pure hunters.
950.m: Golden eagles sometimes eat carrion too.

951.q: In what state are young stone martens born?
a: With open eyes and full fur
951.e: Like many young predators, stone martens are born blind and without fur. That is why they need a lot of care from their mother.
951.m: Young stone martens are born blind.

952.q: Does a chimpanzee have a tail?
a: Yes, but only a short stump
Yes, a gripping tail like some monkeys
952.e: Chimpanzees are great apes and, like humans, have no tail. This makes them different from many other kinds of monkey.

953.q: Which habitat suits the black-backed jackal?
953.e: It lives in open and partly open landscapes in Africa. There it finds food and places for its den.

954.q: What does a cow like to eat most?
954.e: Cows are herbivores and like to eat grass in the field or hay in the barn best. Grass gives them lots of energy.

955.q: Roughly how long is a stone marten’s body, without the tail?
955.e: A stone marten’s body usually measures around 45 centimetres. On top of that comes a bushy tail of about 25 centimetres.
955.m: Stone martens are about as long as a cat.

956.q: Whose old nest does the red kite sometimes use as a base for its own eyrie?
956.e: Instead of always building from scratch, the red kite likes to use old nests of crows or other birds of prey and add to them. This saves it time and energy.
956.m: The red kite often builds on old crows’ nests.

957.q: How do gibbons move on the ground when they do walk?
a: Upright on their back legs, with their arms raised for balance
On all fours with their belly on the ground
957.e: On the ground, gibbons usually walk on two legs and hold their arms up for balance. But they are only rarely on the ground.
957.m: On the ground, gibbons walk upright.

958.q: What does the snow leopard use its very long tail for?
a: For balance and as a warm blanket
958.e: The tail helps it keep its balance on steep rocks. When resting, the animal wraps it around its body and face to keep warm.

959.q: What is the difference between an otter and a beaver?
a: The otter eats fish, the beaver eats plants
959.e: While the otter is a predator and eats fish, the beaver eats plants such as bark and twigs. Both live near water, but they are very different animals.
959.m: Otters eat fish, beavers eat plants.

960.q: Roughly how big is a cuckoo compared with other birds?
a: About as big as a pigeon, but slimmer
960.e: The cuckoo is about as long as a pigeon but looks slimmer because of its long tail and narrow shape. It weighs much less than a pigeon.
960.m: A cuckoo is pigeon-sized but slim.

961.q: Where does the housefly especially like to be, as its name suggests?
961.e: The housefly likes to live near people, in houses, stables and kitchens.
961.m: The housefly likes to live near people.

962.q: What stops a pond skater from sinking into the water?
a: The surface tension of the water
962.e: The surface of the water acts like a thin, stretchy skin. The light pond skater only presses it down a little and is carried.
962.m: The water surface carries the light body.

963.q: What happens if a swift accidentally lands on the ground?
a: It often struggles to take off again
It digs itself in straight away
963.e: Because of its short legs and long wings, the swift has hardly any chance to build up speed on flat ground. It often needs help or a raised place to take off.
963.m: Taking off from the ground is very hard for it.

964.q: Which sea turtle has a particularly strong beak for cracking shellfish?
964.e: The loggerhead turtle has very strong jaws. It uses them to crack hard shellfish and crabs. The leatherback mainly eats jellyfish, and the green turtle eats seagrass.
964.m: A strong beak cracks hard shellfish.

965.q: What does a jellyfish mostly feed on?
965.e: Jellyfish use their tentacles to catch small fish, crustaceans and tiny living things called plankton.
965.m: Jellyfish eat plankton and small fish.

966.q: How many legs does a stork often stand on when it rests?
a: Always on both legs, stretched out
966.e: You often see storks standing on one leg with the other one tucked up. This saves warmth and energy.
966.m: Storks often stand on one leg.

967.q: How do eagle owls usually react when people disturb them near their nesting site?
a: Very sensitively, they may even abandon their eggs
Not at all, they are never disturbed
They move to another town straight away
967.e: Eagle owls are sensitive to disturbance near their nesting site and, in the worst case, may even give up their brood. That is why it is important to leave known nesting cliffs in peace.
967.m: Disturbance can put eagle owl broods at risk.

968.q: What is the larva of a housefly called?
968.e: The larva of the housefly is called a maggot. It is white, has no legs and eats its way through its surroundings.
968.m: A fly’s larva is called a maggot.

969.q: Why is the least weasel useful for farming?
a: It keeps the mouse population down naturally
It spreads diseases among farm animals
969.e: Since mice can damage fields, the least weasel helps as a natural enemy. So farmers benefit indirectly from this small hunter.
969.m: Least weasels help against plagues of mice.

970.q: What do many zoos do to give penguins a good home?
a: They build cool pools with rocks to climb on
They keep them in desert enclosures
They let them fly around freely
970.e: Penguins in zoos need cool water to swim in and rocks to waddle on. That way they feel at home, as in their natural habitat.
970.m: Zoos build cool pools for penguins.

971.q: How does an elk defend itself against a wolf?
a: With powerful kicks of its front legs
971.e: Elk lash out with their hooves. This can seriously injure attackers.
971.m: Elk defend themselves with their hooves.

973.q: Where does the common frog lay its eggs in spring?
a: Under a stone in the forest
973.e: In spring, common frogs travel to ponds. There the females lay their eggs in the water in large clumps.
973.m: Many clumps of spawn can lie in the same pond.

974.q: What does the hedgehog do in winter?
a: It stays awake and keeps hunting
974.e: When it gets cold, the hedgehog can no longer find food, so it hibernates. This saves energy until spring.

975.q: What keeps a polar bear warm in icy water?
975.e: Under its skin, the polar bear has a thick layer of fat. It keeps it warm even when swimming in icy water.
975.m: Fat keeps the polar bear warm in the water.

976.q: What happens to young male elephants when they grow up?
a: They stay with their mother forever
They look after the herd’s calves
976.e: When male elephants grow up, they leave the family herd. They then usually live alone or with other bulls.

977.q: Which emperor penguin usually keeps the egg warm?
a: Both parents at the same time
977.e: In emperor penguins, the male carries the egg on its feet and keeps it warm under a fold of skin. Meanwhile the female goes off to find food.
977.m: The male emperor penguin keeps the egg warm.

978.q: How small can the world’s smallest octopus be?
978.e: There are tiny kinds of octopus that grow only a few centimetres long. Some would even fit in your hand.

979.q: Which kind of hyena is the biggest?
979.e: The spotted hyena grows much bigger than the other kinds. Adults often weigh 40 to 80 kilograms.
979.m: The spotted hyena is the biggest hyena.

981.q: What does an elephant use its trunk for when greeting others of its kind?
981.e: Elephants often touch each other with their trunks. This is how they greet each other and recognise each other by smell.
981.m: The trunk is also used for greeting.

982.q: On which continents do magpies or closely related species live?
982.e: The magpie and its close relatives are found across large parts of Europe and Asia, and related species also live in North America. This makes it one of the most widespread members of the crow family.
982.m: Magpies and their relatives live on several continents.

983.q: Why do dung beetles roll their dung ball away in as straight a line as possible?
a: To get it away from rivals quickly
983.e: Lots of beetles crowd around a dung heap. By taking a straight route, a beetle gets away quickly from rivals that might steal its ball.
983.m: Straight paths protect against ball thieves.

985.q: How small can the smallest kind of jellyfish be?
985.e: Some jellyfish are tiny and measure only a few millimetres. You can hardly see them in the sea.

986.q: Which group of vertebrates does the eel belong to?
986.e: The eel is a bony fish, even though it looks like a snake. It breathes with gills.
986.m: The eel is a fish, not a snake.

987.q: What does a ladybird do before it flies?
a: It first opens its hard wing cases to the side
It first runs off very fast
It dips into the water briefly
987.e: Before a ladybird takes off, it opens its hard wing cases. Only then can it spread the flying wings underneath and fly away.
987.m: First open the wing cases, then fly.

988.q: Which family does the African buffalo belong to?
988.e: The African buffalo is a bovid, like cattle and antelopes. Deer have antlers, not horns.
988.m: African buffalo are bovids, not deer.

989.q: What does a dog use to hear very quiet or high sounds that people cannot hear?
989.e: Dogs can hear much higher sounds than people and pick up noises from further away. Their ears are very mobile.

990.q: Are many kinds of sea turtle in danger today?
a: No, there are far too many of them
Only one single species is in danger
990.e: Sadly, many sea turtles are considered threatened or endangered. Reasons include fishing nets, plastic litter and destroyed beaches.
990.m: Many sea turtles are endangered today.

991.q: Where does the female European pond turtle lay her eggs?
a: In a pit she digs on land
Straight into the water on the bottom
In a nest of twigs in a tree
In a cave in the rocks
991.e: To do this, the female leaves the water and looks for sunny, loose soil. Afterwards she covers the eggs up again.
991.m: The eggs go into a pit on land.

992.q: What does a cat mainly use its miaow for?
992.e: Adult cats hardly miaow at each other, but they miaow a lot to people. This is how they have learnt to tell us what they want.
992.m: Miaowing is mainly meant for people.

993.q: What makes penguin feathers so waterproof?
a: They are packed tightly and oiled with fat
They are very long and soft
