993.e: Penguin feathers lie very close together and are oiled with fat from a gland. This keeps the water out and the skin dry.
993.m: Dense, oiled feathers keep penguins dry.

994.q: How does a garden cross spider usually react to people?
a: It runs away or sits still
It jumps at people straight away
994.e: Garden cross spiders do not attack people. If you come close, it usually runs away or sits completely still.

995.q: Does the barn owl make a deep hooting call like some other owls?
a: Yes, that is exactly what it does
No, it barks like a dog
995.e: The barn owl does not hoot like some other kinds of owl. Its call sounds more like a loud screech.

996.q: How many species of orangutan are there today?
996.e: There is the Bornean orangutan, the Sumatran orangutan and the Tapanuli orangutan. The last one was described as a separate species in 2017.
996.m: There are three species of orangutan.

997.q: What does a fully grown wels catfish eat?
a: Fish, frogs, crayfish and sometimes water birds
997.e: The wels catfish is a predatory fish. It mainly eats fish, but also crayfish, frogs and occasionally small water birds.
997.m: The wels catfish is a predatory fish.

998.q: How does the grey heron sometimes behave towards people’s fish ponds?
a: It sometimes fishes there, which annoys pond owners
It destroys the ponds with its beak
It lays its eggs in them
998.e: Because the grey heron likes eating fish, it also visits artificial fish ponds. This can sometimes be a problem for pond owners.

a: A fork in a branch where it wedges cones
999.e: In a fork like this, the woodpecker holds a cone firmly so it can work on it more easily. This helps it get at the seeds.
999.m: That is where it wedges its cones.

1000.q: How do a duck’s feet help it swim?
a: With a wing on each foot
1000.e: A thin skin is stretched between the duck’s toes. This webbing works like a paddle in the water.

1001.q: How does a donkey often show that it gets on well with another donkey?
a: They often stand close together and doze side by side
They fight each other all the time
1001.e: Donkeys that are friends often stand close together, doze side by side and swish the flies away from each other with their tails. This shows their close bond.
1001.m: Donkeys that are friends stand close together.

1002.e: Depending on the species and the plant, aphids have different colours. Green aphids are well camouflaged on leaves.

1003.q: What does a wasp’s sting contain?
1003.e: When it stings, the wasp injects venom into the skin. That causes the burning pain.

1004.q: Which of a squirrel’s teeth keep growing all its life?
1004.e: A squirrel’s front gnawing teeth keep growing throughout its life. Gnawing keeps them at the right length.

1005.q: Which of these animals is a sign in the Chinese calendar?
1005.e: The Chinese calendar has twelve animal signs, and one of them is the rooster. Each animal year comes round again every twelve years.
1005.m: The rooster is a Chinese zodiac sign.

1006.q: Why are a horse’s nostrils especially large?
a: So it can breathe in lots of air when running
So it can neigh more loudly
1006.e: The large nostrils help the horse breathe lots of air in and out when it runs fast. This is important because horses are long-distance runners.

1007.q: Why is it important to clean a hamster’s cage regularly?
a: So the hamster gets more colours
So the hamster learns to fly
1007.e: A clean cage prevents illness and bad smells. The hamster also feels more comfortable.
1007.m: A clean cage keeps it healthy.

1008.q: How endangered is the ring-tailed lemur in the wild?
1008.e: The number of ring-tailed lemurs living in the wild is falling. That is why the species is listed as endangered on the Red List.
1008.m: Ring-tailed lemurs are endangered in the wild.

1009.q: What covers the barn owl’s face like a veil?
1009.e: Especially fine, white feathers grow all around the barn owl’s face. Together they form a heart-shaped disc called the facial disc.
1009.m: Fine feathers form the facial disc.

1010.q: How does a badger usually react when it meets a person?
a: It stands still and lets you stroke it
1010.e: Badgers are shy by nature and avoid contact with people. If they meet us, they usually vanish quickly into the undergrowth.

1011.q: What can happen if an earwig pinches a finger with its pincers?
1011.e: The pincers are usually too weak for human skin. At most you feel a slight pinch.
1011.m: The pinch is usually barely noticeable.

1012.q: Where in the world is the housefly found?
1012.e: The housefly lives almost all over the world, wherever people live. That is why it is called a species that follows humans.

1013.q: Who looks after bee colonies and harvests the honey?
1013.e: A beekeeper cares for the bee colonies, keeps them healthy and harvests the honey from the combs. There are many beekeepers in Switzerland too.
1013.m: The beekeeper looks after the bees.

1014.q: How does a peregrine falcon usually carry its prey after catching it?
a: Carried through the air in its talons
Swallowed into its crop and brought up again
Never moved, but eaten on the ground
1014.e: After a catch, the peregrine falcon usually carries its prey in its strong talons to a safe place to eat. There it plucks and eats it.

1015.q: How good is a badger’s eyesight?
1015.e: The badger does not see very well. Instead, it relies much more on its nose.

1016.q: What should you do before stroking a dog you do not know?
1016.e: You should always ask the owner first whether you may stroke the dog. That way the dog does not get a fright or feel threatened.

1017.q: Why is the bearded vulture considered important for the mountain ecosystem?
a: It clears away carcass remains that would otherwise be left lying
It spreads flower seeds in the Alps
1017.e: Because the bearded vulture also eats the large bones of dead animals, it helps with the natural ‘clean-up’ in the mountains. That is why it is seen as a kind of health inspector of the mountains.
1017.m: It clears bones from the mountains.

1018.q: How well does a lion see in the dark compared with people?
1018.e: Lions’ eyes are perfectly adapted to the night. This means they can hunt well even in low light.
1018.m: Lions see very well at night.

1019.q: Roughly how heavy can a large male tiger get?
1019.e: Large male tigers can weigh up to 300 kilograms. That is as heavy as several adults put together.
1019.m: A tiger can weigh up to 300 kilograms.

1020.q: How well can a common toad see on land?
a: Only in black and white and shapes
1020.e: The common toad’s eyes are well adapted to life on land. It can recognise prey and danger quite well with them.
1020.m: Common toads see well on land.

1021.q: What is the first thing a bumblebee queen does in spring?
a: She looks for a place for a new nest
She builds honeycombs straight away like a honeybee
1021.e: After hibernating, the queen wakes up and looks for a sheltered spot. There she lays the first eggs for her new colony.
1021.m: In spring the queen looks for a nest.

1022.q: What do we call animals that, like the alpaca, mainly eat plants?
1022.e: Herbivores feed on grasses, leaves and other plants. Cows and sheep are herbivores too.

1023.q: What colour is the European mantis usually?
1023.e: Green or brown matches plants and dry grass well. That way it hardly stands out.

1024.q: What is sensible when hiking in areas with adders?
a: Wear sturdy shoes and do not reach blindly into the grass
Lift stones with your bare hands
1024.e: Sturdy shoes protect against bites. You should also stay on the paths and not put your hands into hiding places.
1024.m: Sturdy shoes, never reach in blindly.

1025.e: By howling, wolves keep in touch with their pack and warn other packs away from their territory. The howling can be heard for kilometres.

1026.q: What does the law of conservation of energy say?
a: Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only converted
Energy keeps appearing out of nothing
1026.e: In a closed system, the total energy always stays the same; it can only change into other forms, for example from kinetic energy into heat. This basic principle applies throughout physics.
1026.m: Energy never disappears, it changes form.

1027.q: What is it called when ducks lose their old feathers each year and grow new ones?
1027.e: Like many birds, ducks change their plumage once a year. This process is called moulting.
1027.m: When birds moult, new feathers grow.

1028.q: Where does the mallard build its nest?
a: On the ground, hidden in the grass near water
On a rock in the mountains
1028.e: The female looks for a well-hidden spot on the ground near the water. There she lines the nest with feathers.
1028.m: Nests are hidden on the ground.

1029.q: What does the alpine salamander do when its surroundings get very dry?
a: It hides so it does not dry out
It drinks large amounts of water from puddles
It changes the colour of its skin
1029.e: Because its skin has to stay moist, the alpine salamander retreats to shady, damp hiding places when it is dry. These animals cope badly with sun and dryness.
1029.m: When it is dry, it hides.

1030.q: How do many seahorse pairs live?
a: They live alone all their lives
1030.e: Some kinds of seahorse stay with the same partner for a long time. They even meet up again regularly.

1031.q: What does a harbour seal need its long whiskers for?
a: To feel fish in the water
1031.e: The whiskers are very sensitive. With them, the seal can feel the movements of fish in the water, even in murky, dark water.

1032.q: What did the jaguar mean to the Aztecs and the Maya?
a: It was seen as a sacred, powerful animal
1032.e: In the cultures of Central America, the jaguar was honoured as a symbol of strength. It appears in art, myths and orders of warriors.
1032.m: The jaguar was a sacred symbol of power.

1033.q: What does an elephant use its trunk for, among other things?
a: Only for singing like a bird
1033.e: The trunk is a combination of nose and upper lip. It is used as a gripping tool, for smelling and for sucking up water.
1033.m: The trunk is both nose and gripping arm.

1034.e: The cross reminds people of the death of Jesus on the cross. You find it on many churches and in Christian homes.
1034.m: The cross is the symbol of Christianity.

1035.q: Roughly how much does an adult bonobo weigh?
1035.e: Males are heavier than females. Overall, adult bonobos weigh about as much as a teenager or an adult human.

1036.q: In which area of Switzerland are you most likely to come across the alpine salamander?
a: In the Alps and the Pre-Alps
In the Swiss Plateau near big cities
Only in Ticino on the lakeshore
1036.e: As its name says, the alpine salamander lives mainly in the Alps and the Pre-Alps. You hardly ever find it in the lower parts of the Swiss Plateau.
1036.m: It lives mainly in the Alps.

1037.q: What does the great spotted woodpecker need its stiff tail for?
a: As a prop when climbing the trunk
1037.e: The tail presses against the bark and helps it not to fall off. This lets it sit upright on the trunk.
1037.m: The tail props it up on the tree.

1038.q: What else is a female hippo called?
1038.e: An adult female hippo is sometimes called a cow. She looks after her calf with great care.
1038.m: A female hippo is called a cow.

1039.q: Why do donkeys cope well with heat and little water?
a: Their ancestors lived in dry deserts
Their ancestors lived in the rainforest
Their ancestors lived at the North Pole
1039.e: The African wild ass, the ancestor of our domestic donkey, lived in dry desert areas. That is why donkeys still cope well with heat and little water today.

1040.q: How many young does a marmot mother usually have?
1040.e: A litter usually has two to four baby marmots. They are born naked and blind in the safety of the burrow.
1040.m: Marmots have only a few young per litter.

1041.q: How can you often tell that a carp is searching for food on the bottom of the water?
a: The water is stirred up and cloudy
1041.e: When a carp roots around on the bottom, it stirs up mud and small particles. This often makes the water cloudy.
1041.m: Carp rooting for food make the water cloudy.

1042.q: Which kind of ladybird has spread to Switzerland and can push out native species?
1042.e: The harlequin ladybird comes from Asia and was brought in to fight pests. Today it also lives in the wild here and eats the food of native ladybirds.
1042.m: The harlequin ladybird came from Asia.

1043.q: How does a swift look different from a pigeon in flight?
a: Its wings are narrow and curved like a sickle
Its wings are broad and rounded
It flies much more slowly than a pigeon
1043.e: Pigeons have broad, rounded wings, while the swift has narrow, curved, sickle-shaped wings. This makes it much faster and more agile in the air.
1043.m: Sickle-shaped wings set it apart from pigeons.

1044.q: Roughly how long do baby tapirs keep their striped pattern?
1044.e: After about six months, the pattern starts to fade. Then the animals look like the adults.
1044.m: The pattern disappears after a few months.

1045.q: How well can a mole see?
a: Very poorly, its eyes are tiny
Just as well as an eagle
It sees only colours, not shapes
1045.e: The mole’s eyes are tiny and almost hidden under its fur. It hardly needs them underground.

1046.q: Where do koalas live in the wild?
1046.e: Koalas are only found in Australia, mainly in the east of the country. There they live in eucalyptus forests.

1047.q: What does an otter’s fur look like?
1047.e: The otter’s fur is evenly brown and especially thick, which helps it stay warm even in cold water. On the belly it is often a bit lighter.

1048.q: How many entrances can a large badger sett have?
1048.e: An old badger sett is often extended over many years. This creates lots of entrances and tunnels.
1048.m: Badger setts often have many entrances.

1049.q: What hatches first from a housefly’s egg?
1049.e: First a white maggot without legs hatches from the egg. Only after some weeks does it turn into a fully grown fly.
1049.m: A maggot hatches from the egg.

1050.q: How do the whale shark and the basking shark feed, even though they are so huge?
a: They filter tiny creatures out of the water
1050.e: Both sharks swim through the water with their mouths open. This way they collect small living things such as plankton.
1050.m: Whale sharks and basking sharks filter their food.

1051.q: What can help protect orangutans in everyday life?
a: Choosing products with sustainable palm oil
1051.e: If you look for sustainably grown palm oil and labels, you can help reduce forest clearing. Less packaging and careful shopping also help.

1052.q: What are materials that do not conduct electricity called?
1052.e: Insulators such as rubber or plastic stop electricity flowing through them. That is why they are wrapped around cables for protection.
1052.m: Insulators stop the flow of electricity.

1053.q: How many eggs does a mute swan usually lay in a nest?
1053.e: A clutch usually has five to eight eggs. The female patiently sits on them until they hatch.
1053.m: Usually five to eight eggs in the nest.

1054.q: Which animal is part of the coat of arms of the Principality of Liechtenstein?
1054.e: Liechtenstein's coat of arms is divided into several fields. One of them shows a black eagle on a gold background. Above it sits the princely crown.
1054.m: Liechtenstein's coat of arms includes an eagle.

1055.q: An apple falls from a tree to the ground. What happens to the energy?
a: Potential energy is converted into kinetic energy
The apple creates new energy out of nothing
1055.e: While the apple hangs high up in the tree, it has stored potential energy. As it falls, this is gradually converted into kinetic energy.
1055.m: Falling converts potential energy into movement.

1056.q: What are the carrion crow’s different calls for?
a: For warning and communicating within the flock
They make no sounds at all
1056.e: Carrion crows use different calls to warn each other or to communicate within the flock. The calls sound different depending on the situation.

1057.q: What is the jellyfish called that is known for living a very long time and being able to turn back into a young form?
1057.e: The so-called immortal jellyfish can turn back into a young form when it is under stress. This way it sometimes escapes death.
1057.m: Some jellyfish can make themselves young again.

a: They sleep with only one half of the brain so they can keep breathing
They sleep for days without surfacing
1058.e: Orcas have to keep coming up to breathe. That is why only one half of their brain sleeps at a time.
1058.m: Orcas sleep with half their brain.

1059.q: Roughly how much does a mole weigh?
a: About as much as a bar of chocolate
Only a few grams, like a mosquito
1059.e: A mole usually weighs between 70 and 120 grams. That is about as much as a bar of chocolate.

1060.q: Which animal belongs, like the sand lizard, to the family of wall lizards (Lacertidae)?
1060.e: The sand lizard and the common wall lizard are both lacertids. Geckos and chameleons form their own families, and the slow worm is a legless lizard of another family.
1060.m: Sand lizards and wall lizards are lacertids.

1061.q: Where does the hippo mainly live?
1061.e: Hippos live in rivers and lakes in Africa, south of the Sahara. There is warm water and plenty of grass there.

1062.q: What does the common earwig feed on?
1062.e: The earwig is an omnivore. For example, it eats parts of plants and small animals.

1063.q: Where do least weasels often get completely white fur in winter?
a: In very cold, snowy regions in the north
1063.e: In regions with long, snowy winters, such as Scandinavia, some least weasels turn white in winter. This gives them good camouflage in the snow.
1063.m: In the far north the least weasel often turns white.

1064.q: Where does the lion mainly live in the wild?
1064.e: Lions live mainly in open grasslands, the savannahs of Africa. There is enough prey and room to hunt there.

1065.q: How does an alpine salamander usually react when a predator threatens it?
a: It often stays still, because its poison protects it
It climbs a tree in a flash
1065.e: Because the poison in its skin puts many predators off, the alpine salamander does not need to flee as fast as other animals. Many predators let go of it again after one bite.
1065.m: Its poison protects it from enemies.

1066.q: How do elephants communicate over long distances too?
a: With deep sounds that are hard to hear
1066.e: Elephants produce infrasound, which means very low sounds. These sounds travel far and can even be passed on through the ground.
1066.m: Elephants use deep sounds to communicate.

1067.q: What happens when an animal moults its skin?
a: The animal sheds its outer covering when it gets too tight
The animal throws off its legs
The animal changes its colour for ever
1067.e: The hard outer skeleton does not grow with the animal. That is why it has to be shed several times so the animal can get bigger.

1068.q: How does the peregrine falcon usually catch its prey?
a: It strikes it in flight with its talons
It digs it out of holes in the ground
It catches it from the water with its beak
1068.e: The peregrine falcon usually catches its victims right in the air by striking them with its strong talons. Then it kills them with a well-aimed bite.
1068.m: Prey is usually struck in mid-air.

1069.q: Which group of animals does the wels catfish belong to?
1069.e: The wels catfish is a bony fish and breathes with gills. It lives only in water.
1069.m: The wels catfish is a fish.

1070.q: How does the adder kill its prey?
a: With a sting in its tail
By crushing it with its teeth
1070.e: It bites and injects venom. Then it swallows the prey whole.

1071.q: Who usually leads a group of chimpanzees?
1071.e: In a group of chimpanzees, there is usually a strong male who leads the group. The others show him respect.
1071.m: A strong male leads the group.

1072.q: What does an eel mainly breathe with in the water?
1072.e: Like other fish, the eel takes oxygen from the water through its gills. It can also take in some extra oxygen through its moist skin.

1073.q: When is the barn owl mainly active?
1073.e: The barn owl is a night animal. During the day it usually sleeps in a hidden place.
1073.m: The barn owl hunts at night.

1074.q: How are young fire salamanders born?
a: As live larvae that can swim in water
As eggs buried in the sand
As fully formed little salamanders with no larval stage
1074.e: The females carry the eggs inside their bodies and release ready-made larvae into the water. This is called giving birth to live young, or ovoviviparity.

1075.q: Where do millipedes usually live in Central Europe?
a: In the soil, under leaves, stones and wood
In the open water of lakes
On mountain peaks in the snow
1075.e: They like it damp and dark. That is why they hide under leaves, bark and stones.
1075.m: They love damp, dark hiding places.

1076.q: Is the black rhino seriously endangered today?
a: Yes, it is threatened with extinction
No, there are lots of them
No, it is not endangered at all
It only lives in zoos now
1076.e: The black rhino is one of the most threatened animals in the world. Only a few thousand still live in the wild.
1076.m: The black rhino is seriously endangered.

1077.q: What happens in the incomplete metamorphosis of an insect like the grasshopper?
a: The larvae already look like the adults
The larva turns completely into a pupa
A flying animal hatches straight from the egg
1077.e: In incomplete metamorphosis, small nymphs that already look like the adults hatch from the egg. They moult several times until they are fully grown.
1077.m: Nymphs already look like the adults.

1078.q: The mute swan’s German name means ‘knob swan’. Where does this name come from?
a: From the knob on its beak
From the humps on its back
From hard lumps on its feet
1078.e: The black knob above the beak gave the bird its German name. It is especially easy to see on males.
1078.m: The knob sits right on the beak.

1079.q: Roughly how long have millipedes existed on Earth?
1079.e: Fossils show that millipedes were among the first land animals. They lived long before the dinosaurs.
1079.m: Millipedes are very old land animals.

1080.q: Why does a cheetah sometimes lose its catch to lions or hyenas?
a: Because it is too exhausted after the sprint to fight
Because it does not like the prey itself
Because it is afraid of its own prey
1080.e: After its fast sprint, the cheetah is very exhausted. Stronger predators such as lions can then simply take the prey away from it.
1080.m: Exhausted cheetahs often lose their prey.

1081.q: What is a male goose called?
1081.e: The male goose is called a gander. It is often a little bigger than the female.
1081.m: A male goose is called a gander.

1082.q: Is the grass snake dangerously venomous to people?
1082.e: The grass snake has no venom that would be dangerous to people. That is why it is harmless.
1082.m: Grass snakes are harmless to people.

1083.q: How do peregrine falcon pairs usually live over the years?
a: They often stay with the same partner for a long time
They never live as a pair
They live in big groups of ten falcons
1083.e: Peregrine falcons usually stay with the same partner for several years and often return to the same nesting site. This loyalty to a place is called site fidelity.
1083.m: Falcon pairs often stay together for a long time.

1084.q: Which beetle belongs, like dung beetles, to the scarab beetles?
1084.e: You can recognise scarab beetles by their antennae with leaf-like plates. The cockchafer has such eye-catching fans.
1084.m: The cockchafer is a relative of dung beetles.

1085.q: What are the marsh frog’s strong back legs especially important for?
a: For powerful jumps and fast swimming
1085.e: The long, muscular back legs with webbed feet help the frog jump on land and swim fast in water. Without them it could hardly escape its enemies.
1085.m: Strong back legs help with jumping and swimming.

1087.q: How can you best tell male and female adult golden eagles apart?
a: By their body size, females are bigger
By the colour of their feathers
By the sound of their calls alone
1087.e: Because the feathers of males and females hardly differ, experts look mainly at body size. Females are clearly bigger and heavier than males.

1088.q: When is the elk rutting season?
1088.e: The elk rut takes place in September and October. Then the bulls fight over the cows.

1089.q: What is the time called when wild boar mate?
1089.e: The mating season of wild boar is called the rut. It usually takes place in winter.
1089.m: The mating season is called the rut.

1090.q: On which animal does Jesus ride into the city of Jerusalem on Palm Sunday?
1090.e: The Bible tells how Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey. Palm Sunday remembers this.
1090.m: The donkey is part of this Bible story.

1091.q: Roughly how long do the young stay with their mother?
a: About one and a half to two years
1091.e: During this time they learn to hunt and climb. Then they look for a territory of their own.
1091.m: The young learn from their mother for about two years.

1092.q: Why does a lion roar so loudly?
1092.e: With its loud roar, the lion shows other lions that an area is already taken. The roar can be heard several kilometres away.

1093.q: Why do the host birds still feed the much bigger cuckoo chick?
a: Because it begs especially loudly and insistently
Because it looks exactly like them
Because the cuckoo brings them food
Because it is not bigger at all
1093.e: The cuckoo chick begs very loudly and opens its beak wide, and this makes the host birds want to feed it. They do not realise that it is not their own chick.
1093.m: Loud begging fools the foster parents.

1094.q: How can you help grass snakes in the garden?
a: With a pond and a pile of leaves
1094.e: A pond provides frogs as food, and leaves are a place to lay eggs. This creates a habitat.
1094.m: A pond and a leaf pile help.

1095.q: What does a brown bear do especially intensely before winter?
a: It eats a lot to build up fat reserves
It looks for a partner to mate with
1095.e: In autumn, a brown bear eats a great deal to store enough fat for its winter rest. It can put on a lot of weight in a short time.
1095.m: Before winter, the bear eats to build up fat.

1096.q: How many bearded vultures have been released into the Alps since the project began?
a: None, they came back on their own
1096.e: Since 1986, young bearded vultures raised in breeding centres have been released again and again in different Alpine countries. In total, several hundred birds have returned to the mountains this way.
1096.m: Hundreds of birds have been released.

1097.q: What is a puma good at doing with its claws?
a: Climbing and holding on to prey
1097.e: Pumas have sharp claws that they can pull in. They help with climbing and grabbing prey.
1097.m: Puma claws are sharp and can be pulled in.

1098.q: What is another word for a sheep’s whole coat of wool?
1098.e: The thick woolly coat of a sheep is also called a fleece. After shearing, the fleece usually stays together in one piece.
1098.m: The woolly coat is also called a fleece.

1099.q: What is a baby pig called?
1099.e: A young pig is called a piglet. It stays with its mother, the sow, for a few weeks.
1099.m: A baby pig is called a piglet.

1100.q: What do sparrow parents feed their little chicks in the nest?
1100.e: Even though adult sparrows like eating seeds, the chicks mainly get insects. These contain lots of protein for growing.

1101.e: Dromedaries are active during the day. In the greatest heat they often rest.

1102.q: What does a young kangaroo do when it is a bit bigger but not yet fully independent?
a: It often just pokes its head out of the pouch
It leaves its mother for ever
It swims away on its own
1102.e: A slightly bigger joey no longer fits completely into the pouch. Often only its head or legs stick out.
1102.m: Bigger babies peek out of the pouch.

1103.q: What colour are a mallard’s feet usually?
1103.e: The mallard’s feet are usually bright orange. It uses them to paddle well in the water.

1104.q: Apart from its crest, what else does the great crested grebe wear on its head in breeding plumage?
1104.e: In breeding plumage, the great crested grebe wears a reddish-brown ruff on the sides of its head as well as its dark crest. In winter both are missing.
1104.m: A crest and a ruff decorate the great crested grebe.

1105.q: At what time of day do llamas usually give birth?
a: During the day, often in the morning
In the middle of the night
1105.e: Llamas often give birth in the morning. This gives the young time to get dry and strong before the cold night.
1105.m: Llamas usually give birth during the day.

1106.q: What do many ants love to eat?
1106.e: Many ants are hunters. They catch small insects and bring them back to the nest as food.

a: The order of who eats whom in nature
A list of foods in a shop
1107.e: A food chain shows how energy is passed from one living thing to the next, for example from plant to plant-eater to meat-eater. In this way all living things in nature are connected.
1107.m: Food chains show who eats whom.

1108.q: How does an adult jaguar usually live?
a: In herds of a hundred animals
1108.e: Jaguars usually move around alone and have their own territory. Males and females only meet in the mating season.

1109.q: How many stomachs does a goat have to digest its food?
1109.e: The goat is a ruminant and has four stomachs. This lets it digest tough grass and leaves well.

1110.q: At what altitudes can the alpine newt be found in the Alps?
1110.e: The alpine newt is surprisingly adaptable and also lives in high mountain waters. In the Alps it is found at heights of over 2500 metres.
1110.m: Alpine newts also live high up in the Alps.

1111.q: What does the female robin build her nest from?
1111.e: The female builds the nest on her own from soft moss, leaves and fine roots. This makes it cosy for the eggs.
1111.m: The nest is made of moss and leaves.

1112.q: Why does a cat often purr?
1112.e: Cats usually purr when they are relaxed and content, for example when being stroked. Angry cats hiss instead.
1112.m: Purring often shows a cat feels good.

1113.q: How do sea turtles find their way on their long journeys through the sea?
a: With a paper map inside them
With their sense of smell for flowers
1113.e: Sea turtles can sense the Earth’s magnetic field and use it to find their way. This lets them find the right route even over huge distances.
1113.m: The Earth’s magnetic field helps them navigate.

1114.q: What is it called when cows are taken up to the alpine pastures in summer?
1114.e: In Switzerland, farmers take their cows up to the alpine pastures in summer, and this is called the Alpaufzug. The cows often wear beautiful flower garlands.
1114.m: In summer cows go up to the alp.

1115.q: How can you easily recognise a common frog?
a: By a dark patch behind the eye
By red stripes on its back
By thick warts on its skin
1115.e: The common frog has a dark patch behind each eye. You can recognise it by this and its brown colour.
1115.m: The dark patch behind the eye is typical.

1116.q: How many wings does a honeybee have?
1116.e: The bee has two pairs of wings, so four wings in total. With them it can fly quickly from flower to flower.

1117.q: Is the hippo more of a herbivore or a carnivore?
1117.e: The hippo eats almost only grass and other plants. Meat is not normally on its menu.

1118.q: How does a slow worm often react when you pick it up?
a: It wriggles and can drop its tail
It stays completely calm and never bites
1118.e: When frightened, it defends itself by wriggling. The dropped tail is meant to distract the enemy. You should not touch wild animals.
1118.m: Better not to touch, it is easily frightened.

1119.q: How soon can a newborn lamb stand and walk?
a: After just a few minutes to hours
1119.e: A newborn lamb can stand and walk on its wobbly legs after a short time. This is important so it can follow the flock.

1120.q: Roughly how fast can a red fox run over a short distance?
1120.e: When fleeing or hunting, a fox can run at up to 50 kilometres per hour for a short time. That is about as fast as a car in town.
1120.m: A fox runs up to 50 km/h.

1121.q: What can some jellyfish do in the dark sea?
1121.e: Some jellyfish can glow in the dark. This is called bioluminescence and helps them confuse enemies.
1121.m: Some jellyfish glow in the dark.

1122.q: How does a mute swan defend its territory?
a: It drives other swans away forcefully
1122.e: Mute swans can be very aggressive when strange swans enter their area. They defend their territory with a lot of strength.
1122.m: Mute swans bravely defend their territory.

1123.q: How does a goose often react when it feels that it or its nest is in danger?
a: It flies far away at once
1123.e: Geese can be very brave when there is danger. They hiss loudly and even run at intruders to defend their nest.

1124.q: What does a sea turtle use to swim through the water?
1124.e: The sea turtle’s legs are shaped into broad flippers. With them it can move gracefully and quickly through the water.
1124.m: Flipper legs make them good swimmers.

1125.q: What do lions drink when they are thirsty?
1125.e: Like most animals, lions drink water from natural watering places. But they can also go a few days without water.

1126.q: What does the abbreviation NGO mean?
a: An organisation that works independently of governments
A department of the European Union
1126.e: NGO stands for “non-governmental organisation”. Such organisations work, for example, for the environment, human rights or development aid, without belonging to a government.

1127.q: Can the garden cross spider fly?
a: Yes, it can fly like a bird
1127.e: The garden cross spider has no wings and cannot fly. Only its young spiders let themselves be carried away by the wind on a thread.
1127.m: Adult spiders do not fly themselves.

1128.q: Which bird of prey is most often mistaken for the red kite?
1128.e: At first glance, the black kite and the red kite look alike. The most important difference is the shape of the tail.
1128.m: The black kite is often mistaken for the red kite.

1129.q: Who normally has young in a pack of African wild dogs?
a: All the females at the same time
A single male without a partner
1129.e: As a rule, it is mainly the alpha pair that has young. The others help to raise them.
1129.m: Usually the leading pair has the young.

1130.q: What does the cuckoo like to eat most?
a: Caterpillars, even poisonous and hairy ones
1130.e: The cuckoo likes eating caterpillars, even ones with poisonous hairs that many other birds avoid. This helps it fight pests in the forest.
1130.m: The cuckoo even eats poisonous caterpillars.

1131.q: Which habitat is especially good for the alpine salamander?
a: Damp mountain forests and stony alpine pastures
Big cities with lots of concrete
1131.e: The alpine salamander prefers damp, cool habitats with stones and hiding places, like those in mountain forests and on alpine pastures. It also finds enough food there.
1131.m: Damp mountain forests are its home.

1132.q: What do hikers sometimes notice after a summer thunderstorm in the mountains?
a: They see more alpine salamanders on the paths
They see no more animals until autumn
1132.e: After rain, alpine salamanders leave their hiding places because the air and ground are damp enough. That is why you meet them more often on hiking paths after a thunderstorm.
1132.m: You see them more often after rain.

1133.q: What does a typical sparrow’s nest usually look like?
a: Very smooth and round like a ball
1133.e: Compared with some other birds, sparrows build their nests in a rather wild and untidy way. Even so, the nest protects the eggs well.

1134.q: In which parts of the world does the Asian elephant live in the wild?
1134.e: The Asian elephant is found from India to Southeast Asia. The two other kinds of elephant live in Africa.
1134.m: Asian elephants live in South and Southeast Asia.

1135.q: What happens when two guinea pigs that do not know each other meet for the first time?
a: They sniff each other to sort out who ranks higher
1135.e: Guinea pigs live in groups with a certain pecking order. When they first meet, they sniff each other carefully and slowly work out who is in charge.
1135.m: New guinea pigs first sort out the pecking order.

1137.q: Which bird also likes to catch salmon?
1137.e: The bald eagle is a large bird of prey that hunts fish. It snatches them out of the water with its talons.
1137.m: Sea eagles catch salmon from the water.

1138.q: Is a garden cross spider’s bite dangerous to people?
a: No, at most it feels like a small prick
Yes, you always have to go to hospital
Yes, it makes you seriously ill at once
1138.e: The garden cross spider rarely bites people, and its venom is harmless to us. At most it feels like a small prick.
1138.m: Its bite is harmless to us.

1139.q: According to estimates, how many beavers were still living in Switzerland before they were reintroduced?
a: None, the beaver had died out
1139.e: In the 19th century, the beaver disappeared completely from Switzerland because it was hunted. Only with planned reintroductions did the species return to the country.
1139.m: The beaver had died out in Switzerland.

1140.q: Which group of animals does the common wall lizard belong to?
1140.e: The common wall lizard has scaly skin and lays eggs, which is typical of reptiles. It breathes with lungs and is not an amphibian.

1141.q: What kind of eater is the grass snake?
1141.e: It feeds only on animals. It does not eat plants.

1142.q: Roughly how old can a harbour seal get?
1142.e: In the wild, harbour seals can get surprisingly old, and some reach over 20 or even 30 years.
1142.m: Harbour seals can get quite old.

1144.q: What does the common buzzard often do high in the sky to use rising air?
a: It circles slowly in wide loops
1144.e: Common buzzards use warm rising air to climb gracefully high into the sky in wide circles. This saves them a lot of energy when flying.

1145.q: What does a robin do when another robin comes into its territory?
a: It threatens it by puffing out its red breast
It shares its food with it
1145.e: A robin shows off its red breast very clearly to warn the intruder. Sometimes there is even a little fight.
1145.m: A red breast shows a threat.

1146.q: How can you often recognise a hunting kestrel from far away?
a: By the way it hovers over one spot in the air
By the loud splash as it dives into water
By running across the ground like an ostrich
1146.e: Hovering in the air, where the kestrel almost stays in one place, is typical of how it hunts. This behaviour is easy to spot from a distance and gives it its well-known hunting look.
1146.m: Hovering in the air gives the kestrel away.

1147.q: The scientific name of the polar bear is Ursus maritimus. Roughly what does that mean?
1147.e: Ursus means bear, and maritimus means belonging to the sea. The polar bear hunts on the sea ice and is an excellent swimmer.
1147.m: The polar bear is called Ursus maritimus, sea bear.

1148.q: How is the carrion crow classed by law in some Swiss cantons?
a: As a bird that may be hunted under certain rules
As a fully protected species with no exceptions
As a species that came from overseas
1148.e: In some Swiss cantons, the carrion crow is a species that may be hunted, and its numbers are controlled to limit damage to farming. The exact rules differ from canton to canton.
1148.m: Carrion crows may sometimes be hunted under rules.

1149.q: What do we call the area that a jaguar defends as its own?
1149.e: Jaguars mark their territory with droppings, urine and scratch marks. This tells other animals that the area is taken.

1150.q: Which animal is one of the natural enemies of the harbour seal?
1150.e: Killer whales, also called orcas, sometimes hunt harbour seals in the sea. For adult seals, they are one of the few real dangers.

1151.q: What does the common buzzard often eat more of in winter, when there are fewer mice?
1151.e: When mice are scarce, the common buzzard switches to carrion, small birds or other prey. Being so adaptable helps it get through hard winters.
1151.m: In winter it also eats carrion.

1152.q: How do dolphins find their prey in murky water?
1152.e: Dolphins send out clicks and listen to the echo that bounces back from objects. This tells them the shape, size and distance of their prey.
1152.m: Dolphins find their prey by echo.

1153.q: Which animal hoots at night and can turn its head very far round?
1153.e: The owl is a night bird that can see and hear very well. It can turn its head almost all the way round.

1154.q: Why can a cat climb trees so well?
a: Because it can pull its sharp claws in and push them out
Because it has suckers on its paws
1154.e: Cats can pull their claws in so they stay sharp, and push them out again when climbing. This gives them a good grip on the bark.
1154.m: Sharp claws that can be pulled in help with climbing.

1155.q: What do harbour seals often do while lying on a sandbank?
a: They lay eggs in the sand
1155.e: Harbour seals spend a lot of time lying on sandbanks and warming up in the sun. This lets them recover from their dives.
1155.m: Harbour seals warm up in the sun.

1156.q: Roughly how tall is a newborn giraffe calf?
a: Just as tall as its mother
1156.e: A giraffe calf drops almost two metres to the ground at birth, but still stands up after a short time. It is very tall right from the start.
1156.m: Giraffe calves are huge from the start.

1158.q: What is the technical word for meat eaters like the African wild dog?
1158.e: Carnivores mainly eat meat. Herbivores eat plants, and omnivores eat both.
1158.m: Meat eaters are also called carnivores.

1159.q: Who often helps to raise the pups in the pack?
a: Nobody, the mother is on her own
1159.e: The pack looks after the young together. Some animals guard them while others go hunting.

1160.q: What are young jaguars usually called?
1160.e: Young big cats are called cubs. The mother raises them on her own.
1160.m: The mother raises the young on her own.

a: It has a beak instead of teeth
1161.e: The hedgehog has lots of small, pointed teeth that it uses to chew up insects. They are typical of insect eaters.
1161.m: Hedgehogs have lots of small, pointed teeth.

1162.q: Which statement about the weight of an adult tawny owl is true?
a: It usually weighs between 400 and 700 grams
It weighs just as much as an eagle owl
1162.e: An adult tawny owl usually weighs between 400 and 700 grams. Its weight also depends on the season and how much food there is.
1162.m: A tawny owl weighs about 400 to 700 grams.

1163.q: Why do earthworms often come to the surface after heavy rain?
a: Because air runs short in their tunnels
Because they are afraid of fish
Because they want to learn to swim
1163.e: When the soil is completely full of water, the worm cannot get enough air any more. So it crawls up to the surface.
1163.m: Water in the soil means no air.

a: Meat, but also fruit and insects
1164.e: Jackals are omnivores. Depending on what is available, they eat small animals, carrion, insects and plants.

1165.q: When can a baby harbour seal swim?
a: Only when it is grown up
1165.e: Baby harbour seals can swim and dive soon after birth. This is important because the tide soon covers their sandbank.

1166.q: Who sits on the eggs of the great crested grebe?
1166.e: The male and female share the job of keeping the eggs warm. This way one parent can always go and look for food.
1166.m: Both parents sit on the eggs together.

1167.q: How does a fire salamander usually move around?
a: Slowly waddling on four short legs
1167.e: With its short legs, the fire salamander moves rather slowly with a waddle. Speed is not its strength.
1167.m: It waddles along at a leisurely pace.

1168.q: How many large eyes does a mosquito have on its head?
1168.e: Mosquitoes have two large compound eyes made up of many tiny single eyes. With them they can spot movement around them well.

1169.q: How does a snake like the grass snake move?
a: By wriggling from side to side
1169.e: It wriggles its body and pushes off against bumps in the ground. It has no legs.

1170.q: Why is the adder endangered in Switzerland?
a: Because it is too cold for it
Because there are too many mice
1170.e: Bogs are being drained and forests are changing. This means habitats are being lost.

a: Yes, they swim better than fish
1171.e: Gorillas usually do not like water much and prefer to stay away from it. They are not good swimmers.

1172.q: Roughly how heavy is a sparrow?
a: About as heavy as a piece of chocolate
About as heavy as a cat
About as heavy as a dog
About as heavy as an apple
1172.e: A sparrow weighs only about 30 grams, which is very light. This helps it fly well.
1172.m: A sparrow weighs only a few grams.

1173.q: What is striking about the puma’s tail?
a: It is short like a stump
It has a tuft like a lion’s
It is bushy like a fox’s
1173.e: The long tail helps the puma keep its balance, for example when climbing and jumping.
1173.m: The long tail helps with balance.

1174.q: What happens to the great crested grebe’s nest when the water level rises a lot?
a: It floats up with it, because it is anchored but built to move
1174.e: The floating nest is anchored in the reeds, but it can float up and down with the water level. This protects the eggs from flooding.
1174.m: The nest adjusts to the water level.

1175.q: What is the special hunting method called in which the peregrine falcon dives at its prey from a great height?
a: The stoop, a steep diving attack
Lying in wait on the ground
1175.e: In this method, the falcon first climbs high and then shoots down at its prey in a steep dive. This hunting technique makes it a feared hunter of the skies.
1175.m: A diving attack from a great height is typical.

1176.q: How does the grey heron usually react when people disturb it?
a: It takes off with a loud call and flies away
1176.e: When disturbed, the grey heron takes off quickly, usually with its croaking call. Then it looks for another quiet place to hunt.
1176.m: When disturbed, it quickly flies off calling.

1177.q: What do mute swans sometimes eat on land too?
1177.e: As well as water plants, swans also like to eat grass on land. You sometimes see them grazing in meadows by the lake.
1177.m: Swans also eat grass on the bank.

1178.q: How many gill slits do most sharks have?
1178.e: Sharks use their gill slits to breathe under water. Most kinds of shark have five on each side.
1178.m: Most sharks have five gill slits.

1179.q: Why do reindeer often move to higher, windier areas in summer?
a: There are fewer annoying insects there
There is more snow to play in
1179.e: Mosquitoes and botflies torment the animals in summer. Wind and cooler air keep the insects away.

1180.q: Which animals are jackals closely related to?
1180.e: Jackals belong to the genus Canis, like wolves and pet dogs. That is why they look quite like dogs. Hyenas look similar but are more closely related to cats.
1180.m: Jackals are related to wolves and dogs.

1181.q: Roughly how old can an Alpine ibex get in the wild?
1181.e: Ibex can get surprisingly old in the wild, and some reach 16 to 20 years. On average, females often live a little longer than males.

a: A canton that historically has only half a cantonal vote
1182.e: In the past a distinction was made between full cantons and half-cantons. Half-cantons, such as Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, only had half a vote when counting the majority of cantons.
1182.m: Half-cantons had half a cantonal vote.

1183.q: How does the red deer usually move forward?
a: Only hopping on all four legs at once
1183.e: The red deer can walk calmly, trot or flee with big leaps. This lets it get over obstacles.
1183.m: Red deer walk, trot and leap.

1184.q: What do sharks use to breathe under water?
1184.e: Water flows through the shark’s gill slits. There the oxygen is taken from the water.

1185.q: Where are the Roman snail’s eyes?
1185.e: The snail’s eyes are at the tips of its long tentacles. With them it can mainly tell light from dark.
1185.m: The eyes sit on long tentacles.

1186.q: Can a whole new starfish grow from a single arm?
a: Yes, if a piece of the centre is attached
1186.e: Some starfish can grow a completely new starfish from an arm that has been cut off. What matters is that part of the centre of the body is still attached to the arm.
1186.m: An arm can grow into a starfish.

1187.q: Which animal appears together with the kangaroo on Australia’s coat of arms?
1187.e: A kangaroo and an emu stand side by side on Australia’s coat of arms. Both animals are at home in Australia.
1187.m: The kangaroo and the emu are on the coat of arms.

1189.q: Which dragonfly has a hint of its colour in its name and is bright red?
1189.e: Male scarlet darters are bright red. The species comes from the Mediterranean and Africa and is spreading into Switzerland as the climate gets warmer.
1189.m: The scarlet darter is bright red.

1190.q: Why should you not feed mute swans with bread?
a: Bread can make them ill and pollute the water
Swans do not like bread at all
Bread is poisonous to swans, like chocolate
1190.e: Bread is unhealthy for swans and can make them ill. Leftover bread also pollutes the water.

1191.q: How widespread is the great crested grebe around the world?
a: It lives on several continents, such as Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia
It is only native to North America
1191.e: The great crested grebe is found on many continents, from Europe across Asia and Africa to Australia. It lives on very different kinds of water.
1191.m: Great crested grebes live on several continents.

1192.q: What colour are a mute swan’s eyes usually?
1192.e: The mute swan’s eyes are usually dark brown. They hardly stand out against the white feathers.

1193.q: What do elk often do in summer against heat and annoying mosquitoes?
a: They bury themselves in the ground
1193.e: Elk cope badly with heat. In the water they cool down, are better protected from biting insects and find water plants.
1193.m: In summer, elk like to head for the water.

1194.q: How do ants usually live together?
a: In big colonies with a queen
1194.e: An ant colony can have thousands of ants. They all work together for the queen and the nest.

1195.q: Is a dog a pure meat eater, or does it eat other things too?
a: It is an omnivore and also eats plant food
1195.e: Scientifically, dogs are omnivores, because they can also digest grain, vegetables and other plant foods. Even so, they need a large share of animal protein.
1195.m: Dogs eat meat and plant food.

1196.q: What happens to an otter’s nose and ears when it dives?
1196.e: Otters can close their nostrils and ears when diving so that no water gets in. This lets them stay under the surface for longer.
1196.m: The nose and ears close when diving.

1197.q: How many legs does a bumblebee have?
1197.e: Like all insects, the bumblebee has six legs. It uses them to crawl over flowers and hold on.
1197.m: Bumblebees have six legs, like all insects.

1198.q: How does a donkey typically behave when it trusts a person?
a: It likes being stroked and follows calmly
1198.e: A donkey that trusts you is usually very friendly, likes being touched and follows its person calmly. Donkeys are known as very friendly animals.
1198.m: Donkeys that trust you are very friendly.

1200.q: On which continent does the Indian rhinoceros live?
1200.e: The Indian rhinoceros lives in Asia, mainly in India and Nepal. It is found there in national parks with tall grass.
1200.m: The Indian rhinoceros lives in Asia.

1201.q: What is typical of many donkeys’ backs?
a: A dark stripe along the back
1201.e: Many donkeys have a dark stripe running along the back. Sometimes there is also a stripe across the shoulders, like a cross.
1201.m: Donkeys often have a stripe along the back.

1202.q: What is special about meerkats when they eat scorpions?
a: They are largely unaffected by the venom
They have to cook them first
It makes them sleepy straight away
1202.e: Meerkats can eat scorpions even though they are venomous. They are quite resistant to the venom.

1203.e: Woodlice crawl on their seven pairs of legs. They are quite quick.

1204.q: Why are host birds sometimes afraid of the cuckoo?
a: Because in flight it looks like a bird of prey
Because it has fiery red eyes
Because it is as huge as an eagle
1204.e: In flight, with its striped underside, the cuckoo looks like a small bird of prey. This scares the host birds off their nest for a moment, so the cuckoo can lay an egg in peace.
1204.m: The cuckoo pretends to be a bird of prey.

1205.q: Which predator is one of the okapi’s natural enemies?
1205.e: Leopards in the African rainforest also hunt okapis. Tigers, polar bears and pumas do not live in the Congo.
1205.m: The leopard is the okapi’s enemy.

1206.q: How can you tell an adult bearded vulture’s head from that of other vultures?
a: Unlike many vultures, it has feathers
It is completely bald and bare
1206.e: While many vultures have bare heads because they push deep into carcasses, the bearded vulture’s head is feathered. It does not need to push into carcasses, because it mainly eats bones.
1206.m: Unlike many vultures, its head has feathers.

1207.q: How well can rabbits see all around them?
a: They can see almost everything around them
1207.e: Rabbits’ eyes are on the sides of their heads, so they can see almost all the way round. This lets them spot enemies early.
1207.m: Rabbits see almost everything around them.

1208.q: What does the elk especially like to eat in winter?
1208.e: In winter there is hardly any grass. Then elk eat shoots, twigs and bark from trees such as willows and pines.

1209.q: What is the leopard's spotted coat mainly for?
1209.e: The spots break up the shape of the body in light and shadow. So the leopard is hard to spot in tall grass and among branches.

1210.q: Which other animals is the ant closely related to?
1210.e: Ants, bees and wasps belong to the same large group of insects. They are called Hymenoptera.

1211.q: What is the great tit especially good at doing with its feet?
a: Holding seeds while pecking them open
1211.e: The great tit holds a seed firmly on a branch with its feet. That way it can open it with its beak.
1211.m: The feet hold seeds while it opens them.

1212.q: What are newborn snow leopards like?
1212.e: The young only open their eyes after several days. At first they are fed with their mother’s milk.
1212.m: The young are blind at first.

1213.q: Where do wasps especially often build their nests?
1213.e: Wasps look for sheltered, dry places for their nest. Lofts, hollow spaces in walls and trees are popular.
1213.m: Wasps like to nest somewhere sheltered.

1214.q: How do penguin parents find their own chick again in a huge colony?
1214.e: Every penguin chick has its own call, which the parents recognise exactly. This lets them find it even among thousands of other chicks.
1214.m: Every chick has its own call.

1215.q: Which animals are a particular danger to young European pond turtles?
1215.e: Because their shells are soft, the little ones are easily hurt. Only as they grow does the shell become hard and protect them better.

1216.q: When is the marsh frog especially active?
a: Mainly during the day, often sunbathing on the bank
Only under water in complete darkness
1216.e: These frogs are active during the day and like to sit in the sun on the bank or on leaves. When there is danger, they jump into the water at once.
1216.m: This frog is mainly active during the day.

1217.q: What is a nuptial flight in ants?
a: The flight in which queens and males mate
A flight by the workers to go shopping
An outing for the whole family
1217.e: In the nuptial flight, young queens and males fly up into the air together. That is when they mate.
1217.m: Ants mate during the nuptial flight.

1218.q: What does research show about how far fire salamanders travel?
a: Many stay near the water where they were born all their lives
They travel to Africa every year
They fly from forest to forest
1218.e: Studies show that fire salamanders are often very loyal to one place and rarely move far from the water where they were born. This makes them vulnerable when their habitat is destroyed.
1218.m: They usually stay in their home area.

1219.q: How have people in Switzerland helped to protect the white stork?
a: With release programmes and protection measures
Not at all, the stork needed no help
1219.e: Because the white stork was doing badly in Switzerland for a while, people started programmes to bring it back. Today there are many storks here again.
1219.m: Release programmes helped the white stork.

1220.q: What was the raven often called in the Middle Ages because it ate carrion?
1220.e: Because ravens also fed on the bodies of executed people, they got the gloomy nickname gallows bird. As a result, they were long seen as eerie animals.
1220.m: Often called the gallows bird because it ate carrion.

1221.q: What does the International Labour Organization (ILO) deal with?
a: Fair working conditions around the world
1221.e: The ILO works for good working conditions, fair pay and protection against child labour. It is based in Geneva and is a specialised agency of the UN.
1221.m: The ILO fights for fair work around the world.

1222.q: How is the European bison different from the American bison?
a: It has longer legs and a less shaggy mane
It is much smaller than a roe deer
1222.e: The European bison usually has longer legs and a less bushy mane. The American bison looks shaggier on the head and front of its body.
1222.m: The American bison is shaggier, the European bison slimmer.

1223.q: Which teeth show that brown bears are omnivores?
a: They have both pointed canines and flatter back teeth
They have only pointed meat-cutting teeth, like pure meat eaters
They have no teeth at all
They have only flat teeth, like pure plant eaters
1223.e: A brown bear’s teeth clearly show that it is an omnivore. Pointed canines are good for meat, while flatter back teeth are good for grinding plants.
1223.m: Bear teeth suit both meat and plants.

1224.q: What is the name of the famous gorge near Solothurn where a saint is said to have lived?
1224.e: According to legend, Saint Verena lived in a cave in the Verena Gorge. Today it is a popular place for outings, with chapels.
1224.m: Saint Verena once lived in the Verena Gorge.

1225.q: Is the least weasel found in Switzerland?
1225.e: The least weasel is found all over Switzerland, though it is rarely seen because it lives so secretly. It lives in fields, meadows and at the edges of woods.

1226.q: What load can domestic camels carry as pack animals?
a: Several dozen up to about 200 kilograms
1226.e: As pack animals, they carry heavy loads over long distances. In the past they were used in caravans.
1226.m: Domestic camels are strong pack animals.

1227.q: Why should you never give chocolate to budgies?
a: Because it is poisonous to them
Because it is hard for people to digest
1227.e: Chocolate contains a substance that is poisonous to birds like the budgie. That is why you must never give it to them.

1228.q: Which larger animal group (phylum) do woodlice belong to?
1228.e: Woodlice have jointed legs and a hard shell, like insects and spiders. That is why they are arthropods.

1229.q: What does a pike’s snout look like?
a: Like a duck’s bill, long and broad
1229.e: The pike has a long, flat snout that looks like a duck’s bill. It is full of sharp teeth.
1229.m: A pike’s snout looks like a duck’s bill.

1230.q: When can you hear the loud concert of croaking marsh frogs at the pond best?
a: On warm days in spring and early summer
Only in the middle of winter
1230.e: Especially in May and June, many males call at the same time to attract females. This loud group calling is called a chorus.
1230.m: Spring and early summer are peak croaking season.

1231.q: How do dung beetles usually roll their dung ball?
a: Not at all, they carry it in their mouth
1231.e: The beetle often props itself on the ground with its front legs. With its back legs it pushes the ball backwards.

1232.q: What is special about a seahorse’s eyes?
a: They can move independently of each other
They are much bigger than its head
1232.e: Each eye can turn on its own without moving the other. This lets the seahorse look in two directions at once.
1232.m: Each eye turns on its own.

1233.q: What is the place called where the mother polar bear spends the winter?
1233.e: In winter, the mother polar bear retreats into a snow den she has dug herself. It is sheltered there and a little warmer.
1233.m: The mother spends the winter in a snow den.

1234.q: Roughly how long is a female dog pregnant?
1234.e: In most dog breeds, pregnancy lasts about nine weeks, so around 63 days. Then the puppies are born.
1234.m: Female dogs are pregnant for about 63 days.

1235.q: How endangered is the Amur leopard?
1235.e: There are only very few Amur leopards left in the wild. It is considered critically endangered.
1235.m: The Amur leopard is extremely rare.

1236.q: Which animal is the giraffe’s closest relative?
1236.e: The okapi from the forests of Africa is the giraffe’s closest living relative. But it looks very different and has a short neck.
1236.m: The okapi is related to the giraffe.

1238.q: In German, the octopus is called ‘Krake’. Where does this name, like the English word ‘kraken’, probably come from?
a: From old stories about sea monsters
From the name of a scientist
1238.e: Old Norse sailors’ tales told of a huge sea monster, the kraken. In German, the name was later also used for the real animals.
1238.m: The name comes from old legends.

1239.q: What body shape does the brown trout have?
1239.e: Its torpedo-like shape lets it glide easily through the water. So it can swim well even in strong currents.

1240.q: What role does the wild boar play for the forest?
a: It loosens the soil and spreads seeds
It is of no use at all
1240.e: By rooting around, wild boar loosen the soil. While doing this, they often spread plant seeds as well.
1240.m: Wild boar help the forest floor.

1241.q: What shape is the pupil of a common frog’s eye?
1241.e: The common frog’s eye has a horizontal pupil. This helps it keep a good watch on its surroundings.
1241.m: The common frog has horizontal pupils.

1242.q: What happens at a traditional Swiss festival when the sheep come back down from the alp?
a: They are often decorated with flowers
They are painted like Easter eggs
They are given shoes to wear
1242.e: When the animals come down from the alp, the sheep are sometimes decorated with flowers and colourful ribbons. The whole village celebrates the animals’ return.
1242.m: When they come down from the alp, the sheep are decorated.

1243.q: Which family does the bison belong to?
1243.e: Like cattle, sheep and goats, bison are bovids. They have horns that are not shed.

1244.q: What should a guinea pig enclosure be like so they have enough room to run?
a: Much bigger than a small cage, with lots of floor space
As small as a shoebox is enough
No enclosure is needed at all
An enclosure for just one day a week
1244.e: Guinea pigs need lots of floor space to run around and move. Small, cramped cages are not enough for a healthy life.
1244.m: Guinea pigs need lots of space.

1245.q: The trout's lateral line is marked in the picture. What is it for?
a: It senses movements in the water
1245.e: The lateral line organ senses the tiniest currents and changes in pressure. So the trout notices prey and enemies, even in murky water.
1245.m: The lateral line senses water movements.

1246.q: How many stomachs does a sheep have?
1246.e: A sheep has four stomachs. This lets it digest tough grass especially well.

1247.q: Which other woodpecker is smaller than the great spotted woodpecker?
1247.e: The lesser spotted woodpecker is even smaller than the great spotted woodpecker. Even so, it looks very like it.
1247.m: The lesser spotted woodpecker is even smaller.

1248.q: What does a brown bear mainly eat?
a: Mostly plants such as berries, roots and grasses
Almost only the meat of other animals
1248.e: Brown bears are omnivores, but a large part of their diet is plant food. Meat, fish and insects are only extras.

1249.q: Roughly how small is a newborn koala baby?
1249.e: A newborn koala is tiny, only about as big as a bean. It crawls into its mother’s pouch by itself to keep growing there.
1249.m: Koala babies are tiny at birth.

1250.q: Which group of frogs does the edible frog belong to?
1250.e: The edible frog is one of the green water frogs. They almost always live near ponds.
1250.m: The edible frog is a water frog.

1251.q: What is true about where the golden jackal lives?
a: It lives in parts of Europe, Asia and North Africa
It lives only on islands in the Pacific
It lives only in South America
It lives only in the Arctic
1251.e: The golden jackal has a large range. It stretches from south-eastern Europe across the Middle East to South Asia.
1251.m: The golden jackal lives on several continents.

a: A constant stream of charged particles that the sun flings into space
An especially strong wind on Earth
Wind blowing from the far side of the moon
1252.e: The sun constantly throws out charged particles such as electrons and protons. When the solar wind meets the Earth’s magnetic field, it causes, among other things, the northern and southern lights.
1252.m: The solar wind is made of charged particles from the sun.

1253.q: Roughly how much does an adult roe deer weigh?
1253.e: Roe deer are quite light animals. They usually weigh between 15 and 30 kilograms, depending on their size.
1253.m: A roe deer weighs about 15 to 30 kilograms.

1254.q: Which bird often sits on buffaloes’ backs and eats insects and ticks?
1254.e: Oxpeckers pick parasites out of the animals’ coats. Both sides benefit, and the bird sometimes also warns the buffaloes of danger.
1254.m: Oxpeckers clean buffaloes and eat parasites.

1255.q: What do wood ants often build their big anthill from?
1255.e: Wood ants collect fir needles and small twigs. They use them to build the well-known anthill.
1255.m: The anthill is made of needles.

a: On your head, left and right
1256.e: Your ears are on the sides of your head and catch sound waves. They help you to hear noises.
1256.m: Ears sit on the left and right of the head.

1257.q: How many eggs does a female budgie usually lay in a clutch?
1257.e: A female budgie usually lays between four and eight small white eggs. She usually lays them a couple of days apart.
1257.m: A clutch usually has 4 to 8 eggs.

1258.q: Which animal has been a symbol of wisdom since ancient times and often appears on university coats of arms?
1258.e: In ancient Greece the owl was the companion animal of Athena, the goddess of wisdom. That is why it still stands for cleverness and knowledge today.

1259.q: What happens to people in a dictatorship who loudly criticise the ruler?
a: They are often punished or locked up.
They are made the new boss.
They are allowed to speak on TV.
1259.e: In a dictatorship criticism is dangerous because the ruler allows no opposing views. Anyone who speaks out anyway risks punishment or prison.

1260.q: Where in Europe is the Alpine marmot originally found?
a: In the Alps and nearby mountains
1260.e: The Alpine marmot is native to the Alps and some other European mountains. Later it was also brought to other mountain ranges.
1260.m: The Alpine marmot lives in Europe’s mountains, especially the Alps.

1261.q: How many toes with sole pads do alpacas have on their feet?
1261.e: Alpacas belong to the camel family and have two toes with soft sole pads. This is gentle on the ground.

1262.q: Which fish is the lake trout especially closely related to?
1262.e: The lake trout and the brown trout belong to the same species. The lake trout grows up in a lake and so gets much bigger.
1262.m: Lake trout and brown trout are closely related.

a: A small, eel-like sea fish that buries itself in the sand
1263.e: Sand eels live in coastal waters and bury themselves in the sand. They are an important food for seabirds.
1263.m: Sand eels bury themselves in the seabed.

1265.q: How long does an octopus usually live?
1265.e: Most kinds of octopus live only one to two years. For such a clever animal, that is a very short time.
1265.m: Octopuses live only a short time.

1266.q: Why do all of today’s Alpine ibex have fairly low genetic diversity?
a: Almost all of them descend from a small remaining population
1266.e: Because almost all ibex descend from the small population in the Gran Paradiso area, their genetic diversity is low today. This is seen as a bottleneck in the history of the species.

1267.q: Can a jellyfish swim against strong ocean currents?
a: No, it usually drifts with the current
Yes, it always swims against it
Yes, it is faster than a shark
No, it always stays in the same place
1267.e: A jellyfish is not very strong and usually drifts along with the current. It can only move a little by itself.
1267.m: Jellyfish often drift with the current.

1269.q: Roughly how heavy can an adult male wild boar get?
1269.e: Large males can weigh well over 100 kilograms. That makes them really heavy forest animals.
1269.m: Male wild boar can get very heavy.

1270.q: When are gibbons usually most active?
1270.e: Gibbons are active during the day. You can often hear them singing early in the morning.

1272.q: Roughly how old can a gorilla get in the wild?
1272.e: Gorillas can get quite old in the wild, similar to some people in earlier times. In zoos they sometimes live even longer.
1272.m: Gorillas can live for over 35 years.

1273.q: How do tawny owl pairs often behave over the years?
a: They usually stay together for life
They form big groups of ten birds
1273.e: Tawny owls are usually monogamous and often stay with the same partner for several years or even for life. They defend their territory together.
1273.m: Tawny owl pairs often stay together for life.

1274.q: What colour are wolf pups’ eyes right after birth?
1274.e: Newborn wolf pups have blue eyes at first, which only later turn yellow or amber. They are also blind and deaf at the start.
1274.m: Pups’ eyes are blue at first.

1275.q: What is the swim bladder of the perch for?
a: To control how it floats in the water
1275.e: The gas-filled swim bladder helps the fish hover at one depth in the water. This saves energy.
1275.m: The swim bladder helps it float.

1276.q: How do bonobos often behave when looking for food?
a: They move to a new country every day
1276.e: During the day the whole group often splits into smaller groups. In the evening or on another day the animals meet up again.
1276.m: Bonobos split up and meet again.

1277.q: How do young millipedes typically grow up?
a: They moult and gain new segments and legs each time
They form a pupa like butterflies
1277.e: In many species, the young hatch with only a few pairs of legs. With every moult, more segments are added.
1277.m: New segments grow with every moult.

1278.e: Gulls and some fish eat starfish. Otters may eat them too.

1279.q: What happens when a jellyfish is lying on the beach?
1279.e: Because a jellyfish is made almost entirely of water, it dries out very quickly on the beach. It shrinks and almost dissolves.
1279.m: Jellyfish dry out on the beach.

1280.q: Why can some jellyfish glow in the dark sea?
a: To confuse enemies or attract prey
1280.e: The glow of some jellyfish is called bioluminescence. It can scare enemies or help attract prey in the dark.
1280.m: A jellyfish’s glow confuses enemies or attracts prey.

1281.q: What is the main difference between a ray and a shark?
a: Rays live only in fresh water
1281.e: Rays are closely related to sharks but have a very flattened body. They usually live on the seabed and move with their large side fins.
1281.m: Rays are flat, sharks are slim.

1282.q: Which statement about the common wall lizard is true?
a: It is one of the most common lizards in warmer parts of Europe
It is threatened with extinction worldwide
It is the largest lizard in the world
1282.e: In warm parts of southern and central Europe, the common wall lizard is widespread and often seen. In Switzerland, however, it is protected in some places.
1282.m: Common in warm parts of Europe.

1284.q: What does the barn swallow’s song sound most like?
a: A loud croak like a raven
1284.e: The barn swallow’s song sounds like a lively, long twittering. The birds often sing while sitting on roofs or wires.
1284.m: Its song is a lively twitter.

1285.q: Which electoral system is mostly used to elect the National Council?
1285.e: With proportional representation, each party gets as many seats as matches its share of the votes.
1285.m: In the National Council, seats are shared out according to party strength.

1286.q: Which fruit is one of ring-tailed lemurs’ favourite foods?
a: The fruit of the tamarind tree
1286.e: Ring-tailed lemurs love eating the fruit of the tamarind tree. The trees also give them leaves and flowers.

1287.q: What are the ears of the African wild dog like?
1287.e: The big, round ears catch your eye straight away. They help the animal hear sounds well.
1287.m: Big round ears are a way to recognise it.

1288.q: Roughly how big is a ring-tailed lemur’s body (without the tail)?
a: About as big as a pet cat
1288.e: The head and body measure about 40 centimetres. That is roughly the size of a pet cat.
1288.m: A ring-tailed lemur is about the size of a cat.

1289.q: What does the great tit do when it collects winter food from the bird table?
a: It takes one seed and flies off
It shares everything with others straight away
1289.e: The great tit often takes a seed from the bird table and flies off with it to a branch. There it holds the seed with its feet and pecks it open.
1289.m: It carries seeds away to eat.

1290.q: How heavy can a very old stork’s nest get over the years?
1290.e: When a stork’s nest is added to for many years, it can weigh over a hundred kilograms. It is made of lots of branches and twigs.
1290.m: Old nests can get very heavy.

1291.q: Roughly how old can a wild tawny owl get?
a: About 5 to 10 years, some much older
1291.e: In the wild, tawny owls often reach five to ten years, and some individuals live much longer. But many die young from accidents or enemies.
1291.m: Tawny owls often live five to ten years.

1292.q: What does the fire salamander do in winter?
a: It rests through the winter in frost-free hiding places
It lies in the blazing sun
1292.e: When it is cold, the fire salamander retreats to frost-free hiding places such as caves or holes in the ground. It stays there until spring.
1292.m: In winter it hides somewhere frost-free.

1293.q: What does a teddy bear hamster’s fur look like?
1293.e: The teddy bear hamster is a type with especially long, soft fur. This makes it look like a little cuddly bear.
1293.m: Teddy bear hamsters have long fur.

1294.q: Where does the cockchafer grub turn into a pupa?
1294.e: In summer, the grub builds itself a hollow in the ground. There it becomes a pupa, from which the beetle hatches.
1294.m: It turns into a pupa in the ground.

1295.q: How does a kingfisher defend its territory along the river?
a: It aggressively drives other kingfishers out of its area
It always shares its territory peacefully with many others
It leaves its territory at once when strangers come
It only sings quietly and does nothing else
1295.e: Kingfishers are loners and defend their hunting area fiercely against others of their kind. Only in the breeding season do they let a partner stay nearby.
1295.m: The kingfisher fiercely defends its territory.

1296.q: Where does the goldfish get its name from?
a: From its often golden orange colour
Because it is made of real gold
Because it lives in a gold mine
1296.e: The name goldfish comes from the bright orange-gold colour that many bred goldfish have. Their wild ancestors, however, had rather dull colours.
1296.m: The name comes from the golden colour.

1297.q: Which bird of prey in the Alps is even bigger than the golden eagle?
1297.e: The golden eagle has a wingspan of over two metres. But the bearded vulture, with a wingspan of up to almost three metres, is even bigger.
1297.m: The bearded vulture is even bigger than the golden eagle.

1298.q: What do rabbits use their long whiskers for?
a: To find their way in narrow tunnels
1298.e: Rabbits feel their surroundings with their whiskers, especially in dark, narrow tunnels. This stops them bumping into everything.
1298.m: Whiskers help them feel their way.

1299.q: What colours can a sheep’s wool be?
1299.e: Sheep’s wool comes in many natural colours such as white, black, brown or patchy. Depending on the breed, the coat looks very different.
1299.m: Sheep’s wool has many natural colours.

a: At dusk and in the evening
At midday in the blazing sun
In the middle of the night, only when there is frost
1300.e: Cockchafers fly mainly at dusk. They are often attracted by light.

1301.q: Which animals are especially dangerous for little cheetah cubs?
1301.e: Lions and hyenas hunt young cheetahs because they are still small and weak. That is why many cubs do not survive their first year.
1301.m: Lions and hyenas are enemies of the cubs.

1302.q: What does a seahorse use to hold on to plants?
1302.e: The seahorse’s tail can wrap around plants like a gripping arm. That way it is not washed away by the current.
1302.m: The tail holds on to plants.

1303.q: Which animals are among the stoat’s natural enemies?
a: Birds of prey, foxes and owls
1303.e: Birds of prey, foxes and owls hunt the stoat and are among its natural enemies. Although it can defend itself well, it must always stay alert.
1303.m: Birds of prey also hunt stoats.

1304.q: What are the main colours of the magpie’s feathers?
a: Black and white with a green and blue sheen
1304.e: At first glance the magpie’s feathers look black and white, but in the light they shimmer metallic green and blue. This sheen is especially easy to see on the tail and wings.
1304.m: Black, white and with a colourful shimmer.

1305.q: Which obstacles do salmon often get over with powerful leaps on their journey?
1305.e: Salmon can leap over smaller waterfalls. But weirs and dams often remain obstacles for them.

1306.q: What does the bearded vulture eat most of all?
1306.e: The bearded vulture specialises in bones and eats almost only the remains of dead animals. Its stomach can even digest large pieces of bone.
1306.m: Bearded vultures love bones, not meat.

1307.q: What does the common frog catch its prey with?
1307.e: The common frog flicks its sticky tongue forward in a flash. The prey sticks to it.
1307.m: The common frog’s tongue is sticky.

1308.q: What is the hole on top of a dolphin’s head that it breathes through called?
1308.e: The blowhole is on top of the head. When it surfaces, the dolphin breathes out through it and takes in fresh air.
1308.m: The blowhole is on top of the head.

1309.q: Which seas are the typical home of many kinds of seahorse?
a: Warm and temperate seas all over the world
1309.e: Seahorses live along many coasts of the world, mainly in warm and mild seas. You hardly find them in icy waters.

1310.q: Roughly how high can a chamois jump?
1310.e: Chamois are excellent jumpers and can jump up to two metres high. This lets them get over steep rocky ledges.
1310.m: Chamois jump up to two metres high.

1311.q: When does the barn owl usually breed?
a: Never at any time of year
1311.e: The barn owl breeds most often in spring and summer. Then there are enough mice to feed the young.
